This is an initial observation that ResNet50 image features likely carry real predictive signal, which makes it less likely that missing image signal explains the concat collapse and points instead toward the fusion step, feature scaling, or the multimodal pipeline. Several things remain open: the chance level (class count is not given), run-to-run variance, whether images add information complementary to RNA, how ViT-L or multiprofile image inputs would compare, and whether weighted fusion (config_017) or normalized concat would recover or exceed the RNA-only anchor. Diagnosing the multimodal pipeline or trying alternative fusion is the natural next test.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: RNA-only PCA-2000 is the anchor at 0.725 accuracy. Image-only ResNet50 reached 0.532, so the image features carry real signal. Yet the multimodal PCA+ResNet50 concat model collapsed to 0.208, well below either unimodal model. That points to a problem in the fusion step, such as feature-scale imbalance or the pipeline itself, rather than a lack of image signal. Multiprofile avgpool gave no clear RNA-only benefit, but that is a single small difference. 2. Test: config_017 changes only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, while keeping the RNA encoder, image encoder and single-profile setting the same as config_016. If accuracy recovers to near or above 0.725, concat was the problem, and weighted fusion becomes a usable path for multimodal models. If it also collapses, the issue is more likely in the multimodal pipeline as a whole. 3. Why now: every remaining multimodal configuration, which is most of the search space, uses either concat or weighted fusion. Settling the fusion question with a one-factor comparison against config_016 is the most efficient way to decide whether those configurations are worth further budget. Encoder and aggregation comparisons can wait.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 made a one-factor change from the collapsed multimodal concat run (llm_summary_003, 0.208 accuracy), switching fusion from concat to weighted while keeping the PCA-2000 RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, and single-profile setting fixed. Validation accuracy recovered to 0.688 (F1 0.659), which points to the concat fusion step, rather than the multimodal pipeline as a whole, as the likely source of the earlier collapse, and suggests weighted fusion is a usable path for multimodal configurations. However, it is still below the RNA-only PCA-2000 anchor (llm_summary_001, 0.725 accuracy / 0.685 F1), so in this setting adding image features gave no gain over RNA alone. Several questions remain open: whether concat failed because of feature-scale imbalance (normalized concat is untested), whether the weighted model under-uses or is degraded by the image branch, run-to-run variance, and whether other encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L) or multiprofile aggregation would let multimodal fusion match or exceed the RNA-only anchor.

selection_reason: Evidence: RNA is the strongest modality so far. RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile scored 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Avgpool multiprofile matched it (0.721) without improving on it. Image-only ResNet50 scored 0.532. Weighted multimodal fusion recovered from the concat collapse (0.688) but still trailed RNA alone. The RNA encoder is the largest untested choice: every RNA-containing run used PCA-2000, so it is unknown whether a learned representation like scVI-200 (or scGPT) extracts more signal. Test: config_004 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200 in the best-performing setting (RNA-only, single-profile). This gives a clean comparison against config_001. Why now: the RNA encoder underlies most of the remaining configurations, including all multimodal ones, so this one experiment improves decisions across much of the search space. It also has a reasonable chance of beating the current best. A scGPT comparison (config_007) can follow to complete the encoder picture.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 made a one-factor change from the RNA-only, single-profile PCA-2000 anchor (llm_summary_001, 0.725 accuracy / 0.685 F1), swapping only the RNA encoder to scVI-200. Validation accuracy fell to 0.530 (F1 0.515), so in this setting the learned scVI-200 representation underperformed PCA-2000 by about 19 points, and PCA-2000 remains the best RNA encoder tested so far. The encoder swap also changes dimensionality (200 vs 2000), and scVI training or tuning settings are unknown, so the drop cannot be attributed to scVI itself rather than reduced dimensionality or suboptimal setup. Run-to-run variance is unknown, and the near-identical scores to the image-only ResNet50 run (llm_summary_004, 0.532 / 0.517) may be coincidental but are worth a quick pipeline sanity check. It remains open whether scGPT (config_007) or a better-configured or higher-dimensional scVI would do better, and whether this result carries over to multiprofile or multimodal configurations.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is the strongest modality so far. RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile scores 0.725 accuracy, above image-only (0.532) and weighted multimodal (0.688). The RNA encoder choice has the largest effect observed: switching to scVI-200 cut accuracy by about 19 points (0.530). However, scGPT, the only remaining RNA encoder, is untested. 2. What this tests: config_007 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT and keeps everything else at the single-profile, RNA-only anchor. This finishes the encoder comparison for the dominant modality. It will show whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding beats PCA or whether learned representations underperform here generally. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: the RNA encoder choice carries into every downstream multiprofile and multimodal configuration. Fixing the best encoder now avoids spending later runs on a weaker backbone. Aggregation (avgpool showed no gain) and image encoders (images are the weaker modality) are lower-priority questions to test afterward, e.g. transformer aggregation via config_003 or ViT-L via config_013.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 made a one-factor change from the RNA-only, single-profile PCA-2000 anchor (llm_summary_001, 0.725 accuracy / 0.685 F1), swapping only the RNA encoder to the pretrained scGPT embedding. It reached 0.532 validation accuracy (F1 0.516), about 19 points below PCA-2000. Both learned RNA encoders tested so far (scGPT and scVI-200) therefore underperformed PCA-2000 in this setting, and PCA-2000 remains the best RNA backbone observed for downstream configurations. However, scGPT, scVI-200 (0.530 / 0.515), and image-only ResNet50 (0.532 / 0.517) now score almost identically despite very different inputs, which is a red flag for a shared pipeline artifact, such as a fallback or default feature path, a dominant-class plateau, or a loading or alignment issue, rather than a true encoder effect. A sanity check of how non-PCA embeddings are loaded, together with a check of per-class predictions, should come before concluding that learned representations are genuinely weaker. Embedding dimensionality, tuning settings, and run-to-run variance also remain unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: PCA-2000 RNA-only single-profile is the best result so far (0.725 accuracy / 0.685 F1). Multiprofile with avgpool (config_002) was about equal or slightly worse (0.721 / 0.681). The only aggregation tested so far is the simplest, parameter-free one, so we do not yet know whether multiprofile input is useless or whether avgpool just failed to use it. 2. Test: config_003 changes one factor from config_002, swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation while keeping the RNA-only setting and the strongest encoder (PCA-2000) fixed. It shows whether learned aggregation over profiles beats both the single-profile and avgpool results. It uses PCA-2000 because scVI and scGPT sit on a suspicious ~0.53 plateau that may be a pipeline artifact. 3. Why now: Aggregation is a key untested design choice that affects about half of the remaining configurations, including the multimodal transformer ones. Testing it on the strongest and most reliable branch gives a clean answer with good upside. A gain would point the search toward transformer-based multiprofile setups. No gain would let us deprioritize multiprofile and focus the budget on fusion and image-encoder questions such as ViT-L.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 changed one factor from the RNA-only PCA-2000 multiprofile avgpool run (llm_summary_002, 0.721 accuracy / 0.681 F1), replacing avgpool with transformer aggregation. Validation accuracy dropped to 0.599 (F1 0.578), about 12 points below both avgpool and the single-profile anchor (llm_summary_001, 0.725 / 0.685). In this setting, learned transformer aggregation therefore underperformed simple pooling, and no tested multiprofile variant has yet beaten single-profile input, which weakens the case for prioritizing multiprofile or transformer-aggregation configurations. The result is a single run with unknown variance and unknown transformer settings (capacity, regularization, training length, number of profiles), so it cannot separate an inherent limit of transformer aggregation from undertraining or overfitting; it also falls between the PCA anchor and the suspicious ~0.53 plateau, and how transformer aggregation behaves in multimodal setups remains untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile (0.725 accuracy / 0.685 F1) is still the best result. Multiprofile input (avgpool 0.721, transformer 0.599) and learned RNA encoders (scVI 0.530, scGPT 0.532) have not beaten it. Weighted fusion with ResNet50 recovered from the concat collapse (0.688) but still fell short of RNA alone. The image encoder is the only major design axis not yet tested: ViT-L has no runs at all. ResNet50 image-only scored 0.532, almost exactly matching the scVI and scGPT runs, which raises concern about a shared pipeline artifact. 2. What this tests: config_013 changes one factor from the ResNet50 image-only run (config_010), swapping the image encoder to ViT-L. It shows whether a stronger image representation lifts the image branch. It also works as a diagnostic: a score well away from about 0.53 makes the plateau more likely a coincidence, while another near-identical result strengthens the case for an artifact. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: a clean single-factor result here decides whether the ViT-L multimodal weighted variants (e.g., config_023) are worth spending budget on. That is more informative than further multiprofile or learned-RNA variants, which current evidence already disfavors.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 changed one factor from the image-only, single-profile ResNet50 run (llm_summary_004, 0.532 accuracy / 0.517 F1), swapping the image encoder to ViT-L. Validation accuracy rose to 0.579 (F1 0.563), which suggests ViT-L gives a stronger image representation than ResNet50 in this setting. It remains well below the RNA-only PCA-2000 anchor (llm_summary_001, 0.725 / 0.685), so image-only models still trail RNA alone. Because the score moved clearly away from the ~0.53 level shared by ResNet50, scVI, and scGPT, the ViT-L branch does not seem to be caught in that shared artifact, which makes coincidence somewhat more plausible, though this does not rule out a loading or plateau issue specific to the earlier runs. Several questions remain open: run-to-run variance (a ~5-point gain from a single run is modest), the chance level, whether ViT-L features are complementary to RNA, and whether ViT-L in weighted multimodal fusion (e.g., config_023) can close or exceed the gap to the RNA-only anchor, which the ResNet50 weighted run (0.688) did not.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: PCA-2000 RNA-only is the best result so far (0.725 accuracy / 0.685 F1). Concat fusion collapsed (0.208), while weighted fusion recovered to 0.688 with ResNet50 but still trailed RNA-only. ViT-L beat ResNet50 in the image-only setting (0.579 vs 0.532), so it is the stronger image representation. 2) Test: config_023 swaps only the image encoder in the weighted multimodal model (ResNet50 → ViT-L), keeping the PCA-2000 encoder, single-profile input and weighted fusion fixed. This shows whether a stronger image branch lets fusion match or beat RNA-only, or whether images add no complementary signal beyond RNA. 3) Why now: it is the most plausible path to beating the anchor and also answers the key open question of whether multimodality is worth pursuing. Multiprofile, transformer aggregation, scVI, scGPT and concat fusion have all underperformed so far, so testing them is lower priority. A clean one-factor comparison against config_017 gives an interpretable answer, which matters under a limited budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 made a one-factor change from the weighted multimodal run (llm_summary_005: PCA-2000 + ResNet50, single-profile, 0.688 accuracy / 0.659 F1), swapping only the image encoder to ViT-L. Validation accuracy fell to 0.520 (F1 0.498). That is about 17 points below the ResNet50 weighted run, about 20 points below the RNA-only PCA-2000 anchor (llm_summary_001, 0.725 / 0.685), and even below ViT-L image-only (llm_summary_009, 0.579). So in this setting the image encoder that scored higher on its own did not carry over to better fusion; combining ViT-L with RNA was associated with a result worse than either branch alone. Because the score sits below both unimodal branches and near the suspicious ~0.53 plateau (ResNet50 image-only, scVI, scGPT), it may reflect a fusion or pipeline problem rather than a lack of complementary image signal: for example, the image branch dominating or destabilizing the weighted fusion, ViT-L feature scale or dimensionality interacting badly with the weighting, or a loading or alignment artifact. These possibilities, along with run-to-run variance and the learned fusion weights, remain unverified, so this single run does not settle whether multimodality is worth pursuing. Pending checks of the fusion weights, per-class predictions, or feature normalization, RNA-only PCA-2000 remains the best configuration observed.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choices matter. 2. Test: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components) is the simplest, lowest-variance configuration. It sets a reference point that later single-factor comparisons can build on: the scVI or scGPT encoder (config_004/007), image-only (config_010), multiprofile avgpool (config_002) and multimodal fusion (config_016). 3. Why now: With a limited budget and no data, a clean baseline is the most informative first step. It avoids assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better, and every later experiment can be read as a change from this baseline.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 set the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA encoder (2000 components) and no image encoder, aggregation or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.421 and validation F1 0.412. The close agreement between accuracy and F1 gives weak evidence that performance is fairly even across classes, but per-class results were not reported. This is a reference point only, since no other configurations have been run. It is not yet known whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image or multimodal inputs, or multiprofile aggregation would do better or worse, and run-to-run variance has not been measured.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.421, F1 0.412). We do not yet know the effect of any major design axis: RNA encoder, modality, profile setting, aggregation or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_002 keeps the same RNA-only PCA encoder and changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This gives a clean one-factor comparison of whether aggregating multiple profiles helps. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: the profile setting applies to most of the remaining configurations, both unimodal and multimodal. Learning its effect early on the cheapest, best-understood pipeline will guide many later choices. Avgpool is the natural first test before trying the more complex transformer aggregator. The result should be read with caution, since run-to-run variance has not been measured.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA encoder (2000 components) from llm_summary_001 and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.421 to 0.653 (about +0.23), and validation F1 rose from 0.412 to 0.628, so the two metrics agree in direction and size. Because only the profile setting and its required aggregation changed, this is fairly clean evidence that multiprofile input with avgpool helps the RNA-only PCA pipeline. However, multiprofile input and avgpool cannot be separated here, and each configuration was run only once, so run-to-run variance is unknown. It is also not yet known whether the gain holds for other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), for image-only or multimodal models, or with a transformer aggregator in place of avgpool.

selection_reason: Evidence: the only comparison so far (config_001 vs config_002) shows that multiprofile input with avgpool raised RNA-only PCA accuracy from 0.421 to 0.653, with F1 rising similarly. This is fairly clean but single-run evidence. Nothing is known about the image modality, yet 42 of the remaining 49 configurations use an image encoder (36 multimodal, 6 image-only). This experiment keeps the multiprofile avgpool setting that worked and swaps the RNA-only PCA input for image-only ResNet50 input, making it a direct modality comparison against config_002. It tests whether imaging carries enough signal on its own to justify exploring image-only and multimodal configurations. Why now: if image-only performance is weak, the many multimodal options become less of a priority. If it is competitive, fusion becomes the main direction to pursue. That makes it the experiment that most reduces uncertainty about the largest part of the search space. The aggregation question (transformer vs avgpool, config_003) and the RNA encoder question (scVI, scGPT) are smaller refinements that can be tested next.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the multiprofile avgpool setting from llm_summary_002 but replaced the RNA-only PCA (2000 components) input with image-only ResNet50 input, with no RNA encoder or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.471 and F1 0.442, well below llm_summary_002 (0.653 / 0.628), so image-only ResNet50 appears to carry less standalone signal than multiprofile RNA PCA in this setup, though it is still above the single-profile RNA baseline (0.421, a comparison that differs in more than one setting). Because modality and encoder changed together, this gap cannot be attributed to imaging versus RNA as such rather than to the ResNet50 versus PCA choice, and with single runs per configuration, run-to-run variance is unknown. Image-only multiprofile is now a weaker reference point, but it remains untested whether image features add complementary signal in multimodal fusion, whether other aggregators (e.g. transformer) change the picture, and how image-only compares under single-profile input.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool gave a large, consistent gain for RNA PCA (0.421 to 0.653 accuracy, with F1 moving the same way). Image-only ResNet50 multiprofile avgpool is much weaker on its own (0.471). It is still unknown whether image features add complementary signal to RNA or just add noise. 2) Test: config_018 keeps the best setup (PCA 2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only the ResNet50 image branch with the simplest fusion, concat. Both of its unimodal components have already been measured (config_002 and config_011), so any gain or loss can be attributed to multimodal fusion. 3) Why now: Whether to use multimodal input is the most important open design choice in this study. This controlled comparison answers it with one run and sets a reference for later tests of weighted fusion, transformer aggregation or other encoders. Alternatives such as a transformer aggregator or an scVI encoder are useful refinements but address narrower questions.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best RNA setup from llm_summary_002 (PCA 2000 components, multiprofile input, avgpool aggregation) and added a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.523 and F1 0.508. That is well below RNA-only llm_summary_002 (0.653 / 0.628) and only modestly above image-only llm_summary_003 (0.471 / 0.442), so in this configuration adding image features through concat fusion was associated with a substantial drop rather than complementary gain, and F1 agrees in direction. Because the image branch and the concat fusion were introduced together, this run cannot tell whether the image features themselves add noise or whether naive concatenation fails to integrate them (for example through feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance). With single runs per configuration, run-to-run variance is unknown, and it remains open whether weighted or gated fusion, other aggregators such as a transformer, or other encoders would let multimodal input match or exceed RNA-only performance.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Multiprofile RNA-only PCA with avgpool is the best result so far (0.653 accuracy / 0.628 F1). Adding a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion (config_018) dropped performance to 0.523 / 0.508. That run cannot tell whether the image features are uninformative or whether naive concatenation fails to combine them, for example because the two feature sets differ in scale or size. 2) Test: config_019 keeps everything in config_018 the same (PCA 2000, ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the fusion from concat to weighted. If weighted fusion recovers or beats the RNA-only result, concatenation was the bottleneck. If it stays well below RNA-only, ResNet50 image features likely add noise in this setup. 3) Why now: Most of the remaining options are multimodal configurations that use one of these two fusion types. A clean single-variable test of fusion therefore decides whether the multimodal part of the search is worth more budget. Encoder or aggregator tweaks to the RNA-only model would only refine one branch. Since these are single runs, any difference should be read as directional rather than conclusive.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 repeated llm_summary_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA 2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool) and changed only the fusion from concat to weighted. It reached validation accuracy 0.632 and F1 0.607, up from 0.523 / 0.508 with concat (about +0.11 accuracy, +0.10 F1, metrics agreeing in direction). Because fusion was the only variable changed, this is fairly clean directional evidence that naive concatenation was a major bottleneck. Even so, the weighted multimodal model still sits slightly below the RNA-only multiprofile best, llm_summary_002 (0.653 / 0.628, about -0.02 on both metrics). So far the ResNet50 image branch has not been shown to add net signal over RNA alone. With single runs per configuration, it is unknown whether the ~0.02 gap to RNA-only falls within run-to-run variance. The learned fusion weights were not reported, so it is also unknown whether the model mostly down-weights the image branch, and it remains untested whether other fusion schemes (e.g. gated), a transformer aggregator or other encoders could let multimodal input surpass RNA-only.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 with avgpool (0.653 accuracy / 0.628 F1). Multiprofile input gave a large gain over single-profile (about +0.23). Multimodal fusion has not beaten RNA-only: weighted fusion reached 0.632, slightly below, and concat fell well below. Aggregation is the main design axis not yet tested. Every multiprofile run used avgpool, so the multiprofile gain cannot be separated from the choice of aggregator. 2. What this tests: Config_003 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only avgpool to a transformer aggregator. This cleanly shows whether learned, attention-based pooling across profiles adds signal beyond simple averaging. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It exploits the strongest current setup while answering a question that applies widely, since about half the remaining configurations differ by aggregator. A gain would point toward transformer variants of the multimodal and other-encoder configurations. No gain or a drop would let us focus on avgpool and spend the remaining budget on encoder choices (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L). Because this is a single run, a small difference should be read with F1 as supporting evidence and not overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_002: RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA 2000 components, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the aggregator from avgpool to a transformer. It reached validation accuracy 0.678 and F1 0.646, up from 0.653 / 0.628 (about +0.025 accuracy, +0.018 F1). The two metrics agree in direction, and this is now the best result in the study. Because aggregation was the only variable changed, this is fairly clean directional evidence that attention-based pooling across profiles may add signal beyond averaging in this pipeline, but the gain is small and each configuration was run only once, so it is unknown whether the difference exceeds run-to-run variance. It also remains untested whether the transformer aggregator helps image-only or multimodal models (for example weighted fusion, which was only about 0.02 behind RNA-only with avgpool) or other RNA encoders such as scVI or scGPT.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only PCA, multiprofile, with a transformer aggregator (config_003: 0.678 accuracy / 0.646 F1). Swapping avgpool for the transformer gave a small but consistent gain (about +0.025 accuracy). Weighted fusion fixed most of the concat failure in multimodal models (0.523 to 0.632). Even so, the weighted multimodal model still trailed RNA-only avgpool by about 0.02, so the ResNet50 image branch has not yet shown net value. 2) This run adds the transformer aggregator to the weighted multimodal setup. It differs by one choice (aggregation) from config_019 and by one choice (adding the ResNet50 branch with weighted fusion) from config_003. It therefore tests two things: whether the transformer gain carries over to multimodal input, and whether images add signal on top of the current best RNA pipeline. 3) Whether multimodal fusion beats RNA-only is the central open design question. This one experiment answers it with clean comparisons and also has a realistic chance of producing a new best. Exploring other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) remains a strong next candidate.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 combined the transformer aggregator with the weighted-fusion multimodal setup (multiprofile, PCA 2000 RNA, ResNet50 image). This makes it a single-variable comparison against two earlier runs: llm_summary_005 (aggregation changed from avgpool) and llm_summary_006 (ResNet50 branch with weighted fusion added to the RNA-only transformer best). It reached validation accuracy 0.713 and F1 0.695, a new best. That is about +0.035 accuracy and +0.048 F1 over RNA-only llm_summary_006 (0.678 / 0.646), and about +0.08 accuracy and +0.09 F1 over avgpool multimodal llm_summary_005 (0.632 / 0.607), with both metrics agreeing in direction. This gives the first directional evidence that the image branch can add net signal over RNA alone, and it suggests a possible interaction: the transformer gain was larger in the multimodal setting than in RNA-only (+0.08 vs +0.025), and images showed net value only under transformer aggregation. However, each configuration was run only once, so it is unknown whether the ~0.035 margin over RNA-only exceeds run-to-run variance. Learned fusion weights were not reported, so how much the model relies on the image branch is unknown, and gated fusion, other image encoders and other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) remain untested in this new best configuration.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_021 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Aggregation and fusion have each been compared one variable at a time, and both transformer aggregation and weighted fusion look clearly helpful. The encoders are the largest untested choice. Only ResNet50 has been tried for images, and its standalone signal was weak (image-only 0.471). The image branch added net value only with the transformer aggregator, a margin of +0.035 over RNA-only. 2) Test: config_027 keeps everything from config_021 and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger image representation adds more complementary signal to the best pipeline, or whether the image contribution is capped regardless of encoder. 3) Why now: it both exploits the strongest direction and resolves a key design question with a clean single-variable comparison against the current best. It is more targeted than starting RNA-encoder sweeps (scVI, scGPT), which can follow once the image-encoder choice is settled.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the current best configuration, llm_summary_007 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA 2000 RNA, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion), and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. It reached validation accuracy 0.650 and F1 0.628, about -0.063 accuracy and -0.067 F1 below llm_summary_007 (0.713 / 0.695), with both metrics agreeing in direction. It also fell below the RNA-only transformer run llm_summary_006 (0.678 / 0.646), so in this pipeline the ViT-L image branch was associated with a net loss rather than a complementary gain, and ResNet50 remains the better-performing image encoder tested so far. Because each configuration was run only once, run-to-run variance is unknown. It is also untested whether the drop reflects weaker ViT-L features for this data or poorer integration (for example feature dimensionality or scale interacting with weighted fusion, or hyperparameters tuned around ResNet50), since image-only ViT-L, learned fusion weights, gated fusion and other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) have not been evaluated.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the current best is config_021 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Profile setting, aggregation, fusion and image encoder have each been probed with single-variable changes. The RNA encoder has never varied: every RNA-containing run used PCA-2000, and RNA is the strongest single modality. This makes the RNA encoder the largest remaining uncertainty about a design choice. 2) Test: config_033 keeps config_021 fixed and swaps only PCA-2000 for scVI-200. This isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional RNA representation improves or degrades the best pipeline. A lower dimension may also change how the RNA and ResNet50 branches balance under weighted fusion. 3) Why now: it is both exploitative and informative. It could yield a new best, and either outcome cleanly answers whether PCA is a bottleneck. That answer then guides whether to test other RNA encoders such as scGPT, or RNA-only scVI runs, with the remaining budget. Because each configuration has a single run, a small difference should be read cautiously, and F1 should be checked as supporting evidence.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the current best configuration, llm_summary_007 (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50 image, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion), and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, the first time the RNA encoder has been varied. It reached validation accuracy 0.530 and F1 0.515, about -0.18 on both metrics below llm_summary_007 (0.713 / 0.695). That places it below the RNA-only PCA transformer run (llm_summary_006, 0.678 / 0.646) and close to the weak concat-fusion multimodal run (llm_summary_004, 0.523 / 0.508). Because only the RNA encoder changed and both metrics agree, this is fairly clean directional evidence that, in this pipeline, scVI-200 performed substantially worse than PCA-2000, so PCA does not appear to be the bottleneck; with a single run per configuration, run-to-run variance is still unmeasured, though the gap is large. It remains untested whether the drop reflects weaker scVI-200 features themselves (no RNA-only scVI run exists) or poorer integration, for example the 200-dimensional RNA branch being outweighed by ResNet50 under weighted fusion (learned fusion weights were not reported), or scVI training and latent-size choices. Other RNA encoders such as scGPT and other scVI dimensions are also untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best run so far is config_021 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1. Single-variable changes away from it have hurt. Swapping the image encoder to ViT-L dropped accuracy to 0.650, and swapping the RNA encoder to scVI-200 dropped it to 0.530. RNA representation therefore looks like a high-impact choice. scGPT is the only RNA encoder never tested in any setting, so it is the largest remaining gap in our knowledge of the representation axis. 2) What this tests: config_045 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT within the best configuration. It asks whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding can match or beat PCA, or whether it fails like scVI. Both scVI and scGPT would then have been compared against PCA under the same aggregation and fusion. 3) Why this is the best use of budget: It is a clean single-variable comparison against the current best. It explores the last untested encoder while keeping some chance of a new best. One limit is that, as with scVI, a drop here would not separate weak scGPT features from poor fusion integration. If both learned encoders underperform, an RNA-only run such as config_009 would be the natural follow-up to disentangle the two.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the current best configuration, llm_summary_007 (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50 image, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion), and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT. This was the first test of scGPT in any setting. It reached validation accuracy 0.629 and F1 0.599, about -0.08 accuracy and -0.10 F1 below llm_summary_007 (0.713 / 0.695), with both metrics agreeing in direction. That is well above scVI-200 in the same pipeline (llm_summary_009, 0.530 / 0.515) but below the RNA-only PCA transformer run (llm_summary_006, 0.678 / 0.646). So in this pipeline both learned RNA encoders underperformed PCA-2000, and scGPT was the less harmful of the two. With single runs per configuration, run-to-run variance is unmeasured. It also remains untested whether the drop reflects weaker scGPT features or poorer integration with ResNet50 under weighted fusion (for example embedding dimensionality or scale, or hyperparameters tuned around PCA), because no RNA-only scGPT or scVI run exists and learned fusion weights were not reported. An RNA-only run with these encoders would help separate the two explanations.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, least confounded baseline. It shows how much signal plain RNA features carry. Every later change (scVI or scGPT encoders, multiprofile aggregation, adding images, fusion type) can then be compared against it one factor at a time. 3) Starting from a cheap, interpretable anchor avoids spending budget on complex multimodal configurations whose results could not be attributed to any single design choice. It also guards against assuming that more complex models are better. The next logical steps are comparisons that change one factor from this baseline, such as an image-only baseline or swapping the RNA encoder.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 set the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder with 2000 components (pca_n2000), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.3275 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.2884. This shows that plain PCA-reduced RNA features carry some signal, but because no other configurations have been run and the number of classes and chance-level accuracy are not given, the result cannot yet be judged as strong or weak. It remains unknown how alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image features, or fusion strategies would compare, and this baseline is best used as the reference point for single-factor comparisons such as an image-only baseline or an RNA encoder swap.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only one result exists, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.328, F1 0.288). Without chance level or any other point of comparison, we cannot tell how much signal RNA carries relative to imaging. That makes the value of the image modality the largest open question, and the answer shapes most of the remaining search space, since about 36 of the 50 untested configurations are multimodal. 2. What this tests: An image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model keeps the simplest setting fixed (single profile, no aggregation, no fusion) and swaps only the modality. Its result will show whether images alone are stronger, weaker or comparable to PCA RNA features. That in turn indicates whether multimodal fusion is likely to help or whether the search should focus on RNA encoders and profile aggregation. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It directly reduces uncertainty about a high-impact design choice and gives a second clean reference point for later single-factor comparisons (image encoder swap, multiprofile aggregation, fusion). It does this before spending budget on more complex configurations whose results could not otherwise be interpreted.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5251 (F1 0.4979), well above the RNA-only PCA (pca_n2000) single-profile baseline from llm_summary_001 (accuracy 0.3275, F1 0.2884). This suggests that image features from ResNet50 carry substantially more class signal than PCA-reduced RNA in the simplest setting, which makes image-containing configurations (image encoder swaps, multiprofile aggregation, fusion) promising directions. However, the comparison changes the modality and the encoder at the same time, rests on single runs with no variance estimates, and lacks a stated chance level, so it remains uncertain whether the gap reflects images versus RNA in general or these specific encoders. It is also untested whether adding RNA through fusion would add complementary signal or mostly noise.

selection_reason: Evidence: in the single-profile setting, image-only ResNet50 (acc 0.525, F1 0.498) clearly beats RNA-only PCA (acc 0.328, F1 0.288). These are single runs with no variance estimates. The biggest open question is whether RNA adds complementary signal to images or mostly noise. config_016 adds PCA RNA features to the ResNet50 image model by simple concatenation and keeps everything else fixed (single-profile, no aggregation). It therefore differs from config_010 only by the added RNA modality, and its result can be read directly against both completed baselines. This is the best next experiment because it tests the core multimodal premise with the simplest fusion method. If fusion helps, the multimodal branches (fusion type, RNA encoder, aggregation) become worth exploring. If it doesn't, the budget can shift toward image-only refinements such as multiprofile aggregation or a ViT-L encoder swap.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested a multimodal, single-profile model that concatenates PCA RNA features (pca_n2000) with ResNet50 image features, with no aggregation. Its only difference from the image-only baseline llm_summary_002 is the added RNA modality. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6878 (F1 0.6585), above both image-only ResNet50 (0.5251 / 0.4979) and RNA-only PCA (0.3275 / 0.2884). Because this comparison isolates the RNA addition under the same encoders and simple concat fusion, it is an initial indication that RNA contributes complementary signal rather than mostly noise, which makes multimodal branches (fusion type, RNA encoder, aggregation) worth exploring. However, all results are single runs with no variance estimates and no stated chance level, so the size and robustness of the roughly 16-point gain are uncertain. It is also untested whether the gain holds with other encoders, fusion methods, or multiprofile aggregation.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is config_016 (multimodal, single-profile, PCA RNA + ResNet50, concat fusion), at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. It clearly beats image-only (0.525) and RNA-only (0.328), which suggests RNA and images carry complementary signal. Profile setting is a major design axis that no experiment has tested yet. Fusion type and encoder swaps are also untested. 2) What this tests: config_018 changes only one thing from the current best, switching to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). Encoders and concat fusion stay the same. This isolates whether pooling information across multiple profiles adds signal on top of the strongest setup. 3) Why it is the best next step: a win would show which part of the large configuration space, mostly multiprofile variants, deserves the remaining budget. A loss or no gain would let later experiments focus on single-profile encoder and fusion choices. Using avgpool first gives a clean, low-complexity test of the profile setting before trying transformer aggregation or weighted fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 changed the best configuration so far (llm_summary_003: multimodal, single-profile, pca_n2000 RNA + ResNet50, concat fusion, 0.6878 accuracy / 0.6585 F1) to a multiprofile setting with avgpool aggregation, keeping the same encoders and concat fusion. Validation accuracy fell to 0.5375 (F1 0.5184), about 15 points lower and close to the image-only baseline (0.5251 / 0.4979), so this multiprofile variant gave no gain and instead performed substantially worse than single-profile. This comparison does not show that multiprofile information is unhelpful in general, because switching to multiprofile also required adding an aggregation step, so the drop could come from mean pooling washing out profile-level signal rather than from the profile setting itself. All results are single runs with no variance estimates or stated chance level, and it remains untested whether stronger aggregators (e.g., transformer or attention pooling), other fusion methods, or other encoders would change the outcome; single-profile encoder and fusion variations currently look like the safer direction, with perhaps one non-avgpool multiprofile check to tell the two explanations apart.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is single-profile multimodal concat (config_016, 0.688 accuracy / 0.659 F1). Switching to multiprofile with avgpool (config_018) dropped accuracy to 0.537. That drop has two possible explanations that cannot yet be separated: multiprofile information may not help, or mean pooling may wash out profile-level signal. 2. What this tests: config_020 differs from config_018 only in using transformer aggregation instead of avgpool, with the same encoders and concat fusion. If accuracy recovers to or beyond 0.688, the earlier drop came from the aggregator. If it stays near 0.54, multiprofile is likely unhelpful in this setup. 3. Why now: Profile setting and aggregation account for a large share of the remaining search space. One controlled run tells us whether to keep exploring multiprofile branches or prune them and focus on single-profile encoder and fusion variants (e.g., ViT-L, scVI or scGPT, weighted fusion). That makes it the most efficient use of the next experiment.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested a multimodal, multiprofile model (pca_n2000 RNA + ResNet50, concat fusion) with transformer aggregation. Its only difference from llm_summary_004 is replacing avgpool with the transformer aggregator. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.7150 (F1 0.6872), which recovers fully from llm_summary_004 (0.5375 / 0.5184) and slightly exceeds the previous best, single-profile llm_summary_003 (0.6878 / 0.6585). Because the comparison with llm_summary_004 isolates the aggregator, it is an initial indication that the earlier multiprofile drop came mainly from mean pooling rather than from multiprofile information being unhelpful, so multiprofile branches look worth keeping rather than pruning. However, the roughly 2.7-point gain over single-profile comes from a comparison that changes both profile setting and aggregation, rests on single runs with no variance estimates or stated chance level, and may be within run-to-run noise; it also remains untested whether other aggregators (e.g., attention pooling), fusion methods, or encoders (e.g., ViT, scVI, scGPT) would strengthen or erase the multiprofile advantage.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.7150 accuracy and 0.6872 F1. Earlier comparisons suggest three things: images carry the most signal, adding RNA helps, and transformer aggregation (not avgpool) makes multiprofile worthwhile. Encoder choice is still completely untested. Every run used ResNet50 and PCA, so we do not know how much these specific encoders limit performance. 2) Test: config_026 keeps the best setup and changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates the effect of image representation in the strongest branch, and image is the modality that carried the most standalone signal. 3) Why now: an encoder swap on the best pipeline is both a logical exploitation step and a test of a major unexplored design axis. Its expected effect is likely larger than switching fusion from concat to weighted. Whether it helps or hurts, the result directly guides the remaining comparisons of ViT-L against ResNet50. RNA encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) on this pipeline remain natural follow-ups.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best pipeline so far, llm_summary_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 RNA, transformer aggregation, concat fusion; 0.7150 accuracy / 0.6872 F1), and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Validation accuracy fell to 0.5988 (F1 0.5777), about 11.6 points lower, and also below single-profile ResNet50 multimodal llm_summary_003 (0.6878). Because only the image encoder changed, this is an initial indication that ViT-L features, used this way, are less effective here than ResNet50, so ResNet50 remains the stronger default image encoder for now. However, this is a single run with no variance estimate or stated chance level, and it is untested whether the drop reflects ViT-L representations themselves or how they fit this specific pipeline (e.g., feature scale or dimensionality under concat fusion, preprocessing, or the transformer aggregator); an image-only or single-profile ViT-L check, or a different fusion method, would help tell these explanations apart, and RNA encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) on the ResNet50 pipeline remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion; 0.7150 acc / 0.6872 F1). Swapping the image encoder to ViT-L hurt, so ResNet50 stays the default image encoder. Two design axes remain completely untested: the RNA encoder and the fusion method. RNA via PCA was weak on its own (0.3275), yet adding it to images gave about a 16-point gain, so the RNA representation is a plausible bottleneck with room to improve. 2) Test: config_032 changes only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200, while keeping the best pipeline fixed. This isolates whether a learned, denoised RNA representation adds more complementary signal than PCA. 3) Value: a single-factor change on the strongest pipeline gives a clean answer about the RNA encoder, a major design choice, and offers real upside if scVI strengthens the RNA contribution. Testing weighted fusion (config_021) remains a natural follow-up.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best pipeline, llm_summary_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50 image encoder, transformer aggregation, concat fusion; 0.7150 accuracy / 0.6872 F1), and changed only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. Validation accuracy collapsed to 0.3316 (F1 0.3150), about 38 points lower. That is roughly the level of the RNA-only PCA baseline (0.3275) and well below image-only ResNet50 (0.5251), so in this pipeline scvi_n200 is an initial negative result and pca_n2000 remains the default RNA encoder. Because adding RNA should not plausibly push a multimodal model below its image-only counterpart, the result may reflect a pipeline or integration problem rather than weak scVI representations. Possible causes include feature scale or a mismatch with concat fusion, a training failure, or the image branch being effectively ignored. The swap also changes dimensionality (200 vs 2000) along with the encoder type, and this is a single run with no variance estimate or stated chance level. An RNA-only scvi_n200 check, or scVI with a different fusion method such as weighted fusion, would help separate these explanations before the scVI branch is pruned.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion), at 0.7150 accuracy and 0.6872 F1. Changing the aggregator, image encoder and RNA encoder has each produced large effects. Fusion is the only design choice never varied: every multimodal run used concat. Two failures may also have come from concat itself: ViT-L dropped to 0.5988, and scVI collapsed to 0.3316, below image-only. Possible causes include feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance between modalities. 2) What this tests: config_021 keeps the best pipeline and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of the fusion method on the strongest configuration. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: It covers an important untested design axis with a clean single-factor comparison. It has a reasonable chance of beating the current best, so it serves both exploitation and exploration. Its result will also show whether weighted fusion is worth carrying into the scVI and ViT-L branches to check whether their poor results were integration problems, which is a better use of budget than testing those weaker branches first.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best pipeline, llm_summary_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 RNA + ResNet50, transformer aggregation; 0.7150 accuracy / 0.6872 F1), and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted. Validation accuracy fell to 0.5200 (F1 0.4791), about 19.5 points lower and slightly below the single-profile image-only ResNet50 baseline (0.5251 / 0.4979). Because only fusion changed, this is an initial indication that weighted fusion, as implemented here, performs much worse than concat on this pipeline, so concat remains the default and weighted fusion currently looks unpromising as a fix for the weak ViT-L and scVI branches. However, this is a single run with no variance estimate or stated chance level, and it is untested whether the drop reflects weighted fusion itself or its implementation and training (e.g., learned weights collapsing onto one modality, normalization, initialization, or a training failure). Landing near image-only level suggests the RNA contribution may have been largely lost, which an inspection of the learned modality weights or a single-profile weighted-fusion check could help clarify.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best pipeline so far is config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion), at 0.7150 accuracy and 0.6872 F1. Single-factor swaps from it have each hurt performance: ViT-L dropped to 0.599, scVI to 0.332 and weighted fusion to 0.520. Transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.715 vs 0.537). The scGPT RNA encoder is the one major design dimension not yet tested anywhere. 2) What this tests: config_044 changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scGPT, keeping everything else in the best pipeline fixed. It shows whether a foundation-model RNA representation adds more complementary signal than PCA. It also shows whether the scVI collapse was specific to scVI or reflects a general problem with integrating non-PCA RNA embeddings in this concat pipeline. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: It is a clean single-factor comparison on the strongest configuration. It has real upside for improving the best result, and it resolves the largest remaining gap in coverage of the RNA-encoder choice. A positive result would open a scGPT branch, while a negative result would strengthen the case for keeping PCA as the RNA encoder.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the best pipeline, llm_summary_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50 image encoder, transformer aggregation, concat fusion; 0.7150 accuracy / 0.6872 F1), and changed only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scGPT. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6776 (F1 0.6464), about 3.7 points below the PCA pipeline. That is far better than the scvi_n200 collapse in llm_summary_007 (0.3316) and roughly on par with single-profile PCA multimodal llm_summary_003 (0.6878). This is an initial indication that scGPT does not improve on pca_n2000 here, so PCA remains the default RNA encoder. It also suggests the scVI collapse was not a general failure of non-PCA RNA embeddings under concat fusion, and was more likely specific to scVI or its setup (e.g., dimensionality, scale, or training). However, this is a single run with no variance estimate or stated chance level, so the modest gap may fall within run-to-run noise and does not firmly rank scGPT below PCA. It also remains untested whether scGPT would benefit from different fusion, feature normalization, or embedding dimensionality, so scGPT may be a viable secondary branch rather than one to prune.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA + ResNet50, transformer, concat; 0.715 accuracy, 0.687 F1). Its edge over single-profile multimodal config_016 (0.688) is small, and that comparison changes both profile setting and aggregation. The RNA contribution was shown only in the single-profile setting (config_010 at 0.525 vs config_016 at 0.688). It is untested whether RNA still adds signal once transformer aggregation over multiple profiles is used, or whether multiprofile transformer aggregation by itself explains most of the gain. 2) What this tests: config_012 is image-only, multiprofile ResNet50 with transformer aggregation. Each comparison changes one factor. Against config_010 it isolates the effect of multiprofile transformer aggregation for images alone. Against config_020 it isolates the RNA contribution inside the best pipeline. Accuracy is the main measure, with F1 as support. 3) Why it is the best next run: Encoder and fusion swaps have mostly been resolved for now, since ViT-L, scVI, scGPT and weighted fusion all did worse. The core design questions about modality and profile/aggregation remain open. If image-only multiprofile approaches 0.715, RNA may be redundant there and simpler models suffice. If it stays near 0.53, that strengthens the case that fusing RNA is the key driver.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested an image-only, multiprofile ResNet50 model with transformer aggregation and no RNA or fusion. It reached 0.5907 validation accuracy (F1 0.5727), which sits between the single-profile image-only baseline llm_summary_002 (0.5251 / 0.4979) and the best multimodal multiprofile pipeline llm_summary_005 (0.7150 / 0.6872). The only change from llm_summary_005 is removing RNA, and accuracy dropped about 12.4 points, an initial indication that PCA RNA still adds substantial complementary signal under multiprofile transformer aggregation and is not redundant there. The roughly 6.6-point gain over llm_summary_002 suggests that multiprofile input with transformer aggregation also helps images alone, but profile setting and aggregator change together, so their separate effects remain unresolved. All results are single runs with no variance estimates or stated chance level, so the gap sizes are uncertain. It is also uncertain whether the multiprofile gain is larger for image-only than for multimodal models (about 6.6 vs 2.7 points against llm_summary_003), since that comparison is confounded; an image-only multiprofile avgpool run could help isolate the aggregator's role.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about the performance scale, which modality carries signal, or whether added complexity helps. 2. What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest, cheapest, least confounded baseline. Later experiments can each change one factor from it: the RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT), profile setting and aggregation (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), adding the image modality, or the fusion method. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: Starting with a minimal reference point makes every later result interpretable as the effect of one design choice. It also avoids assuming that multimodal or multiprofile models are better before any evidence exists.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 set the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a 2000-component PCA RNA encoder, with no image modality, aggregation, or fusion. It was chosen as the simplest and least confounded reference point. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.471 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.442, which shows that RNA expression alone with a linear PCA encoder carries measurable predictive signal. This is only an initial observation. With no prior experiments and no chance-level or class-balance reference given, it is unclear how strong this result is, whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, the image modality, or fusion would help, and how sensitive the result is to the PCA dimensionality or to run-to-run variance.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: we have one baseline, RNA-only single-profile PCA, at 0.471 accuracy and 0.442 F1. We do not yet know whether the image modality carries comparable, weaker, or stronger signal. That is the biggest open question, because it decides whether the many multimodal configurations are worth budget. 2) This run tests an image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model with no aggregation or fusion. Its only difference from the baseline is the modality, so it gives a clean RNA-vs-image comparison. Its result will tell us whether fusion is likely to help and whether image encoder choice deserves more experiments. 3) Most of the remaining search space is multimodal, so settling the value of the image modality early is the most informative next step. If images are weak, we can shift budget to RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation. If they are strong or comparable, multimodal fusion becomes the priority. ResNet50 is the simpler image encoder, which makes it the right single-profile reference point before trying ViT-L.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no aggregation or fusion, as a modality counterpart to the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.411 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.378, about 0.06 below the RNA-only baseline on both metrics (0.471 / 0.442). This suggests that image features from ResNet50 carry measurable but possibly weaker signal than PCA-encoded RNA in the single-profile setting. The comparison changes the encoder along with the modality (ResNet50 vs. PCA-2000), and each result comes from a single run with no variance or chance-level reference, so it remains uncertain whether the gap reflects the modality itself, the encoder choice (e.g., ViT-L might do better), or run-to-run noise, and whether the image signal is complementary enough to RNA for fusion to help.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence so far: two single-profile unimodal baselines. RNA-only PCA-2000 reached 0.471 accuracy and 0.442 F1. Image-only ResNet50 reached 0.411 and 0.378. Both modalities carry signal, but we do not know whether the image signal adds anything beyond RNA or is redundant with it. 2. This experiment adds the image features to RNA through simple concatenation. Config_016 keeps profile setting (single), RNA encoder (PCA-2000), image encoder (ResNet50) and aggregation (none) fixed. Both of its components already have measured baselines, so any change from 0.471 can be attributed mainly to fusion itself, without confounding from a new encoder or from multiprofile aggregation. 3. Whether fusion helps is the decision that splits the search space most: about two-thirds of the remaining configurations are multimodal. A clear gain would justify exploring fusion variants, weighted fusion and multiprofile versions. No gain or a loss would point the budget toward stronger unimodal options, such as other RNA encoders or multiprofile RNA. Concat is the least complex fusion, so it is the logical first test before trying weighted fusion. A single run cannot settle this, but it is a cleanly attributable first comparison.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested multimodal, single-profile fusion by concatenating PCA-2000 RNA features with ResNet50 image features, with no aggregation. Every other setting matched the two unimodal baselines, so the only change was combining the modalities via concat. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.260 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.222. That is well below both RNA-only (0.471 / 0.442) and image-only (0.411 / 0.378), so in this setup naive concatenation degraded performance rather than adding complementary signal. A drop below even the weaker unimodal baseline is unexpected, and this is a single run with no variance estimate. It remains uncertain whether the loss reflects concat fusion itself or fixable factors such as feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance between the two feature sets, optimization or training instability, or a pipeline issue. This result alone should not be taken as evidence that multimodal fusion in general, including weighted fusion or multiprofile variants, cannot help.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: In single runs, RNA-only PCA-2000 (0.471 acc / 0.442 F1) beat image-only ResNet50 (0.411 / 0.378). Concat fusion of the two dropped to 0.260 / 0.222, below either modality alone. That drop is anomalous. It could come from concat itself (for example, scale or dimensionality imbalance between 2000-d PCA and ResNet features), from optimization problems, or from multimodal fusion simply not helping here. 2) What this tests: config_017 keeps everything from config_016 the same (single-profile, PCA-2000, ResNet50) and changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted. If weighted fusion recovers to or above the RNA-only baseline, the failure was specific to concat. If it also collapses, that points to a broader problem with combining modalities in this pipeline. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: Most of the remaining configurations (35 of 48) are multimodal and use either concat or weighted fusion. Settling whether fusion can work at all, and which method to prefer, is the single biggest source of uncertainty for pruning the search space. It is also a clean one-variable comparison. Encoder and multiprofile questions, such as config_002 and config_004, remain good follow-ups after this.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 repeated the multimodal, single-profile PCA-2000 RNA + ResNet50 image configuration from llm_summary_003 with no aggregation, changing only the fusion method from concat to weighted. That makes it a one-variable test of whether the earlier fusion collapse was specific to concat. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.332 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.315. This is above concat fusion (0.260 / 0.222), so the concat failure may have been partly method-specific. It is still well below both image-only (0.411 / 0.378) and RNA-only (0.471 / 0.442), so neither fusion method has yet shown complementary benefit. All results are single runs with no variance estimate, so the size of the weighted-vs-concat gain is uncertain. It also remains unclear whether multimodal underperformance comes from the fusion design, from feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance or optimization problems common to both fusion runs, or from a pipeline issue. This calls for caution before investing heavily in the many remaining single-profile multimodal configurations, though multiprofile or other encoder variants are untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile is the best result so far (0.471 acc / 0.442 F1). Image-only ResNet50 is lower (0.411 / 0.378). Both single-profile fusion attempts fell below either unimodal baseline (concat 0.260, weighted 0.332), so fusion currently looks like a poor investment until the stronger components are better understood. Profile setting and aggregation are completely untested. 2. Test: config_002 keeps the best configuration (RNA-only, PCA-2000) and changes only the profile setting to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles improves on the single-profile baseline. 3. Why now: multiprofile is a major design axis. It appears in many of the remaining configurations, including multimodal ones, so learning its effect cheaply informs a large share of the search space. It also builds directly on the strongest result so far, which balances learning with the chance of improving performance. Avgpool sets a clean reference before trying transformer aggregation or swapping RNA encoders.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best prior configuration (RNA-only, PCA-2000 encoder, no image or fusion) and changed only the profile setting from singleprofile to multiprofile, aggregating profiles with simple average pooling. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.725 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.685. That is a large improvement over the single-profile RNA-only baseline from llm_summary_001 (0.471 / 0.442) and makes this the best result so far. Because this was a near one-variable comparison, multiprofile input with avgpool is strongly associated with the gain, though multiprofile and its aggregation method cannot be separated, and both results are single runs with no variance estimate. It remains untested whether the benefit transfers to image-only or multimodal multiprofile settings, whether transformer aggregation or other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) improve on avgpool/PCA, and whether multiprofile evaluation is directly comparable to single-profile evaluation (e.g., the effective number or grouping of validation samples may differ).

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Moving RNA-only PCA-2000 from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.471 to 0.725 (F1 0.442 to 0.685). This is by far the largest effect seen so far, but it comes from one run on one modality. It is unclear whether the gain reflects multiprofile aggregation in general, something RNA-specific, or a change in how multiprofile evaluation is done. Both single-profile fusion runs fell below the unimodal baselines. 2. What this tests: config_011 changes only the profile setting for the image-only ResNet50 baseline (0.411 / 0.378), from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool. A similarly large gain would show that the multiprofile effect is modality-general. A small or no gain would point to an RNA-specific benefit or an evaluation artifact. It also creates the matched unimodal reference needed to read any multiprofile multimodal result (e.g., config_019). 3. Why now: Profile setting is the design choice with the most evidence of mattering. Checking whether it generalizes clarifies the main driver of performance at the cost of one experiment. It also tells us whether multiprofile fusion is worth budget, which avoids spending runs on the many multimodal configurations blindly. Testing transformer aggregation (config_003) is a reasonable follow-up once this is known.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 changed only the profile setting of the image-only ResNet50 baseline (llm_summary_002) from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, to test whether the large multiprofile gain seen for RNA-only PCA-2000 generalizes across modalities. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.537 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.518, up from 0.411 / 0.378 (about +0.13 accuracy, +0.14 F1). This indicates that the multiprofile benefit is not RNA-specific, though it is roughly half the RNA gain (+0.25 accuracy), so image-only multiprofile remains well below RNA-only multiprofile (0.725 / 0.685) and the modality gap widened from about 0.06 to about 0.19. Uncertainties: these are single runs with no variance estimate; multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation cannot be separated; and a shared change in multiprofile evaluation (e.g., sample grouping) could still inflate both gains, so an evaluation artifact is not ruled out. Matched multiprofile unimodal references now exist for interpreting multiprofile fusion (e.g., config_019), but given the earlier single-profile fusion collapse and the weaker image signal, it is untested whether multiprofile fusion can beat RNA-only multiprofile, and whether transformer aggregation (e.g., config_003) improves on avgpool.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Multiprofile input with avgpool gave the largest gains so far. RNA-only PCA-2000 rose from 0.471 to 0.725 accuracy, and image-only rose from 0.411 to 0.537. That makes RNA-only multiprofile (config_002) the clear leader. However, the aggregation method has never been varied, so the multiprofile benefit cannot be separated from avgpool specifically. Single-profile fusion underperformed both unimodal baselines, which argues for caution before spending heavily on multimodal runs. 2) Test: config_003 changes only the aggregation of the best configuration, from avgpool to transformer. This is a clean one-variable test of whether learned attention over profiles beats simple averaging. 3) Value: It exploits the strongest direction found so far. Its answer also bears on every remaining multiprofile configuration, unimodal and multimodal, which is about half the search space. That will help direct later choices, such as whether multiprofile fusion runs should use avgpool or transformer. It is also a cleaner and more broadly informative use of one experiment than jumping to fusion now.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the leading configuration (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 encoder, no image or fusion; llm_summary_005) and changed only the aggregation method from avgpool to transformer. This made it a one-variable test of whether learned attention over profiles beats simple averaging. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.706 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.667, slightly below avgpool (0.725 / 0.685; about -0.019 accuracy and -0.018 F1). Transformer aggregation therefore gave no improvement here, and avgpool RNA-only multiprofile remains the best result so far. Both results come from single runs with no variance estimate, so this small gap may fall within run-to-run noise and should not be read as evidence that transformer aggregation is reliably worse. It is also untested whether the result holds for image-only or multimodal multiprofile settings, or with transformer tuning (e.g., capacity, regularization, number of profiles). The test does show that the large multiprofile gain does not depend specifically on avgpool, since both aggregators performed far above the single-profile baseline (0.471). However, a shared multiprofile evaluation artifact (e.g., differences in sample grouping) is still not ruled out.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Multiprofile input with avgpool gave large gains for both RNA-only (0.725 / 0.685, the best so far) and image-only (0.537 / 0.518). Transformer aggregation did not beat avgpool for RNA (0.706). Multimodal fusion has only been tested in the single-profile setting, where it fell below both unimodal baselines. Weighted fusion (0.332) did better there than concat (0.260). The key open question is whether fusion can add complementary signal when the inputs are the much stronger multiprofile representations. 2. Test: config_019 uses the same PCA-2000 RNA and ResNet50 image encoders and the same multiprofile avgpool aggregation as config_002 and config_011, and switches to multimodal with weighted fusion. This is a clean comparison against matched unimodal references. It also uses the better-performing fusion method and aggregator, so it gives fusion its fairest test. 3. Why now: Fusion is the design axis behind most of the remaining configurations. A positive result (beating 0.725) would point toward exploiting multimodal multiprofile variants. A negative result would show that the single-profile fusion failure persists, which would justify moving the budget to RNA-encoder tests (scVI, scGPT) on the RNA-only multiprofile setup. Either outcome sharply narrows the search, whereas an encoder swap alone would leave this larger question unresolved.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 (config_019) tested multimodal weighted fusion of PCA-2000 RNA and ResNet50 image features under multiprofile avgpool aggregation, a matched comparison against the RNA-only (llm_summary_005; 0.725 / 0.685) and image-only (llm_summary_006; 0.537 / 0.518) multiprofile references, to see whether fusion adds complementary signal when both inputs are strong. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.573 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.573. That is a large improvement over single-profile weighted fusion (0.332 / 0.315) and modestly above image-only multiprofile, but about 0.15 accuracy below RNA-only multiprofile, so fusion again failed to beat the best unimodal model and RNA-only multiprofile avgpool remains the best result so far. This is consistent with the single-profile fusion underperformance persisting under multiprofile input and supports shifting budget toward RNA-encoder tests (scVI, scGPT) on RNA-only multiprofile. However, these are single runs with no variance estimate, concat fusion, transformer aggregation, and other encoders are untested in multiprofile multimodal settings, and it remains unclear whether the gap reflects fusion design, feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance, optimization issues, or a pipeline problem; a shared multiprofile evaluation artifact also remains unruled out.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Multiprofile input is the dominant factor so far. RNA-only PCA-2000 rose from 0.471 to 0.725 accuracy, image-only from 0.411 to 0.537, and avgpool slightly beat transformer aggregation (0.725 vs 0.706, likely within noise). Fusion has underperformed the best unimodal model in every run, including multiprofile weighted fusion (0.573). The RNA encoder has only ever been PCA-2000, so it is the largest untested design choice on the leading branch. 2) This test: config_005 keeps the best configuration (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. That isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional probabilistic RNA representation beats linear PCA. 3) Why now: it exploits the strongest direction while settling a key representation question with a clean one-variable change. The result will also guide whether later multimodal runs should use scVI, which matters given the open hypothesis that PCA-2000 dimensionality imbalance hurts fusion. The scGPT counterpart (config_008) is a natural follow-up.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the leading configuration (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, no image or fusion; llm_summary_005) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, a one-variable test of whether a learned, lower-dimensional probabilistic representation beats linear PCA. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.512 (primary metric) and F1 of 0.477, far below PCA-2000 under the same setup (0.725 / 0.685; about -0.21 accuracy) and even below image-only multiprofile (0.537 / 0.518). In this setup scVI-200 therefore did not help, and RNA-only multiprofile avgpool with PCA-2000 remains the best result. This argues against simply adopting scVI-200 for later multimodal runs to address the suspected dimensionality imbalance. However, this is a single run with no variance estimate. The encoder swap changes dimensionality (200 vs 2000) and representation type together, so these cannot be separated. It is also untested whether scVI training or tuning (e.g., latent size, gene selection, normalization), a pipeline issue, or the shared multiprofile evaluation setup explains the drop. scGPT (config_008) remains an open comparison.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only multiprofile with avgpool and PCA-2000 is the clear leader (0.725 / 0.685). Transformer aggregation was not better (0.706). Fusion has so far failed to beat the best unimodal model (0.573). Swapping PCA for scVI-200 dropped sharply (0.512). The RNA encoder therefore matters a great deal, but only two encoder types have been compared, and each is a single run. scGPT, a pretrained foundation-model representation, is the remaining untested RNA encoder. 2. What it tests: config_008 keeps the leading setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder to scGPT. It asks whether PCA's advantage is specific to scVI's weaknesses, or whether linear PCA-2000 is generally hard to beat for this task. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: it is a clean one-variable comparison on the strongest pipeline, so it can directly improve on the best result. It also tells us which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal runs, which is the dominant modality's key unresolved choice.
