selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion; 0.653 accuracy / 0.628 F1). It was reached through single-factor changes. Those changes also showed that swapping single changes into this setup hurt it: the transformer aggregator, the ViT-L image encoder and the scVI-200 RNA encoder each dropped accuracy by about 0.14 to 0.18. The one major design axis still untested is the scGPT RNA encoder. It is a pretrained foundation-model representation, so the scVI result does not tell us much about it. 2) Test: config_043 swaps only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT and keeps the best image encoder, aggregation and fusion. This directly shows whether a pretrained RNA representation helps or hurts compared with PCA in the strongest setup. 3) Why now: It completes the planned RNA-encoder comparison as a clean single-factor experiment. It also has real potential to set a new best result, so it serves both exploration and exploitation. If scGPT also falls below PCA, that is strong evidence that PCA-2000 is the right RNA choice. Later runs could then check robustness, for example whether RNA still adds value under multiprofile compared with image-only multiprofile (config_011).
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 changed only the RNA encoder of the current best configuration (llm_summary_006: multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion), swapping PCA-2000 for the pretrained scGPT encoder, and reached validation accuracy 0.573 (F1 0.573), which is about 0.08 below the PCA-2000 version (0.653 / 0.628), with F1 about 0.055 lower. Because this was a single-factor change, it is direct initial evidence that scGPT performed worse than PCA-2000 in this setup, though the drop is clearly smaller than for scVI-200 (llm_summary_008: 0.471), so PCA-2000 remains the reference RNA encoder and the planned RNA-encoder comparison now consistently favors it. scGPT's F1 is nearly equal to its accuracy, unlike the PCA runs where F1 trailed accuracy by about 0.02, which may hint at more balanced per-class behavior, but this is unconfirmed. Uncertainties remain: these are single runs with unknown variance, scGPT results may depend on embedding extraction, normalization, or scale mismatch within weighted fusion, and no image-only multiprofile result is available here, so it is still unknown whether any RNA encoder (PCA or scGPT) adds value beyond images under multiprofile aggregation.

selection_reason: Evidence: the best result so far is multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 + ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion (config_019: 0.653 / 0.628). Swapping in scVI or scGPT lowered performance, and the scVI version (0.471) fell below single-profile image-only (0.532). It is therefore unclear how much RNA contributes once multiprofile aggregation is used. The RNA benefit was only shown under single-profile concat (0.599 vs 0.532). Test: image-only, multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool is the unimodal counterpart of config_018 and config_019. It shows how much multiprofile avgpool helps images alone, compared with the single-profile image-only run (config_010). It also shows how much the PCA RNA branch adds beyond images under aggregation, and whether scGPT (0.573) and scVI (0.471) actually help or hurt compared with images alone. Why now: the modality contribution under multiprofile is the most important unresolved design question. Every RNA-encoder and fusion conclusion depends on knowing this image-only multiprofile reference. This single-factor ablation is cheaper to interpret than further encoder or fusion permutations.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested the image-only counterpart of the leading multiprofile configurations: multiprofile ResNet50 with avgpool aggregation, no RNA branch and no fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.435 (F1 0.423). That is about 0.10 below single-profile image-only ResNet50 (llm_summary_002: 0.532 / 0.516), so multiprofile avgpool appears to hurt the image modality alone even though it helped the PCA+ResNet50 concat model (llm_summary_004 vs 003). Profile setting and aggregation changed together in that comparison, so their separate effects are not isolated. Every multiprofile multimodal ResNet50/avgpool variant scored above this image-only reference: PCA concat 0.632, PCA weighted 0.653, scGPT weighted 0.573, and even scVI weighted 0.471. This is initial evidence that the RNA branch contributes substantially under multiprofile aggregation (about 0.20–0.22 for PCA). It also revises the earlier reading that scVI disrupted fusion, since scVI fell below the single-profile image-only run but not below the multiprofile image-only one. Uncertainties remain: these are single runs with unknown variance, and the modality comparison also differs in whether and how fusion is used. The cause of the image-only multiprofile drop is unresolved and could be averaging that dilutes image features, untuned hyperparameters, or training instability. An RNA-only multiprofile reference has not been run, so how much the multimodal gain reflects true complementarity rather than RNA benefiting more from aggregation is unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we have no information on modality value, encoder quality, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, least confounded configuration. It sets a reference point that later experiments can each change one factor against: encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), modality (image-only, multimodal), and fusion. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: Starting with a clean baseline lets every later result be read as a single-factor comparison. Starting with a complex multimodal or multiprofile model would mix several design choices together. It also guards against assuming that more complex models win, by showing how much a simple model already achieves.
experiment_summary: This first experiment set up a baseline: RNA only, single profile, a PCA encoder with 2000 components, and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It was picked as the simplest and least confounded reference point, so later runs can change one factor at a time (RNA encoder, profile setting with avgpool or transformer aggregation, adding images, fusion). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.653, supported by a validation F1 of 0.628, which shows a simple RNA-only model already does well above trivial performance. There are no other experiments to compare against yet, so this is only an initial observation. We cannot yet say whether other encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, the image modality, or multimodal fusion would improve on it, and we have no estimate of run-to-run variance.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA-2000 baseline reached 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1. We do not yet know how the profile setting, RNA encoder, image modality, or fusion affect performance. 2. This experiment changes one factor: it keeps RNA-only and PCA-2000 and switches from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). It shows directly whether combining multiple profiles helps, and avgpool separates the value of extra profiles from the added complexity of a transformer aggregator. 3. Profile setting affects most of the remaining configurations, including roughly two-thirds of the multimodal ones, so settling it early is the most useful next step. The comparison is clean, cheap, and informative whichever way it turns out. RNA encoder (config_004 or config_007) and image-only baselines (config_010 or config_013) are strong candidates for later runs.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the RNA-only, PCA-2000 setup from llm_summary_001 and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.537, with a supporting F1 of 0.518, about 0.115 accuracy and 0.110 F1 below the single-profile baseline (0.653 and 0.628). So in this RNA-only PCA setting, multiprofile with avgpool did worse than single-profile. The profile setting and the aggregation method changed together, so the drop cannot be attributed to using multiple profiles as such rather than to simple average pooling. It is also unknown whether a transformer aggregator, other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or adding the image modality would change this ranking, and each configuration has only one run with no variance estimate.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: In the RNA-only PCA-2000 setting, switching from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool lowered validation accuracy from 0.653 to 0.537, and F1 fell by a similar amount. Profile setting and aggregation changed together, so we cannot tell whether the multiprofile input itself hurts or whether simple average pooling discards useful information. Each result is a single run with no variance estimate, though a gap of about 0.115 is large. 2. Test: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 and swaps only avgpool for transformer aggregation. If accuracy recovers to near or above the single-profile baseline, the drop was mainly due to avgpool and multiprofile stays a viable direction. If it stays well below 0.653, that is stronger evidence against multiprofile in this setting. 3. Why now: Profile setting and aggregation recur across most of the remaining multiprofile configurations, both RNA-only and multimodal. Settling this with a single one-factor comparison guides many later choices before the budget goes to other encoders or modalities. Those remain important next steps, such as the scVI or scGPT single-profile runs and the image-only baselines.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile setup of llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregation from avgpool to a transformer, as a one-factor test of whether avgpool caused the multiprofile drop. Validation accuracy was 0.485 (F1 0.464), about 0.053 below multiprofile-avgpool (0.537 / 0.518) and about 0.168 below the single-profile baseline (0.653 / 0.628). So in this run the transformer aggregator did not recover performance and did worse than avgpool. This does not support the idea that avgpool alone explained the drop, and it adds evidence against multiprofile input in the RNA-only PCA setting with these two aggregators. Uncertainties remain: each configuration is a single run with no variance estimate, so the smaller avgpool-versus-transformer gap may not be reliable. The transformer's underperformance could reflect untuned hyperparameters or optimization or overfitting issues rather than an inherent limitation. It is also unknown whether multiprofile behaves differently with other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), the image modality, or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: three RNA-only PCA-2000 runs show single-profile (0.653 acc / 0.628 F1) clearly beating multiprofile with avgpool (0.537) and with transformer (0.485). Each is a single run, so this suggests, but does not establish, that single-profile is the better setting. Nothing yet tells us whether the RNA encoder matters or how the image modality performs. 2) Test: config_004 keeps the best-so-far setup (RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion) and changes only the encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. This isolates the effect of RNA representation against the strongest baseline. 3) Why this one: further multiprofile runs look less promising given the consistent drop. Changing the encoder in the best setting is a cheap one-factor experiment that exploits current evidence while resolving a major design uncertainty. Its result will tell us which RNA encoder to carry into later image-only and multimodal comparisons.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the best-so-far setup from llm_summary_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, as a one-factor test of the RNA representation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.411 (F1 0.378), about 0.242 accuracy and 0.250 F1 below the PCA-2000 single-profile baseline (0.653 / 0.628). That makes it the weakest result so far, below both multiprofile PCA runs. Because only the encoder changed, this is direct single-run evidence that scVI-200 did worse than PCA-2000 in this setting, so PCA-2000 is the provisional RNA encoder to carry forward. Uncertainties remain: there is one run per configuration and no variance estimate. The scVI encoder also differs in latent size (200 vs 2000 dimensions) and may have been untrained or untuned, so the gap could reflect dimensionality or training choices rather than scVI itself. Other encoders (e.g., scGPT), the image modality, and multimodal fusion remain untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: All four runs are RNA-only. They provisionally favour PCA-2000 single-profile (0.653 accuracy / 0.628 F1) over multiprofile with avgpool (0.537) or transformer (0.485) and over scVI-200 (0.411). Each result is a single run. The image modality is completely untested, yet most remaining configurations (image-only and all multimodal) depend on it. 2. What this tests: Image-only, single-profile ResNet50 is the simplest image baseline, with no aggregation or fusion to confound it. It shows whether images alone carry useful signal and how they compare to the RNA PCA baseline in the same single-profile setting. It also gives a reference point for later ViT-L, multiprofile and fusion comparisons. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: The RNA axis already has a reasonable provisional winner, and scGPT is just one more encoder variant. Image signal strength is the largest unresolved question, and it decides whether multimodal fusion experiments are worth funding. Testing it in its simplest form isolates one factor and reduces the most uncertainty per experiment.
experiment_summary: This experiment was the first test of the image modality: image-only input, single-profile, a ResNet50 image encoder, and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It serves as the simplest image baseline to compare against the RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.332 (F1 0.315), about 0.321 accuracy and 0.313 F1 below the RNA PCA-2000 single-profile run (0.653 / 0.628) and also below the weakest RNA result, scVI-200 (0.411 / 0.378). In this single run, ResNet50 image features alone carried less discriminative signal than every RNA configuration tested so far. Whether this beats trivial or chance-level performance cannot be judged, because the number of classes and the class balance are not given. Several uncertainties remain: each configuration has only one run and no variance estimate, and ResNet50 may be limited by its pretraining domain, by being frozen or untuned, or by preprocessing choices rather than by weak image signal in general. It is also untested whether a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L), multiprofile image aggregation, or fusion with RNA would add complementary information, even though image-only performance is weak on its own.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is the simple RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000 baseline (0.653 accuracy, 0.628 F1). Multiprofile aggregation (avgpool 0.537, transformer 0.485) and scVI-200 (0.411) both did worse. ResNet50 image-only was weakest (0.332), but it still carries some signal. All results are single runs. The main untested design question is multimodal fusion: whether image features add complementary information to RNA, even though images are weak on their own. 2. What this tests: config_016 adds only the ResNet50 image branch, with concat fusion, to the best configuration. It keeps PCA-2000, single-profile and no aggregation, so any gain or loss is attributable to adding the image modality. Both components already have unimodal baselines, which makes the comparison easy to interpret. 3. Why this is the best next step: Fusion is the central question for multimodal profiling and has not been tested at all. Testing it with the strongest RNA setting and the simplest fusion gives a clean answer. If concat helps, weighted fusion and ViT-L become the logical next tests. If it hurts or does nothing, the budget can shift toward RNA encoders such as scGPT (config_007). This seems more informative than another encoder or aggregation variant along directions that have so far underperformed.
experiment_summary: This experiment was the first test of multimodal fusion. It took the best configuration so far (llm_summary_001: single-profile, PCA-2000 RNA encoder, no aggregation) and added a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion. Validation accuracy was 0.471 (F1 0.442), about 0.182 accuracy and 0.186 F1 below the RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline (0.653 / 0.628), though above ResNet50 image-only (0.332 / 0.315). So in this single run, naive concat fusion with ResNet50 features hurt rather than added complementary information. This gives provisional evidence against this particular fusion setup, but it is uncertain whether the drop reflects uninformative or noisy image features or the concat design itself, since adding the image modality and the fusion method are confounded here (e.g., feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance, optimization, or a frozen or untuned image encoder). Each configuration has only one run with no variance estimate, and weighted fusion, stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), and alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT) remain untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile (config_001: 0.653 accuracy / 0.628 F1) is the best result so far. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_016) dropped performance to 0.471 / 0.442. It is unclear whether that drop comes from uninformative image features or from the naive concat design, for example scale or dimensionality imbalance letting noisy image features dominate. 2. What this tests: config_017 changes only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, keeping single-profile, PCA-2000 and ResNet50 fixed. If weighted fusion recovers to near or above the RNA-only baseline, the concat design was the likely problem and fusion remains a viable direction. If it still underperforms, that is stronger evidence that ResNet50 image features add little. 3. Why this is the best next use of the budget: about half of the remaining configurations are multimodal, and fusion method is a shared factor across all of them. Resolving it with a single, unconfounded experiment efficiently prunes or prioritizes a large part of the search space, which is worth more now than testing another encoder.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the llm_summary_006 multimodal setup fixed (single-profile, PCA-2000 RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, no aggregation) and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted. This one-factor test asked whether the earlier multimodal drop came from the concat design or from uninformative image features. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.721 (F1 0.681), the best result so far. That is about 0.250 accuracy above concat fusion (0.471 / 0.442) and about 0.068 accuracy and 0.053 F1 above the RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline (0.653 / 0.628). Because only the fusion method changed relative to llm_summary_006, this is direct single-run evidence that weighted fusion outperformed concat here, and it suggests the concat drop reflected the fusion design rather than useless image features. The gain over RNA-only provisionally indicates ResNet50 features can add complementary signal when fused this way, which makes weighted multimodal fusion the leading direction. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has one run with no variance estimate, so the size of the gain over RNA-only is not confirmed. It is unknown what weighting the model learned, or whether the gain comes from image information rather than regularization or optimization effects. Whether weighted fusion also helps with multiprofile aggregation, stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), or other RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT) is untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: weighted fusion of PCA-2000 RNA with ResNet50 image features (config_017) gave the best result so far (0.721 acc / 0.681 F1). That beats RNA-only PCA (0.653) and concat fusion (0.471), so images can add useful signal when fused this way. The image branch is still the weakest part: ResNet50 image-only reached only 0.332. Multiprofile aggregation and scVI both hurt in RNA-only runs, which makes those directions less promising for now. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup fixed (single-profile, PCA-2000, weighted fusion) and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. It tests whether a stronger image representation increases the multimodal gain, which isolates the effect of image representation within the leading fusion setup. 3) It is a one-factor extension of the strongest result, so it has good odds of a new best. Either outcome is informative: a clear gain points to image representation as a key lever, and no gain suggests the fusion mechanism, not image quality, drives the improvement. That makes it a better use of the limited budget than revisiting multiprofile or scVI, which have weak evidence so far.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the leading setup from llm_summary_007 fixed (multimodal, single-profile, PCA-2000 RNA encoder, weighted fusion, no aggregation) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, as a one-factor test of whether a stronger image representation increases the multimodal gain. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.532 (F1 0.517). That is about 0.189 accuracy and 0.164 F1 below the ResNet50 weighted-fusion run (0.721 / 0.681) and about 0.121 accuracy below the RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline (0.653 / 0.628), though above ResNet50 concat fusion (0.471 / 0.442). Because only the image encoder changed, this is direct single-run evidence that swapping in ViT-L features hurt within this weighted-fusion setup, and that a larger generic ImageNet backbone did not translate into better multimodal performance here, so ResNet50 with weighted fusion remains the provisional best. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has one run with no variance estimate, so the large gap could partly reflect instability of the weighted fusion. The drop could also stem from ViT-L's higher feature dimensionality or scale interacting with the fusion weights, from frozen or untuned features, preprocessing, or optimization rather than worse image signal as such, and ViT-L image-only performance has not been measured to separate these explanations.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is single-profile PCA-2000 with ResNet50 and weighted fusion (0.721 acc / 0.681 F1). The RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline (0.653) is the strongest single-modality result, so the RNA representation drives most of the performance. Of the three RNA encoders, only two have been tested. scVI-200 did much worse than PCA (0.411), but scGPT is completely unmeasured. Multiprofile input already has two consistent negative results in the RNA-only setting (avgpool 0.537, transformer 0.485), so testing it again now is less informative. 2) What this tests: config_007 changes only the RNA encoder relative to config_001 (single-profile, RNA-only, no image, aggregation or fusion). It is a clean one-factor test of whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding beats or matches PCA-2000. It also helps show whether scVI's poor result reflects learned latent encoders in general or something specific to scVI. 3) Why this is the best use of the next experiment: The RNA encoder is the highest-impact design choice that remains untested. If scGPT matches or exceeds PCA, scGPT with ResNet50 and weighted fusion (config_041) becomes a strong next step. If it underperforms, PCA is confirmed as the RNA backbone, and the remaining budget can focus on multimodal refinements such as multiprofile weighted fusion (config_019).
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the llm_summary_001 baseline fixed (RNA-only, single-profile, no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT, as a one-factor test of whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding matches or beats PCA. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.227 (F1 0.191), the weakest result so far. That is about 0.426 accuracy and 0.438 F1 below PCA-2000 (0.653 / 0.628) and also below scVI-200 (0.411 / 0.378) and ResNet50 image-only (0.332 / 0.315). Because only the encoder changed, this is direct single-run evidence that scGPT did much worse than PCA-2000 in this setting, and together with scVI it provisionally confirms PCA-2000 as the RNA backbone. It also argues against pursuing scGPT with ResNet50 weighted fusion (config_041), with budget better spent on PCA-based multimodal refinements. Uncertainties remain: there is one run with no variance estimate, and the result is low enough to raise the possibility of a pipeline issue (e.g., gene-vocabulary mismatch, preprocessing or normalization, frozen or untuned embeddings, embedding dimensionality) rather than an inherent limitation of scGPT. Chance level cannot be judged because the class count and class balance are unknown, so this does not establish that learned or pretrained RNA encoders are generally inferior.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_017 (multimodal, single-profile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, weighted fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. The encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L) all performed clearly worse, which provisionally fixes PCA-2000 and ResNet50. The profile/aggregation axis has only been tested in the RNA-only setting, where multiprofile hurt and avgpool (0.537) beat transformer (0.485). It is untested whether multiprofile behaves differently once images and weighted fusion are added, since pooling across profiles may help noisier image features. 2) Test: config_019 changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool, relative to the best configuration. This isolates whether multiprofile input helps or hurts in the leading multimodal weighted-fusion setup. 3) Why now: It is a one-factor extension of the strongest configuration and addresses the largest remaining untested interaction. It uses avgpool, the better of the two aggregators in prior evidence. Either outcome is informative: a gain would open a new best direction, and a drop would confirm single-profile as the setting to keep, narrowing the remaining search space.
experiment_summary: This experiment took the best configuration, llm_summary_007 (multimodal, single-profile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, weighted fusion; 0.721 / 0.681). It switched the profile setting to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation to test whether multiprofile behaves differently once images and weighted fusion are added. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.525 (F1 0.498), about 0.196 accuracy and 0.184 F1 below the single-profile weighted-fusion run, and also below the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.653 / 0.628). It was close to the RNA-only multiprofile-avgpool result (0.537 / 0.518). This matches the earlier RNA-only finding that multiprofile hurt, so single-profile is the provisional setting to keep. However, introducing multiprofile input also meant adding avgpool aggregation, so the drop cannot be attributed to multiple profiles as such rather than to the pooling scheme or how it interacts with the fusion weights. Uncertainties remain: there is one run with no variance estimate, weighted fusion has already shown large swings across configurations (possible instability), and transformer or other aggregators have not been tested in the multimodal setting.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2. Test: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, lowest-variance baseline. Every later design choice can be compared against it by changing one factor at a time: scVI or scGPT encoders, multiprofile with avgpool or transformer, image-only, or multimodal fusion. 3. Why now: Under a limited budget, a simple reference point gives the most interpretable anchor. It also guards against assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better, because each later gain can be credited to a single design decision.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) set up an RNA-only, single-profile baseline that uses a PCA encoder with 2000 components (pca_n2000) and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It was chosen as the simplest anchor so that later one-factor changes can be compared against it: alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile settings with avgpool or transformer aggregation, image-only models, and multimodal fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.519, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.480. The F1 being somewhat below accuracy may mean performance is uneven across classes, but per-class results and the class balance were not reported, so this is unconfirmed. This is an initial baseline from a single run with no comparisons yet, so it says nothing about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters, and run-to-run variance is unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (config_001: acc 0.519, F1 0.480). It shows nothing yet about which design choices matter, and run-to-run variance is unknown. 2) Test: config_002 changes one factor, the profile setting. It switches from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and keeps the RNA-only PCA encoder fixed. This isolates whether pooling information across multiple profiles helps. 3) Why now: profile setting cuts across most of the remaining space, since roughly two-thirds of the configurations are multiprofile. Learning early whether multiprofile helps will guide many later choices across encoders, image models and fusion. Avgpool is the cleanest first test of that question; a transformer-aggregation test can follow if multiprofile looks promising. Comparing encoders (scVI, scGPT) or modalities would also be informative single-factor changes, but the profile question has the widest downstream impact.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 tested an RNA-only PCA (pca_n2000) model with a multiprofile setting and avgpool aggregation, with no image encoder or fusion. It differs from the single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001) only in moving to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.519 to 0.678 (+0.159), and validation F1 rose from 0.480 to 0.646, so multiprofile input with avgpool appears clearly beneficial in this RNA-only PCA setting. Uncertainties remain: each configuration was run once and run-to-run variance is unknown; the multiprofile change and the avgpool choice are bundled, so whether other aggregations such as a transformer would do better or worse is untested; it is unknown whether the gain carries over to other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image models, or fusion; and F1 remains slightly below accuracy, which may reflect uneven per-class performance but is unconfirmed.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised RNA-only PCA accuracy from 0.519 to 0.678, and F1 rose by a similar amount (0.480 to 0.646). That makes multiprofile the strongest lead so far. However, the multiprofile change and the avgpool choice were tested together, so it is unclear how much the aggregation method contributes. 2) This experiment keeps everything from config_002 fixed (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) and swaps avgpool for transformer aggregation. It tests whether a learned aggregator adds value beyond simple pooling. 3) It builds directly on the best result with a single-factor change. The answer also decides which aggregation to use in later encoder, image-only and multimodal multiprofile runs, so it saves budget across many later configurations. Each configuration is a single run with unknown variance, so a small difference should not be overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000 setup of llm_summary_002 fixed and replaced avgpool with transformer aggregation (no image encoder or fusion). This single-factor change isolates aggregation within this setting. Validation accuracy rose from 0.678 to 0.713 (+0.035) and validation F1 from 0.646 to 0.695 (+0.048), the best result so far. This suggests learned transformer aggregation may add value over simple pooling for RNA-only PCA multiprofile inputs, though the gain is much smaller than the earlier single-to-multiprofile jump (+0.159). Each configuration was run once with unknown variance, so this modest difference is provisional and could partly reflect run-to-run noise. It is also untested whether the transformer advantage holds for other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only models, or multimodal fusion, and F1 remaining slightly below accuracy may indicate uneven per-class performance, which is unconfirmed.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: All three runs used RNA-only PCA. Moving to multiprofile gave a large gain (accuracy 0.519 to 0.678). Transformer aggregation added a smaller gain (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1), which is provisional because each configuration was run once. The image modality, and therefore fusion, is completely untested, and that is the largest open design question. 2. Test: config_020 keeps the best-known setup fixed (pca_n2000, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) and only adds a resnet50 image encoder with the simplest fusion (concat). Any difference from config_003 can therefore be attributed to adding image information. 3. Why now: This single change builds directly on the strongest configuration while answering whether image data adds value. Its result will guide whether the remaining budget should go to multimodal fusion and image encoder choices or to RNA encoder alternatives (scVI, scGPT). Multimodality is not assumed to help. A null or negative result would be equally informative and would point the search back toward RNA-only variants.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 kept the best-known RNA setup from llm_summary_003 fixed (pca_n2000, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) and added a resnet50 image encoder with concat fusion, making the model multimodal. Validation accuracy fell sharply from 0.713 to 0.422 (-0.291), and validation F1 fell from 0.695 to 0.405. This is below even the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.519), so in this configuration adding images with concat fusion clearly hurt rather than helped, and the strongest result so far remains RNA-only. The image encoder (resnet50) and fusion method (concat) were introduced together and each configuration was run once, so it is uncertain whether the drop reflects image data being unhelpful in general, this particular image encoder, naive concat fusion (for example, imbalance between the modalities' feature dimensions), or training or optimization issues; image-only performance and alternative fusion or encoder choices remain untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: multiprofile input clearly helped RNA-only PCA (+0.159 accuracy), and transformer aggregation gave a smaller, provisional gain (best so far 0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). Adding resnet50 images with concat fusion (config_020) dropped accuracy to 0.422, below even the single-profile RNA baseline (0.519). That drop could come from naive concat fusion, for example the image features swamping the RNA features, or from image data being uninformative, and the two causes are confounded. 2. What this tests: config_021 is identical to config_020 except that it uses weighted fusion instead of concat. This isolates the fusion method in the strongest known setup. If weighted fusion recovers to near or above 0.713, concat fusion was the problem and multimodal models remain worth exploring. If it stays low, the fusion method is less likely to be the cause, which points toward the image modality or encoder. Image-only runs can then confirm that. 3. Why it is the best next step: multimodal models make up most of the remaining search space, and fusion type is a design choice shared across all of them. Resolving this one-factor question first tells us whether that large region is worth spending budget on. Encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) or image-only runs can follow once this is settled.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 kept llm_summary_004's multimodal setup fixed (pca_n2000 RNA, resnet50 images, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) and changed only concat fusion to weighted fusion, isolating the fusion method. Validation accuracy rose modestly from 0.422 to 0.485 (+0.063), and F1 rose from 0.405 to 0.464. That is still far below the best RNA-only result (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1) and below the single-profile RNA baseline (0.519), so weighted fusion may help somewhat over concat but does not recover the multimodal drop. This makes the fusion method an unlikely main cause and points instead toward the resnet50 image features, the image modality itself, or multimodal training or optimization issues. Each configuration was run once with unknown variance, so the small weighted-vs-concat gain is provisional; image-only performance, other image encoders, other fusion designs, and the reason adding images hurts RNA performance all remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is RNA-only pca_n2000 with multiprofile and transformer aggregation (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). Adding resnet50 images cut accuracy to 0.422 with concat fusion and 0.485 with weighted fusion. Both are below even the single-profile RNA baseline. The small concat-vs-weighted difference makes fusion an unlikely main cause. What remains unclear is whether resnet50 image features carry any useful signal on their own. 2) What this tests: image-only resnet50 with the same multiprofile and transformer setup isolates the image modality. If it performs reasonably well, the multimodal drop likely comes from how the modalities are combined or trained, which justifies testing other fusion and encoder choices. If it performs near chance or poorly, resnet50 features are probably weak or noisy, so the next step is either imagenet_vit_l or deprioritizing images. 3) Why this is the best use of the budget: most remaining configurations are multimodal. A single diagnostic run tells us whether that large part of the search space is worth exploring, which is more informative now than a small RNA-encoder exploitation step (for example scvi_n200 with transformer aggregation).
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 was a diagnostic run that isolated the image modality. It used image-only resnet50 with the same multiprofile setting and transformer aggregation as the earlier runs, with no RNA encoder or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.635 (F1 0.618), which is well above both resnet50 multimodal runs (0.422 concat, 0.485 weighted) and the single-profile RNA baseline (0.519), though below the best RNA-only multiprofile transformer result (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). This suggests resnet50 image features carry substantial signal on their own, so weak image features alone seem an unlikely explanation for the multimodal drop. Combining two individually reasonable modalities scoring worse than either alone instead points toward how the modalities are fused, balanced, or optimized, which supports further exploration of fusion and training designs. However, each configuration was run once with unknown variance, and the image-only vs multimodal comparison removes both RNA and fusion together, so the specific cause of the multimodal degradation remains unconfirmed; other image encoders (e.g., imagenet_vit_l), avgpool aggregation for images, and F1 remaining slightly below accuracy (possible uneven per-class performance) are also untested.

selection_reason: Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation with pca_n2000 (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). Multiprofile clearly helped (+0.159), and the transformer gave a smaller provisional gain over avgpool. Both multimodal runs underperformed, and image-only resnet50 scored lower (0.635). The RNA encoder is a major design choice that has not been tested at all, because every RNA run so far used PCA. This experiment keeps the best setup fixed and swaps only pca_n2000 for scvi_n200. That isolates whether a learned, compact RNA representation improves on PCA in the strongest-performing regime. It is the best use of the next run because it exploits the most promising direction while resolving a key uncertainty with a clean one-factor comparison. Its answer also tells us which RNA encoder to carry into later scGPT and multimodal comparisons.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 kept the best-known setup from llm_summary_003 fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, no image encoder or fusion) and replaced the pca_n2000 RNA encoder with scvi_n200, a one-factor test of the RNA encoder. Validation accuracy fell from 0.713 to 0.619 (-0.095), and F1 fell from 0.695 to 0.610. In this regime, scvi_n200 therefore underperformed PCA, landing below the avgpool PCA run (0.678) and the image-only resnet50 run (0.635), so pca_n2000 remains the strongest RNA encoder tested so far. Each configuration was run once with unknown variance, so some of the gap could be run-to-run noise. Several explanations are also bundled and not separated: the scVI model itself, its much smaller latent size (200 vs 2000 dimensions), or scVI training and hyperparameter choices. Whether the result holds under avgpool, single-profile, or multimodal settings, and how scGPT compares, remain untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Each modality works reasonably alone. RNA-only PCA multiprofile with transformer reached 0.713 accuracy, and image-only resnet50 multiprofile with transformer reached 0.635. Yet both multimodal transformer runs fell below either modality alone (0.422 with concat, 0.485 with weighted). Switching from concat to weighted fusion recovered only a little, and image-only results show resnet50 features carry real signal. So the remaining candidate causes are how the multimodal inputs are aggregated across profiles or how the model is trained. 2. Test: This run keeps config_021 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, weighted fusion) and changes only transformer aggregation to avgpool. It shows whether the multimodal collapse is tied to transformer aggregation, for example through overfitting or optimization difficulty with larger fused inputs. If avgpool recovers to at least the single-modality level, aggregation is implicated. If not, the problem lies more in fusion or training. 3. Value: Multimodal configurations make up most of the untested space, so knowing why fusion fails decides whether that space deserves more budget. A clean one-factor diagnostic is a better use of this run than another encoder swap. Exploiting RNA-only with scGPT (config_009) is still a strong candidate for the next run. All conclusions remain tentative because each configuration was run once.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 kept llm_summary_005's multimodal setup fixed (multiprofile, pca_n2000 RNA, resnet50 images, weighted fusion) and changed only the aggregation from transformer to avgpool, as a one-factor test of whether transformer aggregation drives the multimodal collapse. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.639 (+0.154), and F1 rose from 0.464 to 0.620. This implicates transformer aggregation as a major contributor to the multimodal degradation in this setting, although the mechanism (for example, overfitting or optimization difficulty with fused inputs) is not identified. Recovery is only partial: the result roughly matches image-only resnet50 with transformer (0.635), but it stays below RNA-only PCA with avgpool (0.678) and RNA-only with transformer (0.713), so adding images still has not beaten RNA alone, and fusion or training issues may persist. Each configuration was run once with unknown variance, and several comparisons remain untested: avgpool with concat fusion, image-only with avgpool, and other image encoders or fusion designs.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000 with transformer aggregation (0.713 accuracy, 0.695 F1). Every multimodal variant has fallen short of it, with the best reaching 0.639 using avgpool and weighted fusion. Swapping the RNA encoder to scvi_n200 dropped accuracy to 0.619, so encoder choice clearly matters. scGPT is the only RNA encoder not yet tested in the leading setup. 2. What this tests: Keeping RNA-only, multiprofile and transformer aggregation fixed, it changes only the encoder from pca_n2000 to scGPT. This shows whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding beats or trails PCA, and whether scVI's weaker result is specific to scVI or reflects learned embeddings in general. 3. Why now: It extends the strongest direction found so far and could set a new best. It also resolves the main remaining uncertainty about the RNA encoder, which decides which encoder later multimodal runs should use. Running it before more fusion or image-encoder variants keeps the comparison clean and spends the limited budget efficiently. As with earlier runs, a single result is provisional because run-to-run variance is unknown.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 kept the best-known setup from llm_summary_003 fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scGPT, as a one-factor encoder test. Validation accuracy fell sharply from 0.713 to 0.328 (-0.386), and F1 fell from 0.695 to 0.288. This is the lowest result so far, well below scvi_n200 (0.619), the single-profile PCA baseline (0.519), and every multimodal run, so in this setting pca_n2000 remains the strongest RNA encoder tested and both learned embeddings trailed PCA. The drop is unusually large, so it may reflect a setup problem specific to this run (for example, embedding extraction, normalization or gene-vocabulary mismatch, embedding dimensionality, or how the transformer was trained on these inputs) rather than an inherent weakness of scGPT, but these explanations were not separated. Each configuration was run once with unknown variance, and it remains untested whether scGPT behaves differently under avgpool, single-profile, or multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only PCA with multiprofile transformer aggregation (0.713 accuracy). Every multimodal run used resnet50 and none beat RNA-only; the best reached 0.639 with avgpool and weighted fusion. Image-only resnet50 with transformer reached 0.635, so images carry real signal. The image encoder choice is the largest untested design axis: imagenet_vit_l has never been run. 2) What this tests: Running image-only imagenet_vit_l with multiprofile transformer aggregation changes only the encoder relative to config_012 (resnet50, 0.635). This isolates whether ViT-L gives a stronger image representation. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: Testing the encoder inside a multimodal run would mix the encoder effect with fusion and aggregation effects, which the earlier runs showed can collapse performance. This clean comparison says which image encoder to carry forward. If ViT-L clearly beats resnet50, the ViT multimodal configurations (e.g., config_025, avgpool with weighted fusion) become the most promising route to beating the RNA-only result. If it does not, the remaining budget can go to fixing fusion with resnet50 or to refining RNA-only models.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 kept the image-only resnet50 setup of llm_summary_006 fixed (multiprofile, transformer aggregation, no RNA encoder or fusion) and replaced resnet50 with imagenet_vit_l, a one-factor test of the image encoder. Validation accuracy was 0.629 (F1 0.599), slightly below resnet50's 0.635 (F1 0.618). That is a -0.007 accuracy gap and a somewhat larger -0.019 F1 gap. So ViT-L did not show a clear advantage, and the two encoders look roughly comparable in this setting, with resnet50 marginally ahead; both remain well below the best RNA-only PCA transformer result (0.713). Each configuration was run once with unknown variance, so the small difference may be noise. It is also untested whether ViT-L would compare differently under avgpool aggregation, in multimodal configurations (e.g., avgpool with weighted fusion, which gave resnet50 0.639), or with different fine-tuning and feature-extraction choices. The weak image-only evidence therefore does not strongly favor carrying ViT-L forward over resnet50.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 is the simplest configuration: RNA-only, a single profile, and a standard PCA encoder with no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference point for judging every later change. Each added piece, such as a learned encoder (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image features, or fusion, can then be tested one change at a time. 3) With a limited budget, a simple, fast baseline is the most informative first experiment. It avoids assuming that complex multimodal models are better, and it lets later experiments isolate the effect of each design choice.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA encoder (pca_n2000) and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.507 and a validation F1 of 0.455. Because no other experiments have been run, this result is an initial baseline and cannot show whether any design choice helps or hurts. It also remains unknown whether learned RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image features, or fusion would improve on it, so later changes should be compared against this reference one at a time.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Only one experiment has run, an RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.507, F1 0.455). Every design dimension is still untested. 2. Test: config_002 changes a single factor, singleprofile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool), while keeping the RNA-only PCA setup fixed. This isolates whether pooling information across multiple profiles helps, a choice that affects most of the remaining search space. 3. Why now: It is a clean one-variable comparison against the baseline. Using avgpool instead of a transformer separates the effect of the profile setting from the added complexity of learned aggregation. The result will indicate whether multiprofile variants deserve priority before testing encoders, image features or fusion.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 tested an RNA-only PCA (pca_n2000) model with multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation, changing only the profile setting from the llm_summary_001 single-profile baseline (the avgpool aggregation comes with that change). Validation accuracy rose slightly from 0.507 to 0.523 (+0.016), and validation F1 rose more clearly from 0.455 to 0.508 (+0.054). This is an initial signal that pooling across profiles may help, possibly by improving balance across classes. However, the accuracy gain is small and comes from single runs with no variance estimate, so it may fall within run-to-run noise. It also remains unknown whether learned aggregation (e.g., a transformer), other RNA encoders, image features, or fusion would extend or change this trend.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: So far only RNA-only PCA models have been tested. Multiprofile avgpool (config_002) gave a small accuracy gain over single-profile (0.523 vs 0.507) and a clearer F1 gain (0.508 vs 0.455). Nothing is known yet about the image modality, even though most remaining configurations depend on it, either image-only or multimodal. 2) What this tests: config_011 keeps the current best profile setting and aggregation (multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps the RNA PCA input for ResNet50 image features. This isolates the effect of modality and shows how useful image features are on their own. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: the result decides how to spend the rest of the budget. If images are strong or comparable to RNA, the multimodal fusion experiments become a priority. If images are weak, the budget should go to RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and aggregation choices. This one comparison reduces more uncertainty than a further RNA-side tweak would.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 tested an image-only model (ResNet50 features) with multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation, keeping the profile setting and aggregation of llm_summary_002 but replacing the RNA PCA input with image features. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.494 and F1 of 0.453, below the matched RNA-only multiprofile model (0.523 / 0.508) and slightly below the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.507 / 0.455). This is an initial signal that ResNet50 image features alone are somewhat weaker than PCA RNA features in this setup, but they still perform at a broadly comparable level. The results come from single runs with no variance estimate, so the gap may partly reflect noise. It also remains unknown whether image features add complementary information under fusion, or whether other image encoders or aggregation methods would change the comparison.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool RNA-PCA (config_002, 0.523 accuracy / 0.508 F1) slightly beat single-profile RNA. Image-only ResNet50 with the same multiprofile avgpool setting (config_011, 0.494 / 0.453) was somewhat weaker but in a comparable range. These are single runs, so the gaps are small and uncertain. The biggest open question is whether the two modalities carry complementary information. 2. Test: config_018 keeps the exact multiprofile, avgpool, PCA and ResNet50 setup of both unimodal runs and only combines them with simple concat fusion. This gives a clean comparison against both config_002 and config_011, isolating the effect of adding the second modality. 3. Why now: Whether to pursue multimodal configurations at all decides how much of the search space is worth exploring. Answering it with the simplest fusion method, both unimodal baselines already measured and no other variable changed, is the most informative use of the next experiment. Encoder choice (scVI, scGPT, ViT) and transformer aggregation can be tested afterward against whichever setting proves stronger.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 tested a multimodal model that concatenates PCA RNA features (pca_n2000) and ResNet50 image features, using multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation and changing nothing else from the matched unimodal runs (RNA-only llm_summary_002: 0.523 / 0.508; image-only llm_summary_003: 0.494 / 0.453). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.579 and F1 of 0.563, about +0.056 accuracy and +0.055 F1 over the stronger RNA-only model. Because only the added modality differs, this is an initial signal that the two modalities may carry complementary information under simple concat fusion, which supports further exploration of multimodal configurations. However, all results are single runs with no variance estimate. It also remains unknown whether the gain persists with other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image encoders (ViT), transformer aggregation, or alternative fusion methods.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is the multimodal multiprofile PCA+ResNet50 model with avgpool and concat (config_018: 0.579 accuracy / 0.563 F1). It beats both matched unimodal runs. Image-only ResNet50 was the weakest model (0.494), so the image representation is a likely bottleneck. Whether a stronger image encoder helps is untested. 2. Test: config_024 changes only the image encoder, ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps the RNA encoder, multiprofile setting, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion fixed. This isolates the effect of image representation inside the best-performing setup. 3. Why now: it exploits the promising multimodal direction while answering a key design question with a single controlled change. If ViT-L improves results, later aggregation and fusion comparisons can build on the better encoder. If it does not, image-encoder choice is likely less important than RNA encoder, aggregation or fusion, which can be tested next. Single-run noise means a small difference should be treated cautiously.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 tested a multimodal multiprofile model with PCA RNA features (pca_n2000), ImageNet ViT-L image features, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. Its only change from the previous best, llm_summary_004 (ResNet50: 0.579 accuracy / 0.563 F1), was the image encoder. It reached 0.632 validation accuracy and 0.607 F1, gains of about +0.052 accuracy and +0.044 F1. This makes it the best configuration so far and an initial signal that a stronger image representation helps within this fused setup, consistent with the image branch having been a bottleneck. However, all results are single runs with no variance estimate. The ViT-L encoder has not been tested image-only, so it is unclear whether the gain reflects better standalone image features or better complementarity with RNA. It is also unknown whether the improvement holds with other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), transformer aggregation, or alternative fusion methods.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ViT-L image, avgpool, concat) at 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. Three earlier signals support this setup: multiprofile input helped, adding images helped, and a stronger image encoder helped. Aggregation, however, has only ever been tested as avgpool, so whether learned aggregation helps is unknown. 2) What this tests: config_026 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, within the current best setup. This isolates whether attention-based pooling across profiles adds value over simple averaging when the features are strong. 3) Why this is the best next experiment: It exploits the leading configuration while answering an untested design question with a clean one-factor comparison. The multiprofile gain suggests that how profiles are combined matters, so this has a real chance of improving the best result. Whichever way it turns out, the result will guide whether later runs, such as those testing RNA encoders or weighted fusion, should use transformer or avgpool aggregation.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 tested replacing avgpool with transformer aggregation in the previous best configuration (llm_summary_005: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA pca_n2000 RNA, ImageNet ViT-L image, concat fusion; 0.632 accuracy / 0.607 F1), changing only the aggregation. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.224 and F1 to 0.184 (about -0.41 and -0.42). This is far below every earlier run, including the single-profile RNA-only baseline (0.507), so in this setup transformer aggregation did not help and avgpool remains the better-supported choice. Because this is a single run and the drop is very large, it is unclear whether transformer aggregation is inherently worse here or whether the result reflects a training failure such as instability, poor hyperparameters, overfitting, or too little training for the added parameters. Before abandoning learned aggregation, one could rerun it or tune it, or test it in a simpler setting such as RNA-only multiprofile.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best configuration is config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ViT-L image, avgpool, concat; 0.632 accuracy / 0.607 F1). The history so far suggests three things. Multiprofile avgpool helps a little. Adding the image modality helps. A stronger image encoder helps. Transformer aggregation failed badly in this setup, so avgpool is the better-supported choice for now. Fusion method has never been varied; every multimodal run used concat. 2) Test: config_025 changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted, and keeps every other setting from the current best. This isolates the effect of fusion directly. It tells us whether adaptively weighting the two modalities improves on simple concatenation now that both modality branches are reasonably strong. 3) Why now: fusion is a binary choice, so this one run fully answers that question in the most promising context. It is also a low-risk exploitation step that could raise the best score. RNA encoder is the other main untested axis, but scVI and scGPT are two alternatives. Settling fusion first gives a firmer reference point for those later one-factor RNA encoder comparisons. Transformer aggregation is better revisited later in a simpler setting such as config_003. As with earlier runs, a small difference here should not be overinterpreted, since there is no variance estimate.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 tested weighted fusion instead of concat in the previous best configuration (llm_summary_005: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA pca_n2000 RNA, ImageNet ViT-L image, avgpool aggregation; 0.632 accuracy / 0.607 F1), changing only the fusion method. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.328 and F1 to 0.288 (about -0.30 and -0.32). This is below every earlier run except the transformer-aggregation run (0.224), and well below the single-modality models (RNA-only multiprofile 0.523, image-only ResNet50 0.494), so concat remains the better-supported fusion choice in this setup. Because this is a single run with no variance estimate and the drop is very large, it is unclear whether weighted fusion is inherently worse here or whether the result reflects a training or implementation failure such as unstable or collapsed modality weights or poor hyperparameters. That uncertainty means weighted fusion should not yet be ruled out entirely, but llm_summary_005 remains the reference point for the untested RNA encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT).

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best configuration so far is config_024 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ViT-L image, avgpool, concat), at 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1. Changing its aggregation (transformer) or its fusion (weighted) each caused a large collapse in performance, so avgpool and concat are the better-supported choices for now. The RNA encoder is the main design choice not yet tested: every run so far has used PCA. Earlier, upgrading the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L gave about +0.05 accuracy. That suggests representation quality matters, and the RNA branch may now be the bottleneck. 2. What this tests: config_048 keeps config_024 exactly and changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA to scGPT. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation improves the fused model, in the same way the stronger image encoder did. 3. Why this is the best use of the next experiment: It exploits the strongest known setup while answering the largest remaining open question with a clean single-factor comparison. It also avoids spending budget on aggregation or fusion variants that have just failed. The scVI variant (config_036) is the natural follow-up if scGPT does not help, and an image-only ViT-L run (config_014) could later separate standalone image strength from RNA-image complementarity.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 tested an scGPT RNA encoder in place of PCA (pca_n2000) within the previous best configuration (llm_summary_005: multimodal, multiprofile, ImageNet ViT-L image, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion; 0.632 accuracy / 0.607 F1), changing only the RNA encoder. It reached 0.721 validation accuracy and 0.681 F1 (about +0.089 and +0.075), making it the best configuration so far. Because only the RNA encoder changed, this is a single-factor signal that a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation helps in this fused setup, consistent with the RNA branch having been a bottleneck after the image encoder upgrade. However, this is a single run with no variance estimate, so the size of the gain is uncertain. Several questions also remain open: scGPT has not been tested RNA-only, so it is unclear whether the gain reflects stronger standalone RNA features or better complementarity with ViT-L image features; scVI is still untested; and it is unknown whether the improvement holds under other aggregation or fusion choices.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The RNA encoder has had the largest single-factor effect so far. Swapping PCA for scGPT in the best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L image, avgpool, concat) raised accuracy from 0.632 to 0.721 and F1 from 0.607 to 0.681. However, scVI, the third RNA encoder, has never been tested, so we do not know whether the gain is specific to the scGPT foundation model or would come from any learned RNA representation. Transformer aggregation (0.224) and weighted fusion (0.328) both failed badly in single runs. That makes avgpool with concat the reliable backbone to hold fixed. 2. What this tests: config_036 changes only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200, keeping everything else identical to config_048 and config_024. This gives a clean three-way comparison of PCA, scVI and scGPT within the strongest setup. It shows whether the RNA improvement comes from learned representations in general or from scGPT pretraining in particular. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It fills the largest remaining gap on the most impactful design axis. It also has a realistic chance of matching or beating the current best, so it serves both exploration and exploitation. Other questions are lower priority right now: whether scGPT helps on its own (RNA-only config_008), whether ViT-L is strong on its own, and whether multiprofile helps at the top setting. Each of those can follow once the encoder choice is settled.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 tested scVI (scvi_n200) as the RNA encoder in the strongest backbone (multimodal, multiprofile, ImageNet ViT-L image, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion), changing only the RNA encoder from the PCA run (llm_summary_005: 0.632 accuracy / 0.607 F1) and the scGPT run (llm_summary_008: 0.721 / 0.681). Validation accuracy collapsed to 0.208 and F1 to 0.172, the lowest of all runs and below every single-modality model. Within this setup, a learned RNA representation alone therefore did not reproduce the scGPT gain, and scGPT remains the best-supported RNA encoder. However, this is a single run with no variance estimate, and the collapse is similar in size to the transformer-aggregation (0.224) and weighted-fusion (0.328) failures, so it may reflect a training or pipeline failure rather than weak scVI features. Possible causes include the low 200-dimensional embedding being swamped by the high-dimensional ViT-L features under concat, scaling or normalization mismatch, or poor hyperparameters. An RNA-only scVI run or a rerun would help separate encoder quality from an integration failure before ruling scVI out.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_048 (scGPT + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat: 0.721 accuracy / 0.681 F1). Swapping PCA for scGPT gave the largest single-factor gain (+0.089 accuracy). scGPT has never been run without images, so we cannot tell whether that gain comes from strong standalone RNA features or from complementarity with ViT-L. Other changes to this backbone (scVI, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) collapsed. That makes it more valuable to anchor what works than to probe fragile variants. 2) Test: config_008 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scGPT, avgpool) removes only the image branch from config_048. With PCA, adding images gave about +0.11 over RNA-only. If scGPT-only nearly matches 0.721, the image modality adds little once RNA is strong, and the RNA encoder is the dominant factor. If it falls well below, multimodal complementarity holds with a strong RNA encoder. It also gives a direct scGPT vs PCA comparison in the RNA-only setting (vs config_002, 0.523). 3) Why now: this single-factor ablation tests a core design question, whether multimodality is necessary, rather than assuming it. It could also produce a competitive, simpler model. It is a better use of budget than retesting configurations that already failed or than the single-profile ablation, which can follow next.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 tested an RNA-only scGPT model (multiprofile, avgpool, no image encoder or fusion), removing only the ImageNet ViT-L image branch from the best configuration, llm_summary_008 (0.721 accuracy / 0.681 F1). It reached 0.536 validation accuracy and 0.516 F1, about 0.185 accuracy below the fused model and only marginally above the matched RNA-only PCA run (llm_summary_002: 0.523 / 0.508; +0.013 accuracy, +0.008 F1), a gap that may fall within run-to-run noise. This is an initial signal that multimodality remains important even with a strong RNA encoder, and that scGPT's large gain in the fused setup is not matched by a comparable standalone RNA-only advantage over PCA, which is consistent with scGPT and ViT-L features combining well under concat rather than scGPT simply being a much stronger standalone encoder. However, these are single runs with no variance estimates, and ViT-L has not been tested image-only, so how much of the fused performance comes from ViT-L features alone versus a genuine scGPT–image interaction remains unresolved.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about how well any modality performs, which RNA or image encoder is better, or whether multiprofile aggregation or fusion helps. 2. What this tests: config_001 is the simplest RNA-only, single-profile model using a standard PCA encoder. It sets a reference point for validation accuracy and F1. Each later design choice can then be added one at a time against it: a learned RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), the image modality, and fusion. 3. Why now: Under a limited budget, a clean, low-complexity baseline makes every later comparison interpretable as a single-variable change. It also guards against assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models will win. Starting with a complex configuration would mix several factors together and make its result hard to attribute.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA RNA encoder (pca_n2000), no image encoder, no aggregation and no fusion. It was chosen as a low-complexity reference point. It reached validation accuracy 0.523 and validation F1 0.508, and the similar values suggest performance is fairly balanced across classes. Because no other experiments have been run, this is a baseline only. We cannot yet say whether this level is strong or weak, or whether learned RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, the image modality or fusion would do better. Run-to-run variance is unknown, so small differences from this baseline in later single-variable comparisons should be read cautiously.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.523 accuracy and 0.508 F1. We know nothing yet about the image modality, which half of the search space depends on, including every multimodal and fusion configuration. 2) This test: config_010 runs the simplest image-only setup (single-profile, ResNet50, no aggregation, no fusion). It is a direct modality comparison against config_001 at matched complexity, with no confounding from aggregation or fusion. 3) Why now: knowing whether images alone are weaker than, comparable to, or stronger than RNA tells us whether the many multimodal configurations are worth budget, and which modality to prioritize when testing encoders. Comparing RNA encoders (e.g., config_004) is also useful, but it only refines one branch. The modality question reduces more uncertainty across the whole search space.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested the simplest image-only setup: single-profile, ResNet50 image encoder, no RNA encoder, no aggregation and no fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.706 and F1 0.667, well above the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.523 / 0.508). This initial observation suggests the image modality carries substantial predictive signal and supports giving image-containing and multimodal configurations search budget. However, the comparison changes both modality and encoder type (ResNet50 vs. PCA), so it does not show that images are inherently stronger than RNA (a learned RNA encoder might close the gap); it is also a single run with unknown variance, and the wider accuracy–F1 gap (about 0.04 vs. about 0.015) may indicate less balanced per-class performance. Whether other image encoders, multiprofile aggregation or fusion with RNA improve on this result remains untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Two single-profile baselines exist. Image-only ResNet50 reached 0.706 accuracy (F1 0.667). RNA-only PCA reached 0.523 (F1 0.508). So images carry strong signal and PCA RNA is weaker. What we don't know is whether RNA adds information that images lack, or whether it only adds noise. 2. Test: config_016 combines the two encoders already measured (PCA RNA and ResNet50) with simple concat fusion, in the same single-profile setting with no aggregation. Fusion is the only new element, so the result isolates the effect of adding RNA to the image model. A gain, especially in F1, would suggest the modalities are complementary and that multimodal branches deserve budget. No gain or a drop would suggest focusing on image-side choices (encoder, multiprofile aggregation) or on better RNA encoders before fusing. 3. Value: Modality is the largest branching factor in the remaining space, since most untested configurations are multimodal. Testing it with the simplest fusion and known components gives clean evidence for allocating the limited remaining budget. Run-to-run variance is unknown, so a small difference should not be overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested the simplest multimodal setup: single-profile, PCA RNA encoder (pca_n2000) plus ResNet50 image encoder, concat fusion and no aggregation. It combined the two components already tested alone, so that the effect of adding RNA to the image model could be isolated. It reached validation accuracy 0.227 and F1 0.191, far below both the image-only baseline (llm_summary_002: 0.706 / 0.667) and the RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.523 / 0.508), so this concat-fused configuration performed worse than either modality alone. A drop this large, below even the weaker unimodal model, is more consistent with a failure of this specific fusion setup (for example, feature-scale mismatch between PCA and ResNet50 features, or an optimization or training problem) than with RNA simply adding mild noise, but the available evidence cannot tell these explanations apart. It also remains untested whether other fusion methods, feature normalization, learned RNA encoders or multiprofile aggregation would make multimodal models competitive. This is a single run with unknown variance, but the gap is large enough that it is unlikely to be noise alone.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: image-only ResNet50 (0.706 / 0.667) clearly beats RNA-only PCA (0.523 / 0.508). However, multimodal PCA+ResNet50 with concat fusion collapsed to 0.227 / 0.191, well below either modality alone. That drop points to a problem with this specific fusion setup, such as feature-scale mismatch or an optimization issue. The data cannot yet show whether the problem is concat itself or multimodal fusion in general. 2) What this tests: config_017 keeps everything the same (single-profile, PCA, ResNet50) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. If weighted fusion recovers to near or above image-only, the failure was specific to concat. If it also collapses, the problem is likely in combining these features or in the multimodal pipeline itself. 3) Why it is the best use of budget: most of the remaining configurations (about 36 of 48) are multimodal and depend on this fusion question. Settling it now decides whether that large region deserves budget or whether search should focus on image-only extensions such as multiprofile aggregation or ViT-L. Neither of those directions has failed, so they can be tested next.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the failed multimodal configuration fixed (single-profile, pca_n2000 RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, no aggregation) and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted fusion. Weighted fusion reached validation accuracy 0.650 and F1 0.628, recovering sharply from the concat run (llm_summary_003: 0.227 / 0.191) and exceeding RNA-only (llm_summary_001: 0.523 / 0.508). It still fell below image-only ResNet50 (llm_summary_002: 0.706 / 0.667). Because fusion was the only change, this single-variable comparison suggests the concat collapse was tied to concat fusion in this setup rather than to multimodal combination of these features in general, so the multimodal region remains viable. However, adding PCA RNA features through either fusion method has not yet beaten image-only. Open questions: why concat failed (e.g., scale mismatch vs. optimization), whether normalization, learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), stronger image encoders or multiprofile aggregation would let fusion surpass image-only, and how much of the roughly 0.056 deficit to image-only is noise, given single runs with unknown variance.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is image-only ResNet50 single-profile (0.706 accuracy / 0.667 F1). Weighted fusion recovered the multimodal model from the concat collapse but still trailed image-only. The profile setting (multiprofile with aggregation) is a major design axis that has not been tested in any modality. 2) What this tests: config_011 changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, on the strongest configuration. It isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles helps, and avgpool is the simplest aggregation, so it is a clean first test before trying transformer aggregation. 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: It reduces uncertainty about a design choice that applies to almost all remaining configurations (multiprofile accounts for most of them). It also exploits the current best direction, so it is both informative and has a reasonable chance of improving accuracy. Whatever the result, it will guide whether to spend later experiments on multiprofile multimodal variants or on encoder changes such as ViT-L or scVI.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the strongest configuration fixed (image-only, ResNet50 image encoder, no RNA encoder, no fusion) and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, as a first test of the multiprofile axis.
