It reached validation accuracy 0.586 and F1 0.574, a drop of about 0.12 accuracy from image-only single-profile (llm_summary_002: 0.706 / 0.667) and below weighted-fusion multimodal (llm_summary_004: 0.650 / 0.628), though still above RNA-only PCA (llm_summary_001: 0.523 / 0.508); the narrower accuracy–F1 gap (about 0.011 vs. about 0.039) may indicate more balanced but lower per-class performance. Because profile setting was the only change, this single-variable comparison suggests that multiprofile with avgpool aggregation hurt this image-only ResNet50 setup. The comparison cannot separate multiprofile input from the choice of avgpool, so it remains untested whether transformer aggregation, other encoders, or multimodal multiprofile variants would behave differently; this is a single run with unknown variance, although a gap this large is unlikely to be noise alone.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Image-only single-profile ResNet50 is the best result so far (0.706 acc / 0.667 F1). Adding PCA RNA has not beaten it, either with weighted fusion (0.650) or concat fusion (0.227, a collapse). Multiprofile with avgpool also hurt the image model (0.586). The image encoder is the one axis in the strongest modality that has never been tested. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. That isolates the effect of the image representation. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: it balances exploitation and exploration. It has a realistic chance of raising the performance ceiling. The answer also tells us which image backbone to use in the remaining multimodal and multiprofile configurations, so it covers many of them at once. Aggregation (transformer vs. avgpool) and learned RNA encoders remain important open questions. Each of those, however, applies to settings that currently trail the single-profile image baseline, so they are better tested afterward.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best configuration fixed (image-only, single-profile, no RNA encoder, no aggregation, no fusion) and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, to isolate the effect of the image backbone. It reached validation accuracy 0.721 and F1 0.681, a new best that slightly exceeds image-only ResNet50 (llm_summary_002: 0.706 / 0.667). The accuracy–F1 gap (about 0.039) is similar to ResNet50's, which suggests a comparable per-class balance. Because the encoder was the only change, this single-variable comparison tentatively favors ViT-L, but the gain is small (about 0.014 accuracy, 0.014 F1) and comes from single runs with unknown variance, so it may fall within run-to-run noise and should not be treated as a decisive backbone advantage. It remains untested whether ViT-L also helps in the multimodal (weighted fusion) and multiprofile (avgpool or transformer aggregation) settings, and whether it changes how much RNA adds. Other image encoders and learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) are also unexplored, and repeat runs would help establish whether the ViT-L edge is real.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: the RNA encoder is the largest untested design axis. RNA has only been tried with PCA (0.523 / 0.508). Every multimodal run so far used PCA RNA features. Concat fusion collapsed (0.227) and weighted fusion (0.650) still trails image-only (ResNet50 0.706; ViT-L 0.721 / 0.681). So it is unclear whether RNA is weak in itself or only weak as PCA features. 2) What this tests: config_004 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA to scVI, in the simplest setting (RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation, no fusion). This isolates whether a learned RNA representation substantially improves the RNA signal. 3) Why now: the result decides how to spend the remaining budget on many multimodal configurations. If scVI greatly improves RNA-only, scVI-based weighted fusion (e.g., config_035) becomes a strong candidate to beat image-only. If it does not, the budget should shift toward image encoders and aggregation. The ViT-L versus ResNet50 gain is small, so exploiting it now would add less information than resolving the RNA encoder question.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the simplest RNA-only setup fixed (single-profile, no image encoder, no aggregation, no fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200, to test whether a learned RNA representation strengthens the RNA signal. It reached validation accuracy 0.260 and F1 0.222, roughly half of the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.523 / 0.508) and far below image-only ViT-L (llm_summary_006: 0.721 / 0.681). This single-variable comparison suggests that scVI did not improve RNA-only performance in this setup. The result weakens the case for scVI-based weighted fusion (e.g., config_035) as a route to beating image-only and supports shifting budget toward image encoders and aggregation. The comparison cannot separate scVI as a method from its specific settings (n200 latent size vs. 2000 PCA components, scVI training quality, possible optimization failure), and the drop's similarity in size to the concat collapse (0.227) raises the possibility of a training or pipeline problem. This is a single run with unknown variance, though a gap this large is unlikely to be noise alone. Other RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT, other scVI dimensionalities) and scVI's behavior inside weighted fusion remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Image-only single-profile is the strongest region so far (ViT-L 0.721, ResNet50 0.706). Moving ResNet50 image-only to multiprofile with avgpool cut accuracy by about 0.12 (0.586). That run cannot tell whether multiprofile input itself hurts or whether avgpool is a poor way to aggregate profiles. Transformer aggregation is completely untested, and the multiprofile/aggregation axis covers more than half of the remaining configurations. 2) What this tests: config_012 keeps the config_011 setup fixed (image-only, ResNet50, multiprofile) and changes only aggregation from avgpool to transformer. If it recovers to or beats about 0.706, the avgpool choice was the problem and transformer-aggregated multiprofile variants (including ViT-L and multimodal weighted-fusion ones) become worth exploring. If it stays near 0.59 or lower, the multiprofile setting probably hurts in general, and most multiprofile configurations can be deprioritized. 3) Why now: this single-variable comparison resolves uncertainty about a design axis that governs a large share of the remaining space. That is more efficient than a small exploitation step such as ViT-L weighted fusion, or testing scGPT, whose RNA-only results so far (PCA 0.523, scVI 0.260) suggest limited upside.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the image-only, ResNet50, multiprofile setup of llm_summary_005 fixed and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, to test whether avgpool explained the multiprofile drop. It reached validation accuracy 0.629 and F1 0.599, which partly recovers from avgpool (llm_summary_005: 0.586 / 0.574) but remains well below image-only single-profile ResNet50 (llm_summary_002: 0.706 / 0.667) and ViT-L (llm_summary_006: 0.721 / 0.681), and slightly below weighted-fusion multimodal (llm_summary_004: 0.650 / 0.628). The result falls between the two outcomes anticipated when the experiment was selected. The single-variable comparison tentatively suggests that transformer aggregation helps relative to avgpool (about +0.043 accuracy), but a deficit of about 0.08 to single-profile remains, so in this setup multiprofile input appears to underperform with either aggregator, and the multiprofile region looks less promising than single-profile without being clearly ruled out. Uncertainties: these are single runs with unknown variance, so the size of the aggregation gain is not firmly established; the accuracy–F1 gap widened again (about 0.029 vs. about 0.011 for avgpool); and it is untested whether ViT-L, other transformer settings or multimodal weighted-fusion multiprofile variants would close the gap to single-profile.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Image-only single-profile is the strongest region so far (ViT-L 0.721, ResNet50 0.706). Adding PCA RNA features through weighted fusion has not beaten image-only (0.650). scVI RNA-only collapsed (0.260 vs. 0.523 for PCA). scGPT is the only RNA encoder not yet tested, and it appears in 15 of the remaining configurations, including 12 multimodal ones. It is therefore the largest unresolved question about representation. 2. What this tests: config_007 changes only the RNA encoder relative to the PCA RNA-only baseline (config_001) and the scVI run (config_004). It isolates whether scGPT gives a stronger RNA signal. A clearly better result would make scGPT-based weighted fusion a credible route to beating image-only. A weak result would argue for concentrating the remaining budget on image encoders and the PCA or ViT-L fusion region. A low result would also help show whether the scVI failure reflects learned RNA encoders in general or a scVI-specific problem. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: This cheap single-variable experiment resolves uncertainty for a large block of the search space before budget is spent on complex scGPT multimodal or multiprofile runs. Exploiting with ViT-L plus PCA weighted fusion (config_023) can still follow and is expected to be informative, but prior evidence suggests PCA fusion tends to trail image-only.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the RNA-only, single-profile setup fixed (no image encoder, aggregation or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder to scGPT, allowing direct comparison with PCA (llm_summary_001: 0.523 / 0.508) and scVI (llm_summary_007: 0.260 / 0.222). scGPT reached validation accuracy 0.688 and F1 0.659. That is about 0.165 above PCA and far above scVI, approaches image-only ResNet50 (0.706 / 0.667), trails the best result, image-only ViT-L (0.721 / 0.681), and exceeds PCA+ResNet50 weighted fusion (0.650 / 0.628). This single-variable comparison suggests scGPT gives a much stronger RNA representation than PCA or scVI in this setup, so the scVI collapse does not appear to reflect learned RNA encoders in general, and scGPT-based weighted fusion (e.g., with ViT-L) is now a credible candidate for beating image-only. Uncertainties remain: these are single runs with unknown variance; the accuracy–F1 gap is about 0.029, compared with about 0.015 for PCA; and it is untested whether scGPT features complement image features or would hit the fusion problems seen with concat. It is also still unresolved whether scVI failed because of its specific settings or a training or pipeline issue.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scGPT gave a much stronger RNA-only result (0.688/0.659) than PCA (0.523) or scVI (0.260). The best model so far is image-only ViT-L (0.721/0.681), with ResNet50 close behind (0.706). Weighted fusion is the only fusion method that has worked: PCA+ResNet50 reached 0.650, while concat collapsed. The open question is whether a strong RNA representation adds complementary signal to image features or still drags fusion below image-only, as PCA did. 2) This run adds scGPT through weighted fusion to the best image-only setup (single-profile ViT-L), so it compares directly with config_013 (image-only ViT-L) and config_007 (scGPT-only). It tests whether multimodal fusion with a strong RNA encoder can beat the best unimodal model. Weighted fusion avoids the known concat failure, and single-profile avoids the multiprofile drop seen in both aggregation tests. 3) This is the most promising direction the evidence points to and has the highest expected chance of a new best. It also answers the key design question of whether RNA adds value once its representation is strong. If it underperforms, config_041 (scGPT+ResNet50 weighted) can then isolate the RNA-encoder effect against config_017.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 combined the two strongest unimodal components, scGPT RNA and ImageNet ViT-L image encoders, with weighted fusion in a single-profile setting with no aggregation. It tested whether a strong RNA representation adds complementary signal to the best image-only model. It reached validation accuracy 0.527 and F1 0.510. That is far below both of its unimodal components (image-only ViT-L, llm_summary_006: 0.721 / 0.681; scGPT-only, llm_summary_009: 0.688 / 0.659) and below PCA+ResNet50 weighted fusion (llm_summary_004: 0.650 / 0.628), so in this setup fusion did not merely fail to help but substantially hurt, by about 0.19 relative to image-only ViT-L. A drop below even the weaker unimodal component, like the concat collapse, is more consistent with a problem specific to fusing these features (for example, scale or dimensionality mismatch between scGPT and ViT-L embeddings, poorly learned fusion weights, or a training or pipeline issue) than with RNA simply adding mild noise, but the evidence cannot distinguish these explanations. Because both encoders differ from the earlier PCA+ResNet50 weighted run, the cause cannot be attributed to either encoder alone; a scGPT+ResNet50 weighted run (e.g., config_041) or a PCA+ViT-L weighted run would help isolate it, and this remains a single run with unknown variance.

selection_reason: 1. No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000, no aggregation or fusion) sets a simple baseline. Every later design choice can be compared against it one factor at a time: learned RNA encoders (scvi, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image-only models, and multimodal fusion. 3. Under a limited budget, a cheap, interpretable reference point is the most useful first experiment. It lets later gains be attributed to specific design changes, and it avoids assuming that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models will do better.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) set a simple RNA-only, single-profile baseline using a PCA RNA encoder (pca_n2000), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.518 (primary metric) and validation F1 0.484 (supporting). The slightly lower F1 may indicate uneven performance across classes. No other experiments exist yet, so this is an initial reference point and gives no evidence on which design choices matter. It is still unknown whether learned RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image-based models, or multimodal fusion would improve on it, and run-to-run variance has not been measured.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.518, F1 0.484). It tells us nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2. Test: config_002 keeps the same modality and encoder (RNA-only, pca_n2000) and switches only to multiprofile input with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles helps, without confounding it with encoder or modality changes. 3. Why now: Multiprofile is the setting for most of the remaining configurations, including most multimodal ones. Settling whether it helps first will guide many later choices. Using avgpool before the transformer gives a low-complexity reference point, so any later gain from transformer aggregation can be judged against it.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only pca_n2000 setup from llm_summary_001 and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile input with simple average pooling (avgpool), with no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.518 to 0.653 (primary metric), and F1 rose from 0.484 to 0.628 (supporting), which suggests that multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation helps in this RNA-only PCA setting. Multiprofile input and avgpool were introduced together, so their separate contributions cannot be told apart. The comparison also rests on single runs with unmeasured run-to-run variance. It remains unknown whether the gain carries over to learned RNA encoders, image or multimodal models, or whether stronger aggregation (e.g., a transformer) improves on this avgpool reference.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Within RNA-only PCA, multiprofile input with avgpool clearly beat single-profile (accuracy 0.653 vs 0.518, F1 0.628 vs 0.484). These are single runs with unknown variance. Nothing is known yet about the image modality, and image settings appear in 42 of the 49 untested configurations (6 image-only, 36 multimodal). 2) Test: This experiment keeps the best-known setting (multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps RNA for image (resnet50). That isolates how much signal images alone carry, and whether the multiprofile setting looks useful beyond RNA. 3) Why now: Knowing whether images are weak, comparable or strong determines whether spending budget on multimodal fusion and the costlier ViT-L encoder is worthwhile. That makes it more informative right now than refining RNA aggregation or encoder choice, which can follow.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 was the first image-only run: a resnet50 image encoder with multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation, no RNA encoder and no fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.639 (primary) and F1 0.620 (supporting), roughly comparable to the RNA-only pca_n2000 multiprofile/avgpool run (0.653 / 0.628) and well above the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.518 / 0.484), so images alone appear to carry substantial signal. The 0.014 accuracy gap to RNA is small and rests on single runs with unmeasured variance, so it should not be read as RNA being reliably stronger. Several questions remain open: whether multiprofile/avgpool helps the image modality (no single-profile image run exists), whether image and RNA signals are complementary enough to benefit from fusion, and how other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) or stronger aggregation would compare.

selection_reason: Evidence: multiprofile input with avgpool clearly beat single-profile for RNA (pca_n2000: 0.653 vs 0.518 accuracy). Image-only resnet50 under the same multiprofile/avgpool setting reached a similar 0.639. So both modalities carry substantial signal on their own, and the 0.014 gap between them is within plausible run-to-run noise. The biggest open question is whether RNA and image signals are complementary. This experiment tests that directly. It combines the two components already measured under identical profile and aggregation settings (pca_n2000 + resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool) and joins them with simple concat fusion. The change versus the unimodal runs is therefore limited to adding the second modality. If accuracy and F1 clearly exceed about 0.65, multimodal fusion becomes the main direction to exploit, and follow-ups like weighted fusion, transformer aggregation, or other encoders can build on it. If it does not, the budget can shift toward better unimodal encoders or aggregation. Either outcome informs the largest remaining part of the search space, so it is a better use of the next run than a narrower encoder or aggregation tweak.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 combined the two previously tested unimodal components, pca_n2000 RNA and resnet50 image, under the same multiprofile/avgpool setting and joined them with simple concat fusion, so the only change from the unimodal runs was adding the second modality. It reached validation accuracy 0.706 (primary) and F1 0.667 (supporting), above both RNA-only (0.653 / 0.628) and image-only (0.639 / 0.620). This suggests RNA and image signals are at least partly complementary and makes multimodal fusion a promising direction to build on. The roughly 0.05 accuracy gain over the best unimodal run rests on single runs with unmeasured variance, and F1 rose less than accuracy (it is only slightly above the ~0.65 threshold set in advance), which may point to uneven per-class gains. It remains unknown whether weighted or other fusion methods, stronger aggregation (e.g., a transformer), or different RNA/image encoders would add to this concat baseline.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Multiprofile input with avgpool clearly helped RNA-only (0.518 to 0.653). Concat fusion of pca_n2000 and resnet50 under multiprofile/avgpool is the current best (0.706 accuracy, 0.667 F1), above both unimodal runs. Every multiprofile run so far has used avgpool, so it is still unknown whether a learned aggregator does better. 2) Test: config_020 keeps config_018 fixed and changes only aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. This isolates the effect of aggregation strength within the best-performing setup. 3) Why now: Aggregation affects every multiprofile model (RNA, image and multimodal), so the answer will guide many later choices. It also extends the strongest direction found so far, so it serves both exploitation and uncertainty reduction. Fusion type (config_019) and encoder swaps (config_024, config_030) are natural follow-ups once the aggregation question is settled. Any gain or loss should be read cautiously, since run-to-run variance has not been measured.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_004: multimodal pca_n2000 + resnet50, multiprofile, concat fusion) and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer aggregator. Validation accuracy collapsed from 0.706 to 0.260 (primary) and F1 fell from 0.667 to 0.222 (supporting), well below even the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.518 / 0.484). Because aggregation was the only change, this is evidence that the transformer aggregator, as configured here, underperforms avgpool in this setup. However, the drop is so large that it may reflect a training or optimization failure (e.g., hyperparameters, training length, or instability on this data size) rather than a fundamental weakness of learned aggregation, and it comes from a single run with unmeasured variance. It remains unknown whether a tuned or re-run transformer would recover, whether the same degradation appears in RNA-only or image-only multiprofile models, and avgpool should remain the reference aggregation for now while fusion and encoder follow-ups are explored.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_018 (multimodal pca_n2000 + resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat; acc 0.706, F1 0.667). It beat both unimodal runs, so RNA and image signals look complementary. Swapping avgpool for a transformer collapsed performance (0.260), so avgpool stays the reference aggregation. Fusion method is a core design choice that has not been tested at all: only concat has been run. 2) Test: config_019 changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted, keeping the encoders, multiprofile input and avgpool fixed. This cleanly isolates the effect of fusion on the strongest setup. Weighted fusion could also help with the smaller F1 gain, since it lets the model rebalance the modality contributions. 3) Why now: it exploits the most promising direction with a single-variable change, so the result is interpretable whichever way it goes. It also tells us which fusion to carry forward into later encoder comparisons (ViT-L, scVI, scGPT). The transformer-failure diagnostic can wait, because avgpool is already a working reference.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 took the best configuration so far (llm_summary_004: multimodal pca_n2000 + resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) and changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted. Validation accuracy fell from 0.706 to 0.530 (primary) and F1 fell from 0.667 to 0.515 (supporting). This is below both unimodal multiprofile runs (RNA 0.653, image 0.639) and only slightly above the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.518). Because fusion was the only change, this is evidence that weighted fusion, as configured here, underperforms concat in this setup, so concat should remain the reference fusion for upcoming encoder comparisons (e.g., ViT-L, scVI, scGPT). Still, the result comes from a single run with unmeasured variance, and falling below either modality alone suggests a possible optimization or weighting problem (e.g., poorly learned or collapsed modality weights, or hyperparameters) rather than an inherent limit of weighted fusion; whether a tuned weighted or other fusion method could match or beat concat remains unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal pca_n2000 + resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat; acc 0.706, F1 0.667). Changing the aggregation to a transformer (0.260) or the fusion to weighted (0.530) each hurt sharply. These are single runs and may reflect optimization failures, but for now avgpool and concat are the reference choices. Encoder choice is the main design axis not yet tested; all runs so far used pca_n2000 and resnet50. 2. Test: config_024 keeps the best configuration and changes only the image encoder, from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. Any difference can therefore be attributed to image representation quality within the fusion setup that works best. 3. Why now: It exploits the strongest direction while answering a one-variable encoder question. If ViT-L helps, it becomes the new reference for later RNA-encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT). If it does not, resnet50 stays the default and the remaining budget can go to RNA encoders. Small gaps will be read cautiously, with F1 as supporting evidence.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_004: multimodal pca_n2000 RNA, multiprofile, avgpool, concat; 0.706 / 0.667) and changed only the image encoder, from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. Validation accuracy fell to 0.535 (primary) and F1 to 0.519 (supporting). That is below both unimodal multiprofile runs (RNA 0.653, resnet50 image 0.639) and only slightly above the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.518), so resnet50 should stay the reference image encoder for upcoming RNA-encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT). Because the image encoder was the only change, this is evidence that ViT-L, as configured here, underperforms resnet50 in this concat/avgpool setup. Still, this is a single run with unmeasured variance, and a multimodal model scoring below either modality alone points to a possible optimization or integration problem (e.g., embedding dimensionality or scale mismatch with the PCA features under concat, or hyperparameters) rather than worse image features. No image-only ViT-L run exists to separate the encoder's standalone quality from how it interacts with fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_018 (pca_n2000 + resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat; 0.706 accuracy / 0.667 F1). Three single-factor swaps away from it all performed much worse: transformer aggregation, weighted fusion and the ViT-L image encoder. So avgpool, concat and resnet50 are the current reference choices. The RNA encoder is the one major design axis not yet tested; only PCA has been tried. 2) This run changes only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200, and keeps everything else as in config_018. It shows whether a learned RNA representation adds to or weakens the complementary RNA-image signal under concat fusion. Because scVI's 200 dimensions are far fewer than PCA's 2000, it also gives indirect evidence on the dimension-mismatch explanation raised for the ViT-L failure. 3) It is a clean one-factor comparison against the strongest configuration, so it combines exploitation (it could beat 0.706) with exploration of the last untested axis. The result also decides whether to try scGPT next or to return to unimodal diagnostics.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_004: multimodal, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat; 0.706 / 0.667) and changed only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. Validation accuracy fell to 0.520 (primary) and F1 to 0.498 (supporting). That is below both unimodal multiprofile runs (RNA PCA 0.653, resnet50 image 0.639) and about level with the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.518). Because only the RNA encoder changed, this is evidence that scVI, as configured here, underperforms PCA in this concat/avgpool setup, so pca_n2000 should stay the reference RNA encoder. Still, every single-factor swap away from llm_summary_004 has now landed near 0.52–0.53 accuracy (transformer aggregation was lower, at 0.26), with multimodal scores below either modality alone. That pattern could mean a shared optimization or integration fragility (e.g., embedding scale or dimensionality imbalance under concat; 200-d scVI is more mismatched to resnet50's features than 2000-d PCA, but this run does not isolate dimensionality), or that the 0.706 reference is itself an optimistic single run, since run-to-run variance is unmeasured. No RNA-only scVI run exists to separate the encoder's standalone quality from its interaction with fusion, so unimodal diagnostics or repeated runs of the reference configuration may be more informative than trying scGPT next.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is multimodal pca_n2000 + resnet50 with multiprofile, avgpool and concat (0.706 accuracy / 0.667 F1). Every single-factor swap away from it has dropped to about 0.52–0.53, or to 0.26 with the transformer aggregator. Several of these multimodal runs score below either modality alone, which points to a possible fusion or integration fragility rather than a weak component. The scVI swap (config_030, 0.520) cannot tell us which explanation is right, because no RNA-only scVI run exists. 2. What this tests: config_005 is RNA-only scVI with multiprofile and avgpool, so it differs from config_002 (PCA RNA-only multiprofile avgpool, 0.653 / 0.628) only in the RNA encoder. If scVI alone performs near PCA, the multimodal drop likely comes from how the 200-d scVI features interact with resnet50 under concat fusion. If scVI alone is also weak, the encoder itself is the problem. 3. Why it is the best next use of the budget: it isolates one design factor in a cleaner setting with no fusion. It also directly tests the integration-fragility hypothesis that affects how we read the ViT-L and weighted-fusion results. This is more informative than testing scGPT or more multimodal combinations while that confound is unresolved.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 tested RNA-only scvi_n200 with multiprofile input and avgpool, and differs from llm_summary_002 (RNA-only pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool; 0.653 / 0.628) only in the RNA encoder. It reached validation accuracy 0.520 (primary) and F1 0.479 (supporting), about level with the PCA single-profile baseline (0.518 / 0.484). Because only the encoder changed, this is evidence that scVI as configured here is weaker than PCA as a standalone RNA representation. That suggests the low multimodal scVI result (llm_summary_008, 0.520) is at least partly explained by the encoder itself rather than solely by fusion fragility. Even so, the scVI + resnet50 concat run still scored below image-only resnet50 (0.639), so adding scVI failed to help and may have hurt, and an integration problem is not ruled out. This run also does not explain the ViT-L or weighted-fusion drops. It remains unclear whether scVI's weakness reflects its 200-d latent size, its training or hyperparameters, or a genuine limit of the representation, and all comparisons rest on single runs with unmeasured run-to-run variance, including the 0.706 reference.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result is multimodal pca_n2000 + resnet50 with multiprofile, avgpool and concat (0.706 accuracy / 0.667 F1). Every single-factor swap away from it has lost accuracy: weighted fusion, ViT-L, scVI and the transformer aggregator. The RNA-only scVI diagnostic (0.520 vs PCA 0.653) showed that weak multimodal results can come from a weaker encoder itself, not only from fusion fragility. scGPT is the one RNA encoder never tested in any form, so its quality is completely unknown. 2) What this tests: config_008 runs RNA-only scGPT with multiprofile input and avgpool. It differs from the RNA-only PCA run (config_002) only in the RNA encoder, so it measures scGPT's standalone quality without any fusion confound. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: It cheaply reduces the largest remaining uncertainty, an entire untested encoder. If scGPT beats PCA, the logical next step is config_042 (scGPT + resnet50 with concat), a direct extension of the best setup. If scGPT is weak, we can drop all scGPT multimodal configs without spending runs on them. The alternative, image-only ViT-L (config_014), is also diagnostic, but ViT-L already has some evidence against it, whereas scGPT has none.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 tested RNA-only scGPT with multiprofile input and avgpool. It differs from llm_summary_002 (RNA-only pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool; 0.653 / 0.628) only in the RNA encoder, so it measures scGPT's standalone quality without a fusion confound. It reached validation accuracy 0.536 (primary) and F1 0.516 (supporting), well below PCA and only slightly above RNA-only scVI (0.520 / 0.479) and the PCA single-profile baseline (0.518). This is evidence that scGPT, as configured here, is a weaker standalone RNA representation than pca_n2000, so scGPT + resnet50 concat (config_042) looks unlikely to beat the 0.706 reference, and scGPT multimodal configs are a lower priority. Both learned RNA encoders now land near 0.52–0.54, which could reflect real limits of these embeddings or a shared issue in how they are extracted, sized or trained here; this run cannot separate those explanations. All comparisons, including the 0.706 reference, rest on single runs with unmeasured variance.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing about how hard the task is or which design choices matter. 2. Test: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest configuration available. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 against which every later choice can be compared one factor at a time: the RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT), profile setting and aggregation (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), the image modality, and multimodal fusion. 3. Why now: Starting with a complex multimodal or multiprofile model would mix several design choices together, so any result would be hard to attribute. A simple baseline is cheap, interpretable and anchors the search, letting the following experiments change one factor at a time from a known starting point.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion, chosen as the simplest reference configuration. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.688, with a validation F1 of 0.659. The F1 sits slightly below accuracy, which may hint at some unevenness in per-class performance, but this is not established. With no prior experiments for comparison, this is only an initial reference point. It does not yet show whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, the image modality, or multimodal fusion would help or hurt, and run-to-run variance is unknown, so small future differences from this baseline should be read cautiously.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.688, F1 0.659). We know nothing yet about whether the image modality carries useful signal. That matters because 36 of the 50 remaining configurations are multimodal and depend on it. 2. What this tests: An image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model, with no aggregation or fusion, sets a matched baseline for the second modality. It keeps the simple single-profile setting so the comparison with config_001 isolates modality. If image-only performs well, multimodal fusion is worth pursuing. If it performs poorly, the budget can go to RNA encoder and multiprofile questions instead. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: This is the decision with the most downstream consequence for which part of the search space to explore. Testing aggregation or RNA encoders first would refine only a small part of the space while leaving the value of the image modality unknown. One run will not settle the question, but it gives the needed second reference point at minimal cost.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion, as a second-modality reference point to compare against the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.512 (F1 0.477), about 0.18 below the RNA-only baseline's 0.688 (F1 0.659), with F1 again sitting slightly below accuracy. This suggests that, in this single-profile setting, ResNet50 image features alone carry less class signal than PCA-encoded RNA. However, the comparison changes both modality and encoder, so it does not cleanly separate the value of the image modality from the choice of ResNet50, and each configuration has only one run with unknown run-to-run variance. It remains untested whether image features add complementary information when fused with RNA, whether multiprofile aggregation changes the image-only result, or whether other image encoders would close the gap, so this low standalone result should not by itself rule out multimodal configurations.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: We have two single-profile references. RNA-only PCA reached 0.688 accuracy (F1 0.659), and image-only ResNet50 reached 0.512 (F1 0.477). The image result shows that ResNet50 features carry less signal on their own. It does not show whether they add complementary information to RNA, which is the central question for a multimodal study. Each result is a single run, so variance is unknown. 2. What this tests: config_016 adds ResNet50 image features to the config_001 baseline through simple concat fusion. It keeps the same PCA RNA encoder, single-profile setting and no aggregation. Comparing it directly with config_001 isolates the effect of adding the image modality. Using concat, the simplest fusion, avoids mixing in a fusion-strategy question. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: It changes one design factor relative to the strongest baseline and reuses both tested encoders. It addresses the highest-level fork in the search space: multimodal versus RNA-only. A clear gain would justify spending later budget on fusion type, image encoder and aggregation within the multimodal branch. No gain or a loss would argue for focusing on RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation instead. Either outcome usefully narrows a large part of the remaining configurations.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested a multimodal, single-profile model that adds ResNet50 image features to the llm_summary_001 RNA-only baseline (PCA n2000, no aggregation) through simple concat fusion, so adding the image modality via concat is the only change. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.619 (F1 0.610). That is about 0.07 below the RNA-only baseline (0.688, F1 0.659) and above image-only ResNet50 (0.512, F1 0.477), with a smaller gap between F1 and accuracy than either unimodal run. This initial observation suggests that naive concat of ResNet50 features did not add complementary signal and may have diluted the RNA signal in this setting. Each configuration has only one run and variance is unknown. The result applies specifically to concat fusion with ResNet50 and PCA, so it does not rule out benefits from other fusion strategies, image encoders, RNA encoders, or multiprofile aggregation. Within the tested options, RNA-focused configurations currently look stronger.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: All three runs so far are single-profile. RNA-only PCA is the strongest (0.688 accuracy, F1 0.659). Image-only ResNet50 (0.512) and naive concat fusion (0.619) were both lower. The profile-setting axis is completely untested, and it applies to every modality and encoder. 2. What this tests: Moving the best configuration (config_001) to the multiprofile setting with the simplest aggregation (avgpool) changes only the profile and aggregation choice. This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles adds class signal over a single profile. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: It exploits the strongest current direction (RNA-only PCA) while resolving a major design question. Avgpool is the lowest-complexity aggregator, so a result in either direction is easy to interpret. It will guide whether later encoder, transformer-aggregation, or fusion experiments should be run in the single-profile or multiprofile setting. It is preferable to changing the encoder or fusion now, because those questions affect fewer configurations.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 moved the best configuration so far (llm_summary_001: RNA-only, PCA n2000) from single-profile to the multiprofile setting with simple avgpool aggregation, changing only the profile setting and aggregator, to test whether combining multiple profiles adds class signal. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.514 (F1 0.498), about 0.17 below the single-profile RNA-only baseline (0.688, F1 0.659), which puts it roughly at the image-only ResNet50 level (0.512) and below naive concat fusion (0.619). This initial observation suggests that multiprofile with avgpool, as implemented here, loses rather than adds signal for PCA-encoded RNA, possibly because mean-pooling washes out profile-level information. However, multiprofile and avgpool were changed together, so the result does not separate the value of multiprofile input from the choice of aggregator: a learned aggregator such as a transformer could behave differently. With one run per configuration and unknown variance, it also remains untested whether this pattern holds for other encoders or modalities, so the single-profile setting currently looks like the stronger default rather than a settled choice.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only single-profile with PCA n2000 (0.688 acc, 0.659 F1) is clearly ahead so far. Image-only ResNet50 (0.512), naive concat fusion (0.619) and multiprofile avgpool (0.514) all trailed it. Every result so far uses the PCA encoder, so we do not know whether PCA itself is a good RNA representation. That matters because RNA appears to be the dominant signal and the encoder choice sits under most remaining configurations. 2) What this tests: config_004 keeps the best baseline exactly the same (RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion) and swaps only the encoder from PCA n2000 to scVI n200. Any change can therefore be attributed to representation alone. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: if scVI beats PCA, it becomes the stronger RNA base for later aggregation and fusion tests and changes how the many scVI-based options should be prioritized. If it underperforms, PCA's position is strengthened. This is a cleaner, higher-leverage question than retesting aggregation (config_003) or fusion variants, since both of those still depend on which RNA representation is best.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_001: RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA n2000 to scVI n200, to test whether the RNA representation itself limits performance. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.328 (F1 0.288), roughly 0.36 below the PCA baseline (0.688, F1 0.659) and the lowest result so far, well under image-only ResNet50 (0.512). Because only the encoder changed, this suggests that scVI n200 as used here is a much weaker RNA representation than PCA n2000 in this setting, which strengthens PCA as the RNA base for later aggregation and fusion tests. However, the encoder swap also changes the latent dimensionality (200 vs 2000) and may depend on scVI training settings, and the drop is unusually large, so a suboptimal or faulty scVI setup cannot be ruled out. With a single run, unknown variance, and scGPT and other scVI sizes untested, this should not yet be read as ruling out all scVI-based configurations.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA-only single-profile PCA n2000 is the best result so far (0.688 acc, 0.659 F1). scVI n200 under the same setup did far worse (0.328), so the RNA representation clearly matters a great deal. scGPT, the third RNA encoder, is still untested, and many remaining configurations depend on which RNA encoder is used. 2) This experiment changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA to scGPT, relative to the best baseline. It completes the single-profile RNA encoder comparison. It also shows whether PCA's lead reflects a general advantage over learned embeddings or only scVI's weakness or setup. 3) The RNA encoder is the foundation for every later aggregation and fusion test, and scGPT could plausibly beat PCA. Settling this choice with one clean, single-variable comparison is the most efficient way to reduce uncertainty before spending budget on transformer aggregation or fusion variants.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_001: RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA n2000 to scGPT, completing the single-profile RNA encoder comparison. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.224 (F1 0.184), the lowest result so far: about 0.46 below PCA n2000 (0.688, F1 0.659) and below scVI n200 (0.328). Because only the encoder changed, this initial observation suggests that both learned embeddings, as used here, are much weaker RNA representations than PCA n2000 in this setting, which reinforces PCA as the default RNA base for later aggregation and fusion tests. However, each configuration has a single run with unknown variance, and the encoder swap may also change embedding dimensionality. A drop this large, especially for a pretrained foundation model, means a suboptimal setup cannot be ruled out (e.g., preprocessing or gene-vocabulary mismatch, or frozen versus fine-tuned embeddings), so this should not be read as definitively ruling out scGPT-based configurations.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: single-profile RNA-only PCA n2000 is the best result so far (0.688 accuracy, 0.659 F1). The multiprofile run (config_002) dropped sharply to 0.514. That run changed both the profile setting and the aggregator (avgpool), so it is unclear whether multiprofile input itself hurts or whether mean-pooling washes out profile-level signal. 2) What this tests: config_003 keeps config_002 identical except for swapping avgpool for a learned transformer aggregator. This isolates the effect of aggregation and shows whether multiprofile PCA can match or beat the single-profile baseline. 3) Why it is the best next use: most of the remaining configurations are multiprofile. Settling whether multiprofile with a learned aggregator is viable decides whether that large part of the search space should be pursued or set aside. It also uses the strongest RNA encoder, so the answer is not confounded by weak scVI or scGPT embeddings. Testing weighted fusion (config_017) is a good follow-up, but the aggregation question affects more of the remaining choices.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the multiprofile RNA-only PCA n2000 configuration from llm_summary_004 and changed only the aggregator, from avgpool to a learned transformer. The goal was to test whether mean-pooling explained the multiprofile drop. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.540 (F1 0.524), a small gain of about 0.026 in both metrics over avgpool (0.514, F1 0.498), but still about 0.15 below the single-profile PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.688, F1 0.659). This initial observation suggests that the aggregator choice accounts for at most a small part of the multiprofile gap: with PCA RNA, neither aggregator tested brought multiprofile close to single-profile, so multiprofile configurations currently look weaker as implemented. However, with one run per configuration and unknown variance, the modest transformer gain may not be reliable, transformer hyperparameters and other aggregators were not explored, and it remains untested whether multiprofile behaves differently with image or multimodal inputs or whether the deficit comes from the multiprofile data setup itself.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Single-profile RNA-only PCA n2000 is the best result so far (0.688 accuracy, F1 0.659). Multiprofile with either aggregator, the scVI and scGPT encoders, and image-only ResNet50 were all clearly weaker. The one multimodal run (config_016, PCA plus ResNet50 with concat) dropped to 0.619. That drop could mean the images add no complementary signal, or it could mean naive concat diluted the RNA signal. The data cannot yet tell these apart. 2. What this tests: config_017 changes only the fusion strategy, from concat to weighted, keeping PCA n2000, ResNet50 and single-profile fixed. Weighted fusion can learn to down-weight the weaker image stream. If it matches or beats the RNA-only baseline, fusion design was the bottleneck and multimodal remains a live direction. If it still falls short, the case that ResNet50 images add little here gets stronger. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It is a clean one-variable comparison on the most promising backbone. It addresses the largest untested design dimension, fusion strategy, which governs every remaining multimodal configuration. It also has a realistic chance of producing a new best result. Testing the ViT-L image encoder makes sense afterward, once we know whether fusion can use image features at all.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the llm_summary_003 multimodal configuration (single-profile, PCA n2000 RNA, ResNet50 images, no aggregation) and changed only the fusion strategy, from concat to weighted, to test whether a fusion that can down-weight the weaker image stream would recover or beat the RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.688, F1 0.659). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.208 (F1 0.172), the lowest result so far: about 0.41 below concat fusion (0.619, F1 0.610), about 0.48 below RNA-only PCA, and below image-only ResNet50 (0.512) and even scGPT (0.224). Although fusion was the only variable changed, a weighted-fusion model scoring far below either of its unimodal components suggests a likely training or implementation failure (e.g., weight collapse, scale mismatch between streams, or optimization issues) rather than evidence about whether image features add complementary signal. So this run does not resolve the concat-dilution versus no-complementary-signal question; with a single run, unknown variance, and untested weighted-fusion settings or other fusion methods, weighted fusion should be treated as unreliable as implemented rather than ruled out, and RNA-only single-profile PCA n2000 remains the best configuration.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only single-profile PCA n2000 is still best (0.688 accuracy, F1 0.659). Every image-containing run so far used ResNet50. That includes image-only (0.512), concat fusion (0.619, below RNA-only) and weighted fusion (0.208, likely a training failure). So we cannot tell whether the image modality is inherently weak here or whether ResNet50 is the limiting factor. The image encoder is the main design axis not yet tested. 2. What this tests: config_013 keeps the image-only single-profile setup and changes only the encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This cleanly isolates the effect of image representation, the same way the RNA encoder sweep isolated PCA, scVI and scGPT. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: it resolves the key uncertainty that decides whether further multimodal search is worthwhile. If ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50, ViT-L fusion with PCA (e.g., config_022) becomes a logical, well-motivated follow-up. If it does not, the evidence that images add little signal grows stronger, and the remaining budget can go to RNA-focused refinements. Running a multimodal ViT-L configuration directly would mix the encoder effect with the effect of fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the image-only, single-profile setup of llm_summary_002 and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. The goal was to test whether ResNet50, rather than the image modality itself, explained the weak image results. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.427 (F1 0.417), about 0.085 below image-only ResNet50 (0.512, F1 0.477) and about 0.26 below the best configuration, RNA-only single-profile PCA n2000 (0.688, F1 0.659). Because only the encoder changed, this initial observation suggests that ViT-L as used here is not a stronger image representation than ResNet50, which adds to the evidence that images carry less class signal than PCA-encoded RNA in this setting and weakens the case for ViT-L fusion follow-ups such as config_022. However, each configuration has a single run with unknown variance, ViT-L setup details (e.g., frozen versus fine-tuned features, input resolution, or domain mismatch between ImageNet pretraining and cellular images) could be limiting, other image encoders remain untested, and image-only performance does not directly rule out complementary signal under a better-functioning fusion method.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only single-profile PCA n2000 (0.688, F1 0.659) is the best result so far. Multiprofile has only been tested with PCA RNA, where it fell to 0.514 with avgpool and 0.540 with a transformer. The learned aggregator helped slightly. It is still unclear whether multiprofile is generally harmful, which would suggest a data-setup issue, or whether the problem is specific to the RNA representation. Multiprofile is used by most remaining configurations, so this uncertainty affects much of the search space. 2. What this tests: config_012 keeps the image-only ResNet50 setup of config_010 (0.512, F1 0.477). It changes only the profile setting, to multiprofile with the transformer aggregator that did better for RNA. Image features may plausibly gain from pooling several profiles, so this checks whether the multiprofile drop carries over to another modality. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: If image multiprofile also drops, multiprofile looks generally unhelpful, and the many multiprofile multimodal configurations can be deprioritized. If it improves on single-profile ResNet50, multiprofile multimodal options such as config_020 become worth testing. Either outcome narrows the remaining space more than another single-profile fusion variant, such as config_022, given that ViT-L was weaker than ResNet50 on its own.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the image-only ResNet50 setup of llm_summary_002 (single-profile: 0.512, F1 0.477) and switched it to multiprofile input with a transformer aggregator. The aim was to test whether the large multiprofile drop seen with PCA RNA (single-profile 0.688 fell to 0.514 with avgpool and 0.540 with a transformer) carries over to the image modality. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.532 (F1 0.516), a small gain of about 0.020 in accuracy and about 0.039 in F1 over single-profile ResNet50. This initial observation suggests multiprofile is not uniformly harmful across modalities, so the RNA drop may be specific to the PCA RNA representation or its interaction with multiprofile data, rather than a general data-setup failure; multiprofile multimodal configurations (e.g., config_020) therefore should not yet be deprioritized wholesale. However, the result is still about 0.16 below the best configuration (RNA-only single-profile PCA n2000), the gain is small relative to unknown run-to-run variance from single runs, and multiprofile input and the transformer aggregator were introduced together, so it remains unclear whether any benefit comes from pooling multiple profiles or from the learned aggregator, and whether it would survive fusion with RNA.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run, so we have no estimate of baseline performance and no evidence about which design choices matter. 2. Test: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest configuration in the space. It sets a reference point that later experiments can be compared against one factor at a time: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting and aggregation (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), modality (image-only), and fusion (multimodal). 3. Why now: Under a limited budget, a cheap and interpretable baseline is the most efficient first step. It avoids assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models will help, and it lets each later gain be attributed to a single design change rather than several confounded ones.
experiment_summary: This first experiment set a baseline using the simplest configuration: RNA-only, single-profile, a PCA RNA encoder (pca_n2000), and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5176, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.4837. No other experiments exist yet, so this is only an initial reference point, and it says nothing yet about whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image-only models, or multimodal fusion would do better or worse. It also remains unknown how stable this estimate is across runs or seeds, and how hard the task is in absolute terms, so later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons against this baseline should be read with that uncertainty in mind.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (config_001: acc 0.518, F1 0.484). Every other design axis is untested, and we do not know how much run-to-run noise there is. 2) Test: config_002 changes one factor, single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool, while keeping the RNA-only PCA setup fixed. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the profile setting under the simplest aggregation. 3) Why now: the profile setting affects most of the remaining search space, so its effect matters early. Avgpool is the simplest aggregator, so it measures that effect without the extra capacity of a transformer. The result will tell us whether multiprofile variants deserve more of the budget. Encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) and an image-only baseline remain the next one-factor comparisons to run.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the RNA-only PCA setup (pca_n2000, no image encoder, no fusion) from llm_summary_001 and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input, aggregated with avgpool. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5136, slightly below the single-profile baseline's 0.5176 (about -0.004), while validation F1 rose from 0.4837 to 0.4982 (about +0.015). With one run per configuration and unknown run-to-run variance, both differences are small enough that they may be noise, so this is a mixed, inconclusive initial comparison rather than evidence that multiprofile helps or hurts. The change also bundles moving to multiprofile with the specific avgpool aggregator, so it remains untested whether other aggregators (e.g., attention or transformer pooling), other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or repeated seeds would show a clearer profile-setting effect.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only RNA-only PCA configurations have been tested so far. Single-profile reached 0.518 accuracy and multiprofile avgpool reached 0.514. That difference is small and inconclusive, so it is not yet clear whether multiprofile input helps. The largest open question is the modality itself. No experiment has shown whether image features carry useful signal, and most of the remaining space (image-only and every multimodal configuration) depends on that answer. 2. What this tests: config_010 is the simplest image-only setup: single-profile, resnet50, with no aggregation or fusion. It mirrors the RNA single-profile baseline (config_001), so comparing the two gives a clean modality comparison without changing profile setting or aggregation. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: The result will guide where to spend the remaining experiments. If images perform close to or better than RNA, multimodal fusion and image-encoder choices become high priority. If images perform poorly, the budget should shift toward RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and aggregation. This is more informative than another small RNA-side variation, such as a different RNA encoder or transformer aggregation, which would refine only one branch of the search.
experiment_summary: This experiment tested the simplest image-only configuration: single-profile input, a resnet50 image encoder, and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It mirrors the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (llm_summary_001), so the two differ only in modality. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5375 (validation F1 0.5184), about +0.020 accuracy and +0.035 F1 above that baseline (0.5176 / 0.4837). It is also the highest of the three runs so far, above multiprofile RNA avgpool (0.5136 / 0.4982). This is an initial observation that image features carry signal at least comparable to PCA RNA features, and possibly somewhat more. With one run per configuration and unknown seed variance, the size and reliability of the gap are uncertain. The comparison also involves only one encoder per modality (resnet50 vs pca_n2000), so it does not establish that images are generally more informative than RNA. Still untested are other image encoders, stronger RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-side multiprofile aggregation, and whether multimodal fusion improves on either single modality.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: In single-profile mode, resnet50 image-only (0.5375 acc / 0.5184 F1) modestly beat PCA RNA-only (0.5176 / 0.4837). The one multiprofile avgpool run was inconclusive. Fusion is still completely untested. Both unimodal parts of the simplest fusion model now have matched single-profile baselines. 2. Test: config_016 adds PCA RNA to the resnet50 single-profile model with concat fusion and changes nothing else. It directly asks whether combining modalities beats the best single modality, or whether the RNA features add little beyond images. 3. Why now: Multimodal options make up most of the remaining search space, so knowing early whether fusion helps at all tells us how much budget to spend there versus on encoder choices (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L). Using the simplest fusion and the already-measured encoders keeps the comparison clean against both baselines.
experiment_summary: This experiment tested the simplest multimodal fusion: single-profile input, the pca_n2000 RNA encoder and resnet50 image encoder from the matched unimodal baselines (llm_summary_001 and llm_summary_003), combined by concat fusion with no aggregation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6390 (F1 0.6197), about +0.10 accuracy and +0.10 F1 above the best single modality (resnet50 image-only, 0.5375 / 0.5184) and about +0.12 accuracy above PCA RNA-only (0.5176 / 0.4837). This makes it the best run so far and gives initial evidence that the two modalities carry complementary signal under these encoders. The gap is much larger than the earlier differences of about 0.004 to 0.035 between runs, but each configuration still has only one run and seed variance is unknown. It also remains untested whether the gain holds with other fusion methods, stronger encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L), or multiprofile aggregation, and whether part of it reflects the larger combined input rather than cross-modal complementarity.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Concat fusion of pca_n2000 RNA and resnet50 image features (config_016) reached 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. That is about 0.10 above either single modality, a gap much larger than the 0.004 to 0.035 differences seen elsewhere. Fusion is now the most promising direction. However, we do not know whether the gain depends on the fusion method or reflects complementary signal that any reasonable fusion would capture. 2) Test: config_017 keeps everything in config_016 the same (single-profile, pca_n2000, resnet50, no aggregation) and changes only the fusion from concat to weighted. This isolates the effect of the fusion strategy. A similar or better result would suggest the multimodal gain is robust to how the modalities are combined. A clear drop would show that fusion choice matters, so concat should be kept as the default. 3) Why now: It extends the best result by changing a single factor, so the outcome is easy to interpret and could also improve performance. Knowing which fusion works better narrows the large remaining multimodal space (encoder and multiprofile variants) before spending budget on those choices. Multiprofile effects were inconclusive in the RNA-only comparison, so they can be tested afterwards on top of the better fusion method.
experiment_summary: This experiment repeated the best configuration so far (llm_summary_004: multimodal, single-profile, pca_n2000 RNA, resnet50 image, no aggregation) and changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5232 (F1 0.5084), about -0.116 accuracy and -0.111 F1 below concat (0.6390 / 0.6197). That puts it below image-only resnet50 (0.5375 / 0.5184) and only slightly above PCA RNA-only (0.5176 / 0.4837), so the large multimodal gain seen with concat did not appear under weighted fusion. Because only fusion differed, this is initial evidence that fusion choice matters in this setup and supports keeping concat as the default. However, each configuration has a single run with unknown seed variance, and the weighted fusion's implementation and tuning are not described, so it is unclear whether weighted fusion is inherently worse or just poorly suited or configured here, and whether the ranking holds with other encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or other fusion methods (e.g., attention-based).

selection_reason: Evidence: concat fusion of pca_n2000 RNA and resnet50 image features (config_016, 0.639 accuracy / 0.620 F1) beats every other run by about 0.10. Weighted fusion fell back to unimodal levels, so concat is the working fusion choice. The effect of profile setting is still unresolved. Its only test was RNA-only with avgpool, where accuracy moved -0.004 and F1 +0.015, which is inconclusive. Test: config_018 keeps the best configuration fixed (multimodal, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) and changes only singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. This isolates whether multiprofile aggregation helps, hurts or does nothing in the setting that matters most. Why now: it exploits the strongest direction found so far while settling a major open design choice with a single-factor change. The result will guide whether later runs that swap encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L) or try transformer aggregation should use single-profile or multiprofile input.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_004: multimodal, pca_n2000 RNA, resnet50 image, concat fusion) fixed and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5362 (F1 0.5158), about -0.103 accuracy and -0.104 F1 below the single-profile concat run (0.6390 / 0.6197). That erases the multimodal gain and lands at roughly image-only resnet50 level (0.5375 / 0.5184), close to weighted fusion (0.5232 / 0.5084). Because only the profile setting changed, this is initial evidence that multiprofile avgpool input hurts in this multimodal setup, unlike the small, inconclusive change seen in the RNA-only comparison (llm_summary_002 vs 001), so single-profile is the provisional default for upcoming encoder swaps. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has a single run with unknown seed variance, and the change bundles multiprofile input with the specific avgpool aggregator. It is unclear whether the drop comes from multiprofile input itself or from avgpool (for example, averaging may dilute cross-modal alignment before concat). Transformer or attention aggregation and other encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L) could still behave differently.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: single-profile concat fusion of pca_n2000 RNA and resnet50 images is the best run so far (0.639 accuracy, 0.620 F1). Moving to multiprofile with avgpool (config_018) dropped results to about image-only level (0.536 / 0.516). That earlier comparison changed the profile setting and the aggregator together, so we cannot tell whether multiprofile input hurts or averaging profiles hurts, for example by diluting cross-modal alignment before concat. 2. What this tests: config_020 matches config_018 except that avgpool is replaced by transformer aggregation. If transformer aggregation recovers or beats 0.639, avgpool was the problem and multiprofile stays a viable direction. If it stays near 0.53, that strengthens the case for single-profile as the default. 3. Why now: every multiprofile configuration left in the space depends on this answer, including those with stronger encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L). Settling it with one experiment that changes only the aggregator lets later encoder swaps focus on the right profile setting, rather than spending budget on multiprofile variants that may all be limited by the aggregator.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the multimodal multiprofile setup from llm_summary_006 (pca_n2000 RNA, resnet50 image, concat fusion) and changed only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer, to test whether the multiprofile drop came from avgpool. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.2239 (F1 0.1843). That is about -0.31 below avgpool (0.5362 / 0.5158), about -0.42 below the best single-profile concat run (0.6390 / 0.6197), and far below every earlier run, including the unimodal baselines. Transformer aggregation therefore did not recover the single-profile result, and neither tested aggregator has made multiprofile competitive, which strengthens single-profile as the provisional default for upcoming encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L). However, a score this far below all other runs may reflect a training or optimization failure (for example undertraining, instability, or insufficient data for a transformer aggregator) rather than an inherent limit of transformer aggregation or multiprofile input. With a single run, unknown seed variance, and undescribed aggregator tuning, it remains unresolved whether multiprofile input itself hurts or both aggregators are simply ill-suited or misconfigured here.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Single-profile concat fusion with pca_n2000 and resnet50 (config_016) is clearly the best run so far, at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. Every departure from it lost about 0.10 or more: weighted fusion, multiprofile avgpool, and multiprofile transformer. The transformer run may also reflect a training failure. This makes single-profile concat the provisional default, though each result is a single run. The main untested factor is encoder choice. PCA RNA was the weaker unimodal signal (0.518 vs 0.537 for image), so the RNA representation is a plausible bottleneck. 2. Test: Swap only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200, keeping resnet50, single-profile and concat fixed. This isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional RNA representation strengthens the multimodal gain. It also partly checks whether concat's advantage came from cross-modal complementarity rather than the large PCA input size. 3. Why now: It exploits the best-known setup with a clean one-factor change on an important, unexplored design axis (RNA representation). It may produce the highest immediate result. Either outcome is informative: it tells us whether to pursue scGPT next or turn to the image encoder (ViT-L, config_022).
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the best configuration (llm_summary_004: multimodal, single-profile, resnet50 image, concat fusion, no aggregation) fixed and changed only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5420 (F1 0.4833), about -0.097 accuracy and -0.136 F1 below the PCA concat run (0.6390 / 0.6197). That is roughly image-only resnet50 accuracy (0.5375), with F1 below image-only (0.5184) and about equal to PCA RNA-only (0.4837), so swapping in scVI did not strengthen the multimodal gain and largely erased it. Because only the RNA encoder differed, this is initial evidence that RNA encoder choice matters and that pca_n2000 should remain the default for now. Several points are unresolved: there is no scVI RNA-only baseline, so it is unclear whether scvi_n200 is a weaker standalone representation or just combines poorly with resnet50 under concat. The swap also confounds learned versus PCA features with a 10x change in dimensionality (200 vs 2000), so it neither isolates nor rules out an input-size contribution to the concat gain. With single runs, unknown seed variance and untuned scVI settings, the size of the drop is uncertain, and other RNA encoders (scGPT) and image encoders (ViT-L) remain untested in this setup.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best run so far is config_016 (single-profile, pca_n2000 + resnet50, concat fusion) at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. Every one-factor deviation from it has dropped about 0.10 accuracy. Weighted fusion, multiprofile avgpool, transformer aggregation and the scVI RNA encoder all did worse. That makes single-profile, concat and PCA the provisional defaults. The image encoder is the one major design axis not yet varied: resnet50 has been used in every image run. 2) Test: config_022 keeps config_016 fixed and changes only resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. This isolates whether a stronger pretrained image representation adds to the concat multimodal gain or, as with scVI, disrupts it. 3) Why now: It is a clean single-factor test of an unexplored dimension, built on the strongest configuration, so it serves both exploration and exploitation. Swapping in scGPT (config_040) is an alternative, but the RNA-encoder axis already has one data point, so the untested image axis should reduce more uncertainty per experiment.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the best configuration (llm_summary_004: multimodal, single-profile, pca_n2000 RNA, concat fusion, no aggregation) fixed and changed only the image encoder, from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l, the first test of the image-encoder axis. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6186 (F1 0.6103), about -0.020 accuracy and -0.009 F1 below the resnet50 concat run (0.6390 / 0.6197). That makes it the second-best run so far and the only one-factor deviation from the best configuration not to drop about 0.10; the others were weighted fusion, multiprofile avgpool, transformer aggregation and scVI. It also stays about +0.08 accuracy above image-only resnet50 (0.5375), so the concat multimodal gain largely persists with ViT-L, giving initial evidence that it is not specific to resnet50, though ViT-L brought no improvement and resnet50 remains the nominal default. The gap is small, comparable to earlier differences of about 0.004 to 0.035 that were treated as possibly noise, and each configuration has a single run with unknown seed variance, so it is unclear whether ViT-L is truly slightly worse or effectively tied; there is also no ViT-L image-only baseline, so its standalone strength and how well it combines with PCA under concat are unresolved, as are feature-dimensionality and tuning differences between the encoders and untested combinations such as scGPT RNA.

selection_reason: Evidence: the best run so far is single-profile pca_n2000 + resnet50 with concat fusion (config_016, 0.639 / 0.620). Most one-factor changes from it dropped accuracy by about 0.10: weighted fusion, multiprofile avgpool, scVI RNA, and transformer aggregation (which may have failed in training). ViT-L stayed roughly tied. The RNA encoder clearly matters, since switching to scVI erased the multimodal gain. scGPT is the only RNA encoder not yet tried in any setting, so this axis is still largely unexplored. Test: config_040 keeps the best configuration fixed and swaps only pca_n2000 for scGPT. This shows whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation strengthens or weakens the concat multimodal gain. It also helps tell whether the scVI drop reflects learned embeddings in general or something specific to scVI. Why now: it is a clean one-factor comparison against the strongest baseline on the most consequential open axis. It has a real chance of beating 0.639, and the result is informative either way. Unimodal baselines (scVI or scGPT RNA-only, ViT-L image-only) can follow if the result needs explaining.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the best configuration (llm_summary_004: multimodal, single-profile, resnet50 image, concat fusion, no aggregation) fixed and changed only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scGPT, the first test of scGPT in any setting. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6501 (F1 0.6275), about +0.011 accuracy and +0.008 F1 above the PCA concat run (0.6390 / 0.6197), which makes it nominally the best run so far and well above the scVI swap (0.5420 / 0.4833). This gives initial evidence that a pretrained foundation-model RNA embedding can preserve, and possibly slightly strengthen, the concat multimodal gain, and that the scVI drop was not simply caused by using learned rather than PCA embeddings. However, the gain over PCA is within the range of earlier differences (about 0.004 to 0.035) treated as possible noise, and each configuration has a single run with unknown seed variance, so scGPT and PCA may be effectively tied. There is also no scGPT RNA-only baseline, its embedding dimensionality and tuning are not described, and combinations such as scGPT with ViT-L, other fusion methods, or multiprofile input remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 is the simplest RNA-only, single-profile model using the standard pca_n2000 encoder. It sets a reference point for later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons: PCA versus scVI or scGPT, single-profile versus multiprofile with avgpool or transformer aggregation, and RNA versus image or multimodal fusion. 3) Under a limited budget, a cheap baseline first means every later experiment can be read as the effect of a single change, rather than guessing that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models will help.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration as a reference point: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.494 (primary metric), with a supporting validation F1 of 0.453. The F1 being lower than accuracy may point to uneven performance across classes, though this is not confirmed. Because no other experiments have been run, this result is only an initial baseline. It gives no evidence yet about whether alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image-based models, or multimodal fusion would perform better or worse.
