Those questions are best addressed with later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons against this baseline.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: only one result exists so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.494 accuracy and 0.453 F1. We know nothing yet about the image modality, which is the largest open question in the design space. Every multimodal and image-only configuration depends on whether images carry useful signal. 2. Test: config_010 is the simplest image-only setup (single-profile, ResNet50, no aggregation or fusion). It mirrors the baseline in structure, so it gives a clean comparison of modality: RNA versus image under the same single-profile setting. 3. Why now: this result tells us whether to invest the remaining budget in image encoders and fusion or in RNA encoder and aggregation variants. Swapping the RNA encoder or adding aggregation would refine only one branch of the search. Testing the image branch now does the most to reduce uncertainty before committing to more complex multimodal configurations.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested the simplest image-only setup: a single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.536 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.516, both above the RNA-only single-profile PCA (n=2000) baseline from llm_summary_001 (0.494 accuracy, 0.453 F1); its smaller accuracy–F1 gap may hint at more even per-class performance, though this is unconfirmed. This is an initial observation that the image modality carries useful signal, at least as much as the PCA-encoded RNA baseline. However, the comparison changes both the modality and the specific encoder (ResNet50 vs. PCA), each result comes from a single run with no variance estimate, and the ~0.04 accuracy gap cannot be attributed to modality alone, since other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or image encoders might shift the ranking; whether images and RNA are complementary under fusion, and how multiprofile aggregation affects either branch, remain untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: we have two single-profile, single-run baselines. RNA-only with PCA reached 0.494 accuracy and 0.453 F1. Image-only with ResNet50 reached 0.536 accuracy and 0.516 F1. Both modalities carry signal, but we do not know whether they are complementary. 2. What this tests: config_016 is the simplest multimodal setup. It combines exactly these two encoders with concat fusion in the single-profile setting. Encoders and profile setting stay fixed, so any difference from the unimodal baselines can be attributed to adding the second modality. If it beats 0.536, that is evidence that combining modalities helps. If it does not, more complex multimodal settings should be deprioritised in favour of better unimodal encoders or multiprofile aggregation. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: the multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space. Testing them with the simplest fusion first prevents spending budget on a large region whose basic premise is unverified. It also sets a fusion reference point for later one-factor comparisons, such as concat vs. weighted fusion, other encoders, and multiprofile aggregation.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested the simplest multimodal setup: a single-profile model that concatenates the same encoders used in the two unimodal baselines, PCA (n=2000) for RNA and ResNet50 for images, with no aggregation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.715 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.687. Both are well above the image-only result (0.536 accuracy, 0.516 F1; llm_summary_002) and the RNA-only result (0.494 accuracy, 0.453 F1; llm_summary_001). Because encoders and profile setting were held fixed, this gain of about 0.18 accuracy is reasonably attributed to adding the second modality via concat fusion, and it is initial evidence that RNA and image signals are complementary, which supports prioritising the multimodal region of the search space. However, every result comes from a single run with no variance estimate, and only concat fusion with these two encoders has been tried. It is therefore unknown whether other fusion methods (e.g., weighted), other encoders (scVI, scGPT, other image models), or multiprofile aggregation would add further gains, or whether the size of the multimodal benefit depends on the specific encoder pairing.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The multimodal concat model (config_016, PCA + ResNet50, single-profile) reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. That is far above either unimodal baseline (0.536 image-only, 0.494 RNA-only), so the multimodal region is clearly worth exploiting. The profile setting, however, has not been tested in any modality, and it is one of the main design axes the study aims to understand. 2. Test: config_018 keeps the encoders (PCA n=2000, ResNet50) and fusion (concat) fixed and switches only from single-profile to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregator (avgpool). Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to using multiple profiles. Aggregation is necessarily introduced along with the multiprofile setting, but avgpool is its least complex form. 3. Why now: This is a clean one-factor extension of the current best configuration. It answers a question that affects roughly half of the remaining search space. If multiprofile helps, later comparisons of transformer aggregation, fusion type, and encoders can be run in that setting. If it does not, the budget can stay focused on single-profile variants such as weighted fusion or alternative encoders.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 changed only the profile setting of the current best configuration (multimodal, PCA n=2000 + ResNet50, concat fusion), switching from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, which is the simplest aggregator. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.520 (primary metric), with F1 at 0.479, compared with 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1 for the single-profile counterpart (llm_summary_003). This places it below the image-only baseline (0.536) and only slightly above the RNA-only baseline (0.494), so this multiprofile-avgpool variant is an initial negative observation, and for now single-profile looks like the stronger setting for further exploitation. However, multiprofile and avgpool aggregation were necessarily introduced together, so the drop cannot be attributed to multiprofile input itself rather than to mean-pooling (which may wash out profile-level signal). Every result is also a single run with no variance estimate, and it remains untested whether a learned aggregator (e.g., transformer), other fusion methods, or other encoders would change the conclusion about multiprofile.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: single-profile multimodal concat (PCA n2000 + ResNet50) is the best result so far, at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Switching to multiprofile with avgpool dropped accuracy to 0.520. Because multiprofile and avgpool were introduced together, we cannot tell whether multiprofile input is inherently worse or whether mean-pooling washed out the profile-level signal. 2. What this tests: config_020 keeps everything from config_018 fixed and changes only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer. This directly tests whether a learned aggregator recovers the multiprofile setting, giving a clean one-factor comparison against both config_018 (same profile setting) and config_016 (single-profile). 3. Why it is the best use of budget: multiprofile configurations make up a large share of the remaining search space. Learning early whether the multiprofile drop is specific to avgpool tells us whether to prune or pursue that region. This is more informative than a small single-profile tweak such as weighted fusion or an encoder swap, which can be explored afterward with a better-understood profile setting.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the multiprofile multimodal configuration from llm_summary_004 fixed (PCA n=2000 + ResNet50, concat fusion) and changed only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer. Validation accuracy rose to 0.721 (primary metric), with F1 at 0.681, compared with 0.520/0.479 for multiprofile-avgpool, and it roughly matched the single-profile counterpart from llm_summary_003 (0.715 accuracy, 0.687 F1). This one-factor comparison suggests the earlier multiprofile drop was tied to avgpool aggregation rather than to multiprofile input itself, so the multiprofile region should not be pruned. The small accuracy edge over single-profile (~0.006) and slightly lower F1 do not show that multiprofile is better, since every result is a single run with no variance estimate. It also remains untested whether the transformer aggregator's benefit holds with other fusion methods (e.g., weighted) or encoders (scVI, scGPT, other image models), and whether multiprofile with a learned aggregator can be pushed clearly beyond the single-profile setting.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Multimodal concat clearly beats either single modality (about 0.715–0.721 vs. 0.49–0.54 accuracy). Multiprofile only works with a learned aggregator: transformer gave 0.721, while avgpool gave 0.520. All multimodal runs so far used concat fusion, so fusion is the one major design axis not yet tested. 2) What this tests: config_021 changes only the fusion method (concat to weighted) relative to the current best, config_020 (multiprofile, PCA n=2000 + ResNet50, transformer). It shows whether weighted fusion adds gains on top of the transformer aggregator or whether concat is enough. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: it is a clean one-factor comparison on the strongest configuration, so it is both exploitation (a possible new best) and exploration (a first reading on the fusion axis). The answer tells us which fusion setting to carry forward before spending runs on the larger encoder sweeps (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L). Any small difference should be read cautiously, since each result is a single run with no variance estimate.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 changed only the fusion method of the current best configuration (llm_summary_005: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n=2000 + ResNet50, transformer aggregation), switching from concat to weighted fusion. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.537 (primary metric), with F1 at 0.518, compared with 0.721/0.681 for the concat counterpart. That is roughly the level of the image-only baseline (0.536/0.516; llm_summary_002) and far below both concat multimodal runs. Because this is a clean one-factor comparison, it is initial evidence that weighted fusion performed much worse than concat in this setting, and that concat should be carried forward for now. The result's closeness to image-only may hint that the weighted fusion is down-weighting or failing to use the RNA branch, but this is unconfirmed. It is also still a single run with no variance estimate, so it is unknown whether the drop reflects weighted fusion in general, its specific implementation or optimisation (e.g., weight initialisation or training instability), or an interaction with the transformer aggregator or multiprofile input. Weighted fusion has not been tried in the single-profile setting or with other encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L).

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Concat fusion clearly beat weighted fusion (0.721 vs 0.537), and transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool (0.721 vs 0.520). The best setup, config_020 (multiprofile, transformer, concat, PCA + ResNet50), is about tied with its single-profile counterpart (0.715). Encoder choice is the largest untested factor: every multimodal run so far used PCA + ResNet50. 2. What this tests: config_026 changes only the image encoder of config_020, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether a stronger pretrained image representation improves the best fusion and aggregation setup. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It exploits the settings already supported by evidence while answering a new, important question about representation, with a single-factor change. The result also tells us whether to carry ViT-L into later RNA-encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT).
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 changed only the image encoder of the current best configuration (llm_summary_005: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, transformer aggregation, concat fusion), swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This was the first test of the encoder axis in a multimodal run. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.507 (primary metric), with F1 at 0.455, compared with 0.721/0.681 for the ResNet50 counterpart. That is below the image-only ResNet50 baseline (0.536) and close to the RNA-only PCA baseline (0.494/0.453; llm_summary_001), so this one-factor comparison is initial evidence that ViT-L did not improve, and apparently hurt, this setup; ResNet50 should be carried forward for now, including into later RNA-encoder swaps. The closeness to the RNA-only level may hint that the ViT-L image branch contributed little useful signal under this pipeline, but this is unconfirmed. Because this is a single run with no variance estimate, it is unknown whether the drop reflects ViT-L representations themselves, a mismatch with this pipeline (e.g., feature dimensionality or scale under concat, preprocessing, or optimisation), or an interaction with multiprofile transformer aggregation. ViT-L has not been tested image-only or in the single-profile multimodal setting, either of which could help localise the failure.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n=2000 + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. One-factor tests from that configuration showed large drops when concat was replaced by weighted fusion (0.537) or ResNet50 by ViT-L (0.507). So concat and ResNet50 are the current choices to keep. The RNA encoder is the one major design axis still untested: every run so far has used PCA n=2000. 2. What this tests: config_032 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA to scVI (n=200), and keeps everything else in the best configuration fixed. This shows whether a learned, compact RNA representation adds to or weakens the RNA–image complementarity behind the roughly 0.18 multimodal gain. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: it isolates the last unexplored factor directly against the current best, so it can either improve the top result or confirm that PCA should be kept. The choice between scVI and scGPT is somewhat arbitrary. A drop would point to scGPT (config_044) as the natural follow-up. An unclear result could be checked with the single-profile counterpart (config_028).
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 changed only the RNA encoder of the current best configuration (llm_summary_005: multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion), replacing PCA (n=2000) with scVI (n=200). This was the first test of a non-PCA RNA encoder. Validation accuracy fell to 0.579 (primary metric), with F1 at 0.563, compared with 0.721/0.681 for the PCA counterpart. That is a smaller drop than the weighted-fusion (0.537) or ViT-L (0.507) swaps and still above both unimodal baselines (image-only 0.536, RNA-only PCA 0.494), so this one-factor comparison is initial evidence that PCA should be kept for now, while scVI appears to retain some, but not all, of the multimodal benefit. Because this is a single run with no variance estimate, it is unclear whether the drop reflects scVI representations themselves, the much smaller latent dimensionality (200 vs. 2000, which may shift the RNA–image balance under concat), scVI training or hyperparameters, or an interaction with multiprofile transformer aggregation. scVI has not been tested RNA-only or in single-profile multimodal (e.g., config_028), and scGPT (config_044) remains untested, so it is unknown whether any learned RNA encoder can match PCA.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_020 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n=2000 + ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. One-factor swaps from it have each hurt sharply: weighted fusion fell to 0.537, ViT-L to 0.507 and scVI to 0.579. The only encoder level never tested is scGPT. So we do not yet know whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA encoder can match or beat PCA, or whether scVI's drop says something about learned RNA encoders in general. 2. What this tests: config_044 changes only the RNA encoder of the best configuration, from PCA to scGPT, and keeps everything else fixed. It completes the RNA-encoder comparison against the current best. It will show whether PCA's advantage is broad or specific to scVI (for example, scVI's low 200-dimension latent), and it is the only untested option in this direction that could plausibly beat the current best. 3. Why it is the best use of the next run: The fusion and image-encoder axes already have clear negative results, so this is the most important design axis that remains unresolved. A clean one-factor swap answers it directly, combining exploitation of the best setup with exploration of the last untested encoder. Re-testing scVI or ViT-L in other settings, or running unimodal multiprofile checks, would help localise past failures, but is less likely to change which configuration we carry forward.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 changed only the RNA encoder of the current best configuration (llm_summary_005: multimodal, multiprofile, ResNet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion), replacing PCA (n=2000) with scGPT. This completes the one-factor RNA-encoder comparison. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.525 (primary metric), with F1 at 0.498, compared with 0.721/0.681 for PCA and 0.579/0.563 for scVI (llm_summary_008). That places scGPT below scVI and slightly below the image-only ResNet50 baseline (0.536), so neither learned RNA encoder matched PCA in this setup and PCA should be carried forward. The closeness to image-only may hint that the scGPT branch added little usable signal under concat, but this is unconfirmed. Because each result is a single run with no variance estimate, it is unknown whether the drop reflects scGPT embeddings themselves, a pipeline mismatch (e.g., embedding dimensionality or scale under concat, preprocessing, gene-vocabulary coverage, or frozen vs. fine-tuned use), or an interaction with multiprofile transformer aggregation. scGPT has not been tested RNA-only or in single-profile multimodal, and the setup with no clear one-factor improvement remains config_020/llm_summary_005, roughly matched by single-profile llm_summary_003.

selection_reason:
1. Evidence and uncertainty: the two strongest results are nearly tied. These are multiprofile-transformer concat (config_020, 0.721 accuracy) and single-profile concat (config_016, 0.715 accuracy), both using PCA + ResNet50. Weighted fusion has been tested only once, in the multiprofile-transformer setting. There it collapsed to about the image-only level (0.537). That single result cannot tell us whether weighted fusion fails in general or only interacts badly with transformer aggregation over multiple profiles. Fusion is a core design axis with just one comparison behind it.

2. What this tests: config_017 changes only the fusion method of config_016, from concat to weighted, keeping single-profile and PCA + ResNet50 fixed. This is a clean one-factor test of whether concat's advantage holds without the multiprofile aggregator. If weighted fusion matches or beats about 0.715, the earlier failure was an interaction and weighted fusion stays a candidate. If it again drops to around 0.54, the evidence that weighted fusion ignores the RNA branch becomes much stronger. We could then drop every weighted-fusion configuration, about half of the remaining space.

3. Why this is the best next use of the budget: the encoder axes have already been checked one factor at a time against the best setup, so fusion is the least-resolved axis. It is tested here on the simpler single-profile path with known strong encoders. The result either keeps a plausible improvement in play or efficiently prunes a large part of the search space.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 changed only the fusion method of the single-profile multimodal configuration (llm_summary_003: PCA n=2000 + ResNet50, no aggregation), switching from concat to weighted fusion to check whether weighted fusion's earlier failure in the multiprofile-transformer setting (llm_summary_006, 0.537) was an interaction effect. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.471 (primary metric), with F1 at 0.442, compared with 0.715/0.687 for the concat counterpart. That is below both unimodal baselines (image-only 0.536, RNA-only PCA 0.494), so weighted fusion has now underperformed concat by roughly 0.18–0.24 accuracy in two clean one-factor comparisons across both profile settings. This is fairly consistent evidence for deprioritising or pruning weighted-fusion configurations under this pipeline, with concat carried forward. Unlike the multiprofile run, this result falls below image-only rather than near it, so the earlier hint that weighted fusion simply ignores the RNA branch is not clearly supported, and the failure mechanism is unknown. Possible explanations include weighted fusion itself, its implementation or optimisation (e.g., weight initialisation, feature scale mismatch, training instability), or something else. Each result is still a single run with no variance estimate. Weighted fusion has also not been tested with other encoders, so a general verdict on weighted fusion is not established.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, cheapest baseline in the space. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that every later change can be compared against: swapping the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), adding multiprofile aggregation, adding the image modality, or adding fusion. 3) With a limited budget, a simple anchor point makes each later experiment a one-factor comparison. That lets us credit a gain or loss to a specific design choice rather than to several changes at once, and it avoids assuming that more complex multimodal setups will win.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first reference point in the search: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.5399, with validation F1 of 0.5245 as supporting evidence. Because it is the first completed experiment, this is an initial baseline and not evidence that any design choice helps or hurts. It remains unknown how alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, adding the image modality, or fusion strategies would compare. Variability across runs or seeds is also uncharacterized, so small future differences from this baseline should be interpreted cautiously, ideally through one-factor-at-a-time comparisons.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one completed run, the RNA-only, single-profile PCA (n=2000) baseline (val acc 0.540, F1 0.524). No design choice has been compared yet, and run-to-run variability is unknown. 2) Test: config_002 changes one factor. It keeps the same RNA-only PCA encoder and switches from single-profile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation. This shows whether pooling multiple profiles improves accuracy and F1, without confounding from a new encoder, a new modality, or a learned aggregator. 3) Why now: profile setting affects about two-thirds of the remaining configurations (all multiprofile variants), so this result guides much of the search. Avgpool is the simplest aggregation, so it gives a clean first estimate of the multiprofile effect before testing transformer aggregation. Alternative RNA encoders (config_004, config_007) or image-only baselines (config_010, config_013) are natural follow-up single-factor tests.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested a single-factor change from the llm_summary_001 baseline. It kept the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) encoder with no image encoder or fusion, and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy was 0.5203 versus 0.5399 for the single-profile baseline, and validation F1 was 0.4982 versus 0.5245. This is an initial observation that multiprofile input with simple average pooling did not improve on single-profile input under this RNA-only PCA configuration and may have slightly reduced performance. However, the gap is about 2 points from a single run each, run-to-run variability is uncharacterized, and the comparison changes both profile setting and the introduction of avgpool aggregation, so it should not be taken as evidence that multiprofile input is generally unhelpful. Learned aggregators (e.g., transformer), other RNA encoders, and the image modality may behave differently.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: So far we have only two RNA-only PCA runs. The single-profile baseline reached 0.540 accuracy (F1 0.524). Multiprofile with avgpool was slightly lower at 0.520 (F1 0.498), but a gap of about 2 points from one run each is weak evidence. The biggest gap in our knowledge is the image modality. We have no image-only result, so we cannot judge whether images carry useful signal or whether the roughly 36 multimodal configurations are worth exploring. 2. What this tests: config_010 is an image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model with no aggregation or fusion. It mirrors the single-profile setting of the RNA baseline, so the comparison isolates the effect of modality. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: knowing how informative images are by themselves decides how much budget should go to multimodal fusion versus RNA encoder and aggregation refinements. Comparing RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or the transformer aggregator would refine a narrower question, and those can follow once this reference point is set.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 established the first image-only reference point: a single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion, chosen to mirror the single-profile RNA-only PCA (n=2000) baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached validation accuracy 0.5121 (F1 0.4771), versus 0.5399 (F1 0.5245) for the RNA baseline. This is an initial observation that images alone, with this encoder, performed somewhat below RNA alone, and that F1 dropped more than accuracy. Because modality and encoder change together, the single-run gap of about 3 points (variability uncharacterized, chance level not stated) cannot be attributed to modality itself. Whether images add complementary signal in multimodal fusion, and whether other image encoders would close the gap, remains untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: the single-profile RNA-only PCA baseline reached 0.540 accuracy (F1 0.524). Image-only ResNet50 single-profile reached 0.512 (F1 0.477). Multiprofile avgpool on RNA reached 0.520 and did not help. Each is a single run, so these gaps are small and uncertain. The largest untested design question is whether the two modalities carry complementary signal. 2) config_016 fuses exactly the two encoders already tested (PCA n2000 + ResNet50) in the single-profile setting with simple concat fusion. It is a clean one-step extension of both unimodal baselines: it adds the second modality while holding encoders and profile setting fixed. It directly tests whether fusion beats the best unimodal result (0.540). 3) This is the best use of the next experiment because multimodality accounts for most of the remaining search space. The result tells us whether to keep investing in fusion and image encoders or to focus on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT). Concat is the simplest fusion baseline, so it sets a reference before testing weighted fusion or multiprofile variants.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested simple concat fusion of the two previously tested single-profile encoders (RNA PCA n=2000 + image ResNet50), holding encoders and profile setting fixed relative to the unimodal baselines. It reached validation accuracy 0.5070 (F1 0.4548), below both RNA-only (0.5399, F1 0.5245) and image-only (0.5121, F1 0.4771). This is an initial observation that naive concat fusion did not show complementary benefit in this configuration and may have slightly underperformed either modality alone, with F1 again dropping more than accuracy. Because each result is a single run with uncharacterized variability, the gaps of about 0.5 to 3 points are small and uncertain, and the result does not establish that the modalities lack complementary signal. Other fusion strategies (e.g., weighted or learned fusion, modality balancing or normalization), other encoders, or multiprofile variants remain untested and could behave differently.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: naive concat fusion of RNA PCA (n=2000) and ResNet50 images (config_016) reached 0.5070 accuracy and 0.4548 F1. That is below both RNA-only (0.5399) and image-only (0.5121), and F1 dropped more than accuracy. This leaves open whether the modalities lack complementary signal or whether simple concatenation handles them poorly, for example through imbalance between modalities. These are single runs with unknown variability, so the gaps are suggestive but uncertain. 2) Test: config_017 keeps the encoders and single-profile setting identical to config_016 and changes only concat to weighted fusion. Any difference can therefore be attributed to the fusion strategy. 3) Why now: most of the remaining search space is multimodal, so learning whether a better fusion method can recover or exceed unimodal performance strongly shapes where to spend the budget. If weighted fusion still trails RNA-only, effort should shift toward RNA encoder alternatives such as scVI and scGPT. If it closes the gap, multimodal variants become worth exploiting.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 changed only the fusion strategy from concat (llm_summary_004) to weighted fusion, keeping the single-profile multimodal setup with RNA PCA (n=2000) and ResNet50 image encoders. It reached validation accuracy 0.7250 (F1 0.6847), versus 0.5070 (F1 0.4548) for concat, 0.5399 (F1 0.5245) for RNA-only, and 0.5121 (F1 0.4771) for image-only. Because fusion was the only factor changed, this is the first isolated evidence that fusion strategy strongly affects multimodal performance here. The ~22-point gain over concat and ~18-point gain over RNA-only are much larger than earlier gaps, which suggests the two modalities do carry complementary signal and that concat's poor result likely reflected how it combined them. Several points remain uncertain: each result is a single run with uncharacterized variability, the gain is unusually large and is worth replicating or checking for setup differences, and the mechanism is unknown (e.g., whether weighting corrects modality imbalance). It is also untested whether the benefit holds with other encoders (scVI, scGPT, other image models) or with multiprofile aggregation, so multimodal weighted-fusion variants now look like the most promising direction to exploit.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: weighted fusion (config_017, acc 0.725, F1 0.685) beat concat fusion (0.507) and both single-modality baselines by about 18-22 points. This is the strongest signal so far, but it comes from a single run with one encoder pair (PCA n=2000 + ResNet50), and the image encoder is the weakest tested component (image-only 0.512). The one multiprofile result so far (avgpool, RNA-only) was slightly worse than single-profile, so moving to multiprofile is a less promising extension at this point. 2) Test: keep everything from config_017 fixed (multimodal, single-profile, PCA RNA encoder, weighted fusion) and swap only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This shows whether the image representation matters within the best fusion setup, and whether the weighted-fusion gain holds with a different encoder. 3) Why now: it is a clean one-factor extension of the best configuration, so it exploits the strongest evidence while answering an untested question about image representation. Both outcomes are useful: an improvement would point to a better encoder, and a similar or lower result would suggest that fusion strategy, not the image encoder, drives the gain.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best configuration so far fixed (llm_summary_005: multimodal, single-profile, RNA PCA n=2000, weighted fusion) and changed only the image encoder, swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. Validation accuracy was 0.2596 (F1 0.2217), compared with 0.7250 (F1 0.6847) for the ResNet50 version, and it fell far below every earlier result, including RNA-only (0.5399), image-only ResNet50 (0.5121) and concat fusion (0.5070). Because the encoder was the only factor changed, this is isolated evidence that the weighted-fusion result is highly sensitive to the image representation and does not carry over to ViT-L in this setup. However, a drop to roughly half the RNA-only accuracy is unusually large, which suggests a possible failure mode rather than simply weaker image features; candidates include feature scale or dimensionality mismatch in the fusion weights, training instability, or a pipeline issue. With single runs, no ViT-L image-only baseline, and the large llm_summary_005 gain still unreplicated, the robustness of the weighted-fusion gain and the reason for this collapse remain open.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Weighted fusion of RNA PCA (n=2000) with ResNet50 (config_017) is the clear best so far, at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. That is roughly 18 to 22 points above every other run, but it comes from a single unreplicated run. Swapping the image encoder to ViT-L collapsed performance, so the weighted-fusion gain looks fragile. In the RNA-only setting, multiprofile with avgpool was about 2 points worse than single-profile, but that is a small single-run gap and may not transfer to multimodal models. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile. Avgpool is the simplest aggregation required by multiprofile input. It tests whether multiprofile input helps or hurts in the best-performing regime. It also checks whether the large weighted-fusion gain holds in a closely related setup. Using avgpool rather than transformer keeps the aggregation identical to the RNA-only multiprofile run (config_002), so the two profile effects can be compared directly. 3) Why now: Profile setting is a major design axis that has only been tested in a weak unimodal baseline. Running it next to the strongest configuration both exploits the most promising direction and resolves an important uncertainty. A similar accuracy and F1 would support robustness of weighted fusion. A gain would point to multiprofile weighted variants, including transformer aggregation, as the next step. A drop would focus later experiments on single-profile encoder variants such as scVI or scGPT with weighted fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best configuration (llm_summary_005: multimodal, RNA PCA n=2000 + ResNet50, weighted fusion) fixed and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation, mirroring the RNA-only profile comparison (llm_summary_001 vs 002). It reached validation accuracy 0.7207 (F1 0.6815), essentially matching the single-profile version (0.7250, F1 0.6847); the ~0.4-point gap is smaller than the ~2-point drop seen for the same change in the RNA-only setting. This is an initial observation that multiprofile avgpool input neither clearly helps nor clearly hurts in the weighted-fusion regime. Because a closely related setup again landed near 0.72, it also gives partial support that the large weighted-fusion gain is not a one-off, though it is not a true replicate. Run-to-run variability remains uncharacterized, so the small difference cannot be interpreted. Open questions include whether learned aggregation (e.g., transformer) would make multiprofile input beneficial, how other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) behave with weighted fusion, and why ViT-L collapsed.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Weighted fusion is the clear driver of performance so far. Single-profile RNA PCA plus ResNet50 reached 0.725 accuracy (F1 0.685). The multiprofile avgpool variant landed at 0.721, which suggests the gain is not a one-off and that avgpool aggregation is roughly neutral. Swapping in the ViT-L image encoder collapsed accuracy to 0.26, so the weighted-fusion result is highly sensitive to the encoder representation. However, the RNA encoder has never been varied anywhere in the search. Every run has used PCA n2000, and scVI and scGPT are untested. 2) What this tests: config_029 changes only the RNA encoder (PCA n2000 to scVI n200) relative to the best configuration, config_017. Profile setting, image encoder and weighted fusion stay fixed, so this isolates the effect of RNA representation in the best-performing regime. Because scVI produces a much lower-dimensional embedding, it also gives indirect evidence on whether feature dimensionality or scale mismatch matters for weighted fusion, one candidate explanation for the ViT-L collapse. 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: the RNA encoder is the largest unexplored design dimension. It is tested here in the regime that matters most, with a clean one-factor comparison. A gain would open a new exploitation direction, and a drop would show that PCA is part of what makes weighted fusion work. Learned (transformer) aggregation can be tested afterwards, since avgpool already suggests multiprofile input adds little.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best configuration fixed (llm_summary_005: multimodal, single-profile, ResNet50 image encoder, weighted fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA n=2000 to scVI n=200. This was the first time the RNA encoder was varied in the search. Validation accuracy was 0.4942 (F1 0.4533), well below the PCA version (0.7250, F1 0.6847) and also below RNA-only PCA (0.5399), image-only ResNet50 (0.5121) and concat fusion (0.5070), though it did not collapse as far as the ViT-L swap (0.2596). Because only the RNA encoder changed, this is isolated single-run evidence that the weighted-fusion gain does not carry over to scVI n=200 in this setup, and that the strong result depends on the specific encoder pairing rather than weighted fusion alone. It remains uncertain whether the drop reflects weaker scVI features, a dimensionality or scale mismatch in the fusion weights (both encoder swaps away from the 005 setup now fail, which is consistent with but does not establish this), or tuning or pipeline issues. Also unresolved are the lack of an scVI RNA-only baseline, uncharacterized run-to-run variability, and untested alternatives such as scGPT or feature normalization before fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Weighted fusion with RNA PCA n=2000 plus ResNet50 is the only strong regime found so far. It reached 0.725 accuracy single-profile (config_017) and 0.721 multiprofile with avgpool (config_019). Swapping either encoder collapsed performance: ViT-L gave 0.260 and scVI gave 0.494. So encoder swaps look risky. Aggregation has only been tried as simple avgpool, which was neutral here and slightly harmful in the RNA-only setting. 2. Test: config_021 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, relative to config_019, with encoders, fusion and profile setting held fixed. It isolates whether learned aggregation over multiple profiles adds value beyond averaging. It also gives a third data point in the strong regime, which helps judge whether the roughly 0.72 weighted-fusion result is robust. 3. Why now: Aggregation is a core design axis that is entirely untested beyond avgpool. This is a clean one-factor comparison inside the best-performing setup. It balances exploitation (a plausible chance of beating 0.725) with resolving whether multiprofile input is worth pursuing. Its F1 alongside accuracy will help judge any small differences.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the multiprofile weighted-fusion setup from llm_summary_007 (RNA PCA n=2000 + ResNet50) fixed and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. Validation accuracy was 0.6287 (F1 0.5993), about 9 points below avgpool (0.7207, F1 0.6815) and the single-profile version (0.7250, F1 0.6847), though still well above RNA-only, image-only and concat fusion (about 0.51 to 0.54). Because aggregation was the only factor changed, this is isolated single-run evidence that transformer aggregation did not add value over averaging in this setup and may have hurt. It also adds that the strong weighted-fusion regime is sensitive to aggregation as well as to encoder choice. It remains uncertain whether the drop reflects the transformer itself or untuned training (e.g., learning rate, depth, data size for a learned aggregator, overfitting) or pipeline effects, and run-to-run variability is still uncharacterized; so far no tested multiprofile variant has beaten single-profile input.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: weighted fusion with RNA PCA n=2000 plus ResNet50 is clearly the strongest regime, at about 0.72 accuracy in both single-profile (0.7250) and multiprofile avgpool (0.7207) runs. Every departure from that pairing has hurt. Swapping the image encoder to ViT-L collapsed accuracy to 0.26, swapping the RNA encoder to scVI n=200 dropped it to 0.49, and transformer aggregation lowered it to 0.63. It is still unclear whether the gain needs the PCA encoder specifically or whether scVI was a special case (weaker features or a mismatch in fusion scale or dimensionality). scGPT, the third RNA encoder, has not been tested anywhere. 2. Test: config_041 changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT, keeping single-profile input, ResNet50 and weighted fusion as in the best run. If it reaches about 0.72 or higher, weighted fusion works across RNA encoders and scVI looks like the outlier, and scGPT could become a new best. If it also drops, that adds evidence that the strong result depends on PCA features specifically. 3. Why now: this is a clean one-factor comparison against the best configuration on the dimension most likely to matter, encoder choice. It covers an entirely unexplored encoder and has a real chance of improving accuracy. Diagnostic unimodal baselines such as scVI or ViT-L alone are useful but less likely to change which direction the search exploits next.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the best configuration fixed (llm_summary_005: multimodal, single-profile, ResNet50, weighted fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA n=2000 to scGPT, which had not been tested anywhere before. Validation accuracy was 0.5729 (F1 0.5730), well below the PCA version (0.7250, F1 0.6847). It was above the scVI n=200 swap (0.4942) and modestly above RNA-only PCA (0.5399), image-only ResNet50 (0.5121) and concat fusion (0.5070), and its F1 was close to its accuracy, unlike most earlier runs. Because only the encoder changed, this is isolated single-run evidence that the large weighted-fusion gain did not carry over to scGPT either. It adds to the scVI result in suggesting that the strong ~0.72 regime depends on the PCA n=2000 + ResNet50 pairing rather than on weighted fusion alone, and that scVI was not a unique outlier. It remains uncertain whether this reflects weaker scGPT features, a scale or dimensionality mismatch in the fusion weights (now consistent across all three encoder swaps but not established), or untuned training or pipeline effects. There are still no scGPT or scVI RNA-only baselines, the PCA result has not been replicated, and run-to-run variability is uncharacterized.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so we have no evidence about the scale of performance or which design choices matter. 2) config_001 is the simplest setup: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (2000 components), with no aggregation or fusion. It sets a low-complexity reference point. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time against it: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting and aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image-only models, and multimodal fusion. 3) With a limited budget and no prior data, a clean, cheap baseline is the most useful first run. It shows whether gains from more complex encoders, multiple profiles, or multimodal fusion are real or just added complexity, and it avoids changing several design choices before we have a reference.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder with 2000 components and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.6287, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.5993. This is an initial reference point only. With no prior experiments to compare against, nothing yet indicates whether this performance is strong or weak, or which design choices matter. Open questions include whether alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multi-profile aggregation, image-based models, or multimodal fusion improve on this baseline. Single-factor comparisons against this configuration are needed to attribute any gains.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: There is only one result so far, the RNA-only, single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (accuracy 0.6287, F1 0.5993). We do not yet know which design choices matter. 2. Test: config_002 keeps the modality and encoder fixed (RNA-only, PCA-2000) and changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps on its own, without the extra capacity of a transformer aggregator. 3. Why now: Profile setting is a structural choice that affects about two-thirds of the remaining search space, including most image-only and multimodal configurations. Settling it early, through a clean single-factor comparison against the baseline, will narrow later choices more than testing an encoder swap or jumping to multimodal fusion, where several factors would change at once.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA-2000 setup from llm_summary_001 and changed the profile setting from single-profile to multiprofile, which also required adding avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy fell from 0.6287 to 0.5070, about 12 points, and supporting F1 fell from 0.5993 to 0.4548, so multiprofile with avgpool performed clearly worse than the single-profile baseline in this RNA-only setting. Because multiprofile and avgpool were introduced together, the evidence cannot separate a drawback of using multiple profiles from a drawback of simple mean pooling. It is also unclear whether a learned aggregator (e.g., a transformer) would close the gap, whether the result holds for other RNA encoders or for image and multimodal settings, and how much of the difference reflects run-to-run variance, since each configuration has only one run.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: With the RNA-only PCA-2000 setup, moving from single-profile (0.6287 accuracy, 0.5993 F1) to multiprofile with avgpool (0.5070 accuracy, 0.4548 F1) caused a large drop. Because multiprofile and avgpool were introduced together, we cannot tell whether using multiple profiles hurts or whether simple mean pooling discards useful information. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a learned transformer. This is a clean single-factor test of the aggregation choice. If accuracy recovers to near or above the single-profile baseline, avgpool was the bottleneck and multiprofile remains viable. If accuracy stays well below, the evidence points against multiprofile in general. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: Roughly two-thirds of the remaining configurations are multiprofile, so this one run decides whether a large part of the search space is worth exploring, across RNA, image and multimodal settings. That makes it a better use of limited budget than first testing a new encoder or modality. Since each configuration has only one run, the result should be read as directional rather than conclusive.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only, multiprofile PCA-2000 setup from llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to a learned transformer, which makes it a clean single-factor test of aggregation. Validation accuracy fell further, from 0.5070 to 0.4214 (about 8.6 points), and supporting F1 fell from 0.4548 to 0.4124 (about 4.2 points). Both values are well below the single-profile baseline of 0.6287 accuracy and 0.5993 F1, so in this setting the transformer did not recover the multiprofile gap and performed worse than mean pooling. With one run per configuration and no tuning of the transformer (e.g., capacity, regularization, training budget), it remains uncertain whether this reflects a general drawback of multiprofile input, an under-optimized aggregator, or run-to-run variance, and whether the pattern holds for other RNA encoders or for image and multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: three RNA-only PCA-2000 runs show single-profile (0.629 acc / 0.599 F1) clearly beating multiprofile with avgpool (0.507) and with a transformer (0.421). Each configuration has one run, so this is suggestive rather than settled. The image modality is completely untested, so we do not know whether images carry useful signal or whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing. 2) This experiment tests an image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model. It sets an image baseline that can be compared directly with the RNA single-profile baseline, it isolates the value of the image modality, and it serves as the reference for the later fusion configurations (e.g., config_016 and config_017, which pair PCA-2000 with ResNet50). 3) It is the best use of the next experiment because it explores the largest remaining unknown, the image modality, which most of the remaining configurations depend on. It also keeps the profile setting that has worked best so far. Testing RNA encoders or more multiprofile variants first would leave the fusion branch of the search uninformed.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 established the first image-only baseline: a single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849, with a supporting F1 of 0.4639. This is well below the RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (0.6287 acc / 0.5993 F1), which suggests that in this setup images alone carry less directly usable signal than RNA, though they do perform above the RNA multiprofile transformer run (0.4214). With one run, no tuning of the image encoder (e.g., pretraining, fine-tuning strategy, augmentation), and no fusion runs yet, it remains uncertain whether the gap reflects the modality itself, an under-optimized image pipeline, or run-to-run variance, and whether images add complementary information when fused with RNA (e.g., config_016/017).

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: single-profile RNA (PCA-2000) is the strongest result so far (0.629 acc / 0.599 F1). Image-only ResNet50 is clearly weaker (0.485 / 0.464). Multiprofile hurt RNA-only with both avgpool and the transformer. No experiment has tested fusion yet, so we do not know whether images add complementary signal to RNA. 2. What this tests: config_016 combines the two single-profile components we already measured (PCA-2000 RNA and ResNet50 images) using the simplest fusion, concat. Both unimodal baselines exist, so any gain or loss can be attributed to adding the image modality. It avoids the multiprofile setting that has so far performed poorly. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: whether multimodal fusion helps is the most important open design question. The answer will decide whether the large multimodal part of the search space is worth further budget. It will also set up a clean concat-versus-weighted comparison next (config_017). Encoder swaps such as scVI or ViT-L are useful but secondary, and they can follow once the value of fusion is known.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 was the first multimodal fusion test. It combined the two previously measured single-profile components, PCA-2000 RNA and ResNet50 images, using simple concat fusion and no aggregation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5362 (supporting F1 0.5158). That is about 9 points below the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.6287 / 0.5993) and about 5 points above the image-only baseline (0.4849 / 0.4639). So in this configuration, adding the image modality through concat did not improve on RNA alone and was associated with worse performance. Because each configuration has a single run and the image pipeline and fusion are untuned, it remains uncertain whether this reflects a lack of complementary image signal, the naive concat fusion (e.g., the image features drowning out the stronger RNA signal, or poor feature scaling), under-optimized training, or run-to-run variance. The planned concat-versus-weighted comparison (config_017) would help separate the fusion method from the value of the image modality itself.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 (config_001) is the best result so far at 0.629 accuracy and 0.599 F1. Image-only ResNet50 is much weaker at 0.485. Concat fusion of the two (config_016) reached 0.536, below RNA alone. So naive fusion hurt. It is unclear whether the images lack useful complementary signal or whether concat simply lets the weaker, poorly scaled image features dilute the RNA signal. 2. What this tests: config_017 keeps everything from config_016 the same (single-profile, PCA-2000, ResNet50) and changes only the fusion, from concat to weighted. This cleanly isolates the effect of the fusion method. If weighted fusion recovers or beats RNA-only performance, concat was the problem and multimodal is worth exploring further. If it stays well below RNA-only, that points to limited value from the ResNet50 image features. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: whether fusion can ever beat the RNA-only baseline is the central open question. Testing it with a single-factor change before expanding to other encoders or multiprofile settings avoids wasting runs on a fusion design that may be flawed. It also uses the already-measured components, so the result is directly interpretable.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the single-profile multimodal setup from llm_summary_005 (PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 images, no aggregation) and changed only the fusion, from concat to weighted, making it a clean single-factor test of the fusion method. Validation accuracy fell sharply, from 0.5362 to 0.3275 (about 21 points), and supporting F1 fell from 0.5158 to 0.2884. This is the lowest result so far, well below the RNA-only baseline (0.6287 / 0.5993) and also below image-only ResNet50 (0.4849 / 0.4639). So in this configuration weighted fusion did not recover RNA-only performance and did substantially worse than concat. Because a fused model scoring below both of its unimodal parts suggests a possible optimization or implementation problem with the weighted fusion (e.g., weight initialization, normalization, or training instability) rather than clear evidence about the value of the image signal, it remains uncertain whether the images add any complementary information. With one run per configuration, run-to-run variance and untuned fusion hyperparameters are also unresolved, and it is not yet known whether any fusion design can beat the RNA-only baseline.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is still the simplest model, RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 (0.629 acc / 0.599 F1). Every added complexity has hurt in single runs: multiprofile with avgpool or transformer, image-only ResNet50, and concat or weighted fusion. The RNA encoder, the factor most likely to matter given that RNA is the strongest modality, has not been varied at all. 2) This run keeps RNA-only and single-profile fixed and swaps only the encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT. It is a clean single-factor test of whether a pretrained foundation-model representation beats a linear PCA representation. 3) It isolates representation, a major open design choice, on the strongest known setting. It also has real potential to set a new best score. Whatever the outcome, it tells us which RNA encoder to use in later profile, aggregation and fusion experiments, so it is more informative than further tests of the multiprofile or fusion variants that have already underperformed.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the strongest setting, RNA-only and single-profile with no image encoder, aggregation or fusion, and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to pretrained scGPT, making it a clean single-factor test of RNA representation. Validation accuracy fell from 0.6287 to 0.5729 (about 5.6 points). Supporting F1 fell less, from 0.5993 to 0.5730 (about 2.6 points). So in this setup scGPT embeddings did not beat the linear PCA representation, and PCA-2000 RNA-only single-profile remains the best configuration so far. With one run per configuration and no tuning of how scGPT is used (e.g., frozen vs. fine-tuned embeddings, gene vocabulary overlap, downstream head capacity), it remains uncertain whether the gap reflects the representation itself, an under-optimized scGPT pipeline, or run-to-run variance. It is also unknown whether other encoders (e.g., scVI) or scGPT in multiprofile or fusion settings would behave differently.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA-only single-profile is the strongest setting so far. PCA-2000 reached 0.629 accuracy and 0.599 F1, and scGPT reached 0.573 and 0.573. Multiprofile aggregation (avgpool and transformer) and fusion (concat and weighted) have both hurt performance with PCA. That leaves the RNA representation as the most promising axis that is still unresolved. scVI is the only RNA encoder not yet tested. 2) Test: config_004 keeps the best setting (RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion) and changes only the encoder, from PCA-2000 or scGPT to scVI-200. This is a clean single-factor comparison that completes the RNA encoder axis. It shows whether a compact learned latent space beats the linear PCA baseline, or whether PCA is consistently the best choice across representation types. 3) Value: under a limited budget, this has the highest expected immediate payoff because it varies the strongest setting. It also has high information value, because the best RNA encoder determines which encoder to carry into any later multiprofile or fusion experiments. That avoids spending runs on complex combinations built on a weaker RNA representation.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the strongest setting (RNA-only, single-profile, no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder to scVI with a 200-dimensional latent space, completing a clean single-factor comparison of RNA encoders. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5321 (supporting F1 0.5172). That is about 9.7 points below PCA-2000 (0.6287 / 0.5993) and about 4.1 points below scGPT (0.5729 / 0.5730), so in this setup the ranking is PCA-2000 > scGPT > scVI-200, and PCA-2000 remains the best RNA encoder and the best configuration so far. Uncertainties remain because each configuration has one run and scVI is untuned. Run-to-run variance is unknown, and the result may reflect scVI training choices (e.g., latent size, epochs, preprocessing or batch handling) or simply the smaller representation (200 vs. 2000 dimensions) rather than the learned latent approach itself. It is also untested whether the encoder ranking holds in multiprofile or fusion settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: PCA-2000 RNA-only single-profile is the best so far (0.629 acc / 0.599 F1). Multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer) and the alternative RNA encoders (scGPT, scVI) both did worse. Multimodal fusion with ResNet50 also fell short of RNA-only: concat reached 0.536 and weighted 0.328. The image side has only been tested with ResNet50 (0.485 acc), so we cannot tell whether images carry little signal or ResNet50 is just a weak representation. 2. Test: image-only, single-profile, swapping only ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. This is a clean single-factor test of image representation, the one major design axis not yet examined. 3. Why now: every remaining multimodal configuration depends on how useful the image features are. If ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50, fusing it with PCA (e.g., config_022) becomes a promising next step. If it does not, that supports deprioritizing image and fusion configurations and focusing the remaining budget elsewhere. Either outcome narrows a large part of the untested space at low cost.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the image-only, single-profile setup from llm_summary_004 (no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, a clean single-factor test of image representation. Validation accuracy rose modestly from 0.4849 to 0.5200 (about 3.5 points), and supporting F1 rose from 0.4639 to 0.4791 (about 1.5 points). Image-only ViT-L is still well below the best RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile configuration (0.6287 / 0.5993) and slightly below the PCA-2000 + ResNet50 concat fusion (0.5362), so a better image representation helped but did not close the gap to RNA alone. With one run per configuration, a gain of this size may partly reflect run-to-run variance. Encoder usage was also untuned (e.g., frozen vs. fine-tuned features, input resolution, augmentation). It remains untested whether ViT-L features would add complementary signal when fused with PCA-2000 (e.g., config_022 with concat). The modest image-only improvement makes that test plausible but not clearly promising.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: PCA-2000 RNA-only single-profile is the best configuration so far (0.6287 acc / 0.5993 F1). Multiprofile hurt RNA-only performance with both aggregators, and alternative RNA encoders ranked below PCA. Concat fusion with ResNet50 (0.5362) underperformed RNA alone, and weighted fusion was much worse. ViT-L improved image-only accuracy over ResNet50 (0.5200 vs 0.4849, F1 0.4791 vs 0.4639). The key open question is whether a stronger image representation can add complementary signal to PCA RNA, or whether fusion in this setup simply dilutes the RNA signal. 2) Test: config_022 keeps PCA-2000, single-profile and concat fusion fixed, the best choices for each factor so far, and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L. This is a clean single-factor comparison against config_016. If fusion approaches or beats the RNA-only baseline, image quality is the bottleneck and multimodal search is worth continuing. If it stays well below 0.6287, that is stronger evidence that fusion is not helping here regardless of image encoder. 3) Why now: this is the most plausible remaining route to beating the baseline, and either outcome narrows a large share of the remaining multimodal configurations. Multiprofile or weighted variants are less promising given the consistent negative evidence for them, and they would confound more factors.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the single-profile PCA-2000 + concat fusion setup from llm_summary_005 and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, a clean single-factor test of image representation within fusion. Validation accuracy fell from 0.5362 to 0.4348 (about 10 points) and supporting F1 fell from 0.5158 to 0.4234, about 19 points below the RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline (0.6287 / 0.5993). The result also fell below both of its unimodal components, image-only ViT-L (0.5200) and image-only ResNet50 (0.4849). So the stronger image-only encoder did not carry over to fusion, and concat fusion has now failed to beat RNA alone with both image encoders, which weakens the case that image quality is the bottleneck. Because a fused model scoring below its own unimodal parts suggests a possible optimization or integration problem (e.g., feature scaling or normalization between PCA and ViT-L features, dimensionality imbalance, or training instability) rather than clean evidence that images lack complementary signal, and because each configuration has only one run with untuned fusion, it remains uncertain whether any fusion design in this pipeline could add value over PCA-2000 RNA-only, which remains the best configuration so far.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2. Test: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, cheapest configuration in the space, with no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that later experiments can be compared against one factor at a time. Next steps could swap the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), switch to multiprofile, or compare against an image-only baseline. 3. Why now: Under a limited budget, a simple baseline makes every later result easier to interpret. It lets us measure whether extra complexity actually helps, rather than assuming that multimodal or multiprofile models are better.
experiment_summary: The first completed experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest configuration in the search space: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.586 (primary metric), with a similar validation F1 of 0.574, which suggests performance is fairly balanced across classes rather than driven by one majority class. Because no other experiments have been run, this is only a baseline. It shows nothing yet about whether alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile settings, image modalities, aggregation, or fusion would help or hurt. It is also unknown how much this result would vary with a different seed or data split, so single-run differences in later comparisons should be interpreted cautiously.

selection_reason: Evidence: the only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.586, F1 0.574). Nothing is known about the image modality, which appears in about two-thirds of the remaining configurations (all image-only and multimodal ones). Test: config_010 is the simplest image-only setup (single-profile ResNet50, no aggregation or fusion). Why now: this one run sharply reduces uncertainty about whether images are informative. That determines whether multimodal fusion is worth budget or whether the search should focus on RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation. One run is not decisive, but it guides the largest share of the search space.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 tested the simplest image-only setup: a single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.520 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.498, below the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.586 accuracy, 0.574 F1). This is an initial observation that images alone carry some usable signal but less than RNA in these simple settings, with a slightly larger accuracy–F1 gap that may hint at less balanced per-class performance. The comparison changes both the modality and the encoder (ResNet50 vs. PCA), so it cannot attribute the gap to modality alone, and with single runs and unknown seed or split variance the size of the gap is uncertain. It remains unknown whether other image encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion with RNA would add complementary value beyond RNA alone.

selection_reason:
1. Evidence and uncertainty: There are only two baselines. RNA-only PCA single-profile reached 0.586 accuracy (F1 0.574). Image-only ResNet50 single-profile reached 0.520 accuracy (F1 0.498). RNA looks stronger on its own, but we do not know whether the image signal complements RNA or is redundant. That is one of the most consequential questions in the search space, because it decides whether the large multimodal branch is worth exploring.

2. What this tests: config_016 combines exactly the two tested unimodal components, PCA RNA and ResNet50 images, in the single-profile setting. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: The outcome guides many later choices. If fusion clearly beats 0.586 on accuracy and F1, multimodal configurations deserve priority, and encoder, aggregation and fusion type can be refined later. If it does not, the budget can shift toward RNA encoder and multiprofile comparisons. Given single-run variance, a gain of only one or two points would be treated as tentative rather than conclusive.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 tested the simplest multimodal configuration: single-profile, PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder plus ResNet50 image encoder, concat fusion, no aggregation. It combines exactly the two components from the unimodal baselines, so comparing against them isolates the effect of adding a modality. It reached 0.591 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.573 F1, essentially matching the RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.586 accuracy, 0.574 F1) and clearly exceeding image-only (llm_summary_002: 0.520 / 0.498). This suggests that, in this simple setup, adding ResNet50 image features to PCA RNA gives at most a negligible benefit. The ~0.5-point accuracy gain with flat F1 is within plausible single-run variance and falls below the one-to-two-point threshold set beforehand as only tentative evidence. It remains uncertain whether image signal is truly redundant with RNA or whether naive concat fusion, the image encoder choice, lack of multiprofile aggregation, or seed/split variance hides complementary value. Alternative fusion methods, encoders, and repeated runs would be needed to tell these apart.

What this tests: config_002 keeps the strongest simple baseline (RNA-only, PCA 2000) and changes only one thing, single-profile to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 changed one variable from the RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_001), switching from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation and keeping the PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image modality. Because only the profile setting and its aggregation changed, this is an initial observation that multiprofile with simple average pooling does not help, and may hurt, in this RNA-only setup. It is a single run, and seed or split variance is unknown. experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 changed only the RNA encoder relative to the RNA-only single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001), swapping PCA (2000 components) for scVI (200 dimensions) with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached 0.532 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.516 F1, about 5.4 and 5.8 points below the PCA baseline (0.586 / 0.574). Because the encoder is the only difference, this is an initial single-run observation that this scVI representation underperforms PCA in the simplest setting, which would favor keeping PCA as the default RNA encoder for now. Several questions remain open. Seed or split variance is unknown. The comparison cannot separate the scVI method from its much lower dimensionality (200 vs. 2000) or its training and hyperparameter choices. It is also untested whether scVI would behave differently in multiprofile or multimodal settings, or how scGPT (config_007) would compare.
