experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 changed only the RNA encoder relative to the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (llm_summary_001), swapping PCA (2000 components) for the pretrained scGPT representation, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached 0.519 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.480 F1. That is about 6.7 and 9.5 points below PCA (0.586 / 0.574) and slightly below scVI (llm_summary_005: 0.532 / 0.516), making scGPT the weakest RNA encoder tested so far and similar to image-only ResNet50 (0.520 / 0.498). Its larger accuracy–F1 gap may hint at less balanced per-class performance. Because the encoder is the only change, this is an initial single-run observation that favors keeping PCA as the default RNA encoder. Seed or split variance is still unknown, and the comparison cannot separate the scGPT model from how its embeddings were extracted or used (e.g., no fine-tuning, embedding dimensionality, downstream classifier settings). It also remains untested whether scGPT would behave differently in multiprofile or multimodal configurations.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: PCA single-profile is the best RNA-only setup so far (0.586 accuracy). Multiprofile with avgpool (config_002) dropped about 4.6 points. That result cannot separate multiprofile itself from the simple average-pooling aggregator. Most of the remaining search space is multiprofile, so this uncertainty matters a lot. 2) Test: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA) and swaps only avgpool for transformer aggregation. This isolates the effect of aggregation and shows whether learned aggregation can recover or beat single-profile performance. 3) Why now: the result will strongly shape the rest of the search. If transformer aggregation also underperforms, multiprofile configurations can be deprioritized and the budget shifted to single-profile image-encoder (ViT-L) and fusion comparisons. If it helps, multiprofile-transformer becomes a promising base for multimodal extensions. Either outcome is informative at the cost of one run, though as a single run it should be treated as tentative.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with the PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and transformer aggregation. It differs from llm_summary_004 only in the aggregator (transformer instead of avgpool), so that comparison isolates the aggregation choice. It reached 0.632 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.607 F1. That is about 9.2 and 8.2 points above multiprofile avgpool (0.540 / 0.524) and about 4.6 and 3.2 points above the single-profile PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.586 / 0.574), making it the best configuration so far. The result suggests that the earlier multiprofile drop was tied to avgpool rather than to multiprofile itself, and that learned aggregation over multiple profiles can beat single-profile RNA. Multiprofile-transformer therefore looks like a promising base for multimodal extensions. However, the single-profile comparison changes both the profile setting and the aggregation, so it cannot attribute the gain to multiprofile data versus transformer capacity. All results are single runs with unknown seed or split variance. It also remains untested whether the gain carries over to image or multimodal multiprofile setups, other fusion methods, or other RNA encoders.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only multiprofile with PCA and transformer aggregation (config_003: 0.632 acc / 0.607 F1). It beats single-profile PCA by about 4.6 points and multiprofile avgpool by about 9 points, so learned aggregation over profiles looks like the key positive design choice. In the single-profile setting, adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion gave only a negligible change (0.591 vs 0.586). The open question is whether image signal is redundant with RNA or whether it becomes complementary when aggregated across multiple profiles. 2) Test: config_020 adds ResNet50 images with concat fusion to the config_003 setup, changing only the modality. Compared with config_003, it isolates the value of images in the strongest RNA setting. Compared with config_016, it shows whether the multiprofile-transformer gain carries over to multimodal models. 3) Why now: It exploits the most promising direction found so far while answering a central question about multimodal fusion, using the simplest fusion and the image encoder already tested so the comparison stays clean. If images add nothing here, the budget can shift to RNA-side or encoder questions. If they help, weighted fusion (config_021) or the ViT-L encoder (config_026) are natural one-variable follow-ups. Since every result is a single run, I would treat a difference of only about a point as tentative.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 added ResNet50 image features with concat fusion to the best configuration so far (llm_summary_007: RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000, transformer aggregation), changing only the modality. It reached 0.332 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.315 F1, about 30 and 29 points below llm_summary_007 (0.632 / 0.607) and also below every earlier run, including image-only single-profile (0.520) and single-profile multimodal concat (0.591). Because modality is the only isolated change, this single run indicates that this multimodal multiprofile-transformer-concat setup performs far worse than its RNA-only counterpart, even though adding images was roughly neutral in the single-profile setting. The collapse is too large to be ordinary seed variance, but the cause is unresolved: it could reflect genuine interference from image features, optimization or training instability (e.g., scale mismatch between concatenated features under transformer aggregation), or an implementation or pipeline issue. A rerun or sanity checks, and alternatives such as weighted fusion (config_021) or a different image encoder, would be needed before concluding that images hurt in multiprofile models.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only multiprofile PCA-2000 with transformer aggregation (config_003) is the best result so far (0.632 accuracy / 0.607 F1). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion on that same base (config_020) collapsed to 0.332 / 0.315, far below every other run. In the single-profile setting, concat fusion was roughly neutral (0.591 vs 0.586). The cause of the collapse is unknown. Possible causes are naive concat (for example, feature-scale mismatch with the 2000-dimensional PCA input under transformer aggregation), interference from the image features themselves, or a pipeline problem. 2) What this tests: config_021 differs from config_020 only in fusion (weighted instead of concat), with the same RNA encoder, image encoder, profile setting and aggregation. It directly tests whether the collapse is specific to concat fusion. If weighted fusion recovers to or above about 0.63, it points to concat as the culprit and could give a new best multimodal model. If it also collapses, that points to image features or multimodal transformer training more broadly, and image-only multiprofile transformer (config_012) or a ViT encoder would be the next diagnostics. 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: it is a single-variable comparison at the most important open decision point, the multimodal extension of the best configuration. It is both informative and has real upside for accuracy.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 changed only the fusion method relative to llm_summary_008 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 images, transformer aggregation), using weighted fusion instead of concat. This isolates the fusion choice as a test of whether the earlier collapse was specific to concat. It reached 0.507 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.455 F1, about 17.5 and 14 points above the concat version (0.332 / 0.315). It remained about 12.5 and 15 points below the RNA-only multiprofile-transformer best (llm_summary_007: 0.632 / 0.607) and below image-only single-profile (0.520 / 0.498). Within this single-run comparison, concat appears to account for part of the collapse, but weighted fusion did not reach the ~0.63 recovery threshold set beforehand. Multimodal multiprofile-transformer models therefore still substantially underperform their RNA-only counterpart, and the widened accuracy–F1 gap may hint at less balanced per-class performance. It remains unresolved whether the remaining deficit comes from interference by the ResNet50 image features, multimodal transformer optimization issues (e.g., feature-scale mismatch), or a shared pipeline problem. Seed or split variance is unknown, so diagnostics such as image-only multiprofile transformer (config_012), a ViT encoder, or a rerun would help separate these explanations.

selection_reason:
1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only multiprofile with transformer aggregation (config_003) is the best run so far (0.632 accuracy / 0.607 F1). Adding ResNet50 images to that setup made results much worse, falling to 0.332 with concat fusion and 0.507 with weighted fusion. In the single-profile setting, adding images was roughly neutral (0.591 vs 0.586). We do not know whether this multimodal multiprofile drop comes from the ResNet50 image features themselves under multiprofile transformer aggregation, from the fusion step, or from a pipeline problem. Image features have never been tested in a multiprofile setting on their own.

2. What this tests: config_012 changes only the modality relative to config_020/021. It removes RNA and keeps ResNet50, multiprofile and the transformer aggregator. It is also the multiprofile-transformer counterpart of image-only single-profile (config_010, 0.520). If image-only multiprofile transformer reaches or beats 0.52, the image path works and the deficit likely comes from how RNA and image features are fused. If it collapses well below 0.52, the image features or the image multiprofile pipeline under this aggregator are the likely cause.

3. Why it is the best next run: the multimodal multiprofile collapse is the biggest unexplained result, and it blocks decisions about the whole multimodal branch, including ViT and other fusion variants. One isolated diagnostic run is a better use of the limited budget than trying more multimodal combinations blindly. Testing the transformer with other RNA encoders (e.g., config_006) is less urgent, because both scVI and scGPT already trail PCA.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 was a diagnostic run for the multimodal multiprofile collapse. It tested image-only, multiprofile, ResNet50 with transformer aggregation, which differs from the multimodal multiprofile runs (llm_summary_008/009) only by removing RNA. It reached 0.535 validation accuracy (primary metric) and 0.519 F1, slightly above image-only single-profile (llm_summary_002: 0.520 / 0.498) and well above the multimodal multiprofile runs (concat 0.332, weighted 0.507), though far below the RNA-only multiprofile-transformer best (llm_summary_007: 0.632 / 0.607). This meets the pre-set ≥0.52 criterion, so as an initial observation the ResNet50 image path does not collapse under multiprofile transformer aggregation; since both RNA-only and image-only multiprofile runs outperform their combination, the multimodal deficit more likely arises from how RNA and image features are combined (fusion, feature-scale interaction, or a multimodal-specific pipeline issue) rather than from the image features alone. Uncertainties remain: the ~1.5-point gain over single-profile is within plausible single-run variance and confounds profile setting with aggregation, seed or split variance is unknown, and the exact multimodal failure mechanism (e.g., normalization or scale mismatch versus a bug) has not been isolated.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest baseline in the space. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that later experiments can be compared against, one factor at a time: encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), modality (image-only), and fusion (multimodal). 3) Starting from the simplest configuration avoids assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better. It lets each later experiment isolate one design choice, so the limited budget is spent on interpretable contrasts rather than confounded jumps.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration in the search space: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.573 (primary metric), with a closely matching validation F1 of 0.573, which suggests performance is fairly balanced across classes rather than driven by one class. No other experiments have been completed, so this is an initial baseline. It does not show whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile settings (avgpool or transformer), image-only models, or multimodal fusion would do better or worse. Variability across seeds or splits is also unknown, so later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons against this reference should treat small differences cautiously.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001), with accuracy 0.573 and a matching F1. We know nothing yet about the image modality. Most of the remaining search space (the image-only and all multimodal configurations) depends on whether image features carry useful signal for this task. 2. What it tests: The image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model with no aggregation or fusion is the image counterpart of the RNA baseline. Comparing the two shows how informative image features are on their own. That tells us whether fusion is likely to help, and whether image encoder choices are worth budget. 3. Why now: Encoder or profile tweaks within RNA-only would refine only one branch. This experiment resolves the biggest structural uncertainty with a single, simple run. A strong image result would justify exploring multimodal fusion and multiprofile setups, while a weak one would point the budget toward RNA encoders and profile settings.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion, as the image counterpart to the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.422 (primary metric) with a slightly lower validation F1 of 0.405, well below the RNA-only baseline's 0.573 accuracy and 0.573 F1. This is an initial observation that, under these specific encoder choices, ResNet50 image features alone carry less discriminative signal than PCA RNA features. Because the two runs differ in both modality and encoder, the gap cannot be attributed to modality alone. Several questions remain open: whether other image encoders or multiprofile aggregation would narrow the gap, whether image features add complementary information under multimodal fusion despite weaker standalone performance, and how large seed- or split-level variability is.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA single-profile reached 0.573 accuracy and 0.573 F1. Image-only ResNet50 single-profile reached only 0.422 accuracy and 0.405 F1. So the RNA features carry more standalone signal, but each result comes from a single run. We still do not know whether the weaker image features add complementary information when combined with RNA. This is a central design question for the search. 2. What this tests: config_016 adds the same ResNet50 image features to the RNA baseline (config_001) using concat fusion. The RNA encoder and single-profile setting stay fixed. This isolates whether adding image information helps, hurts or does nothing, and both of its components have already been measured alone. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: the modality question decides whether the large multimodal part of the search space (most remaining configs) is worth exploring. If fusion gives a clear gain, later runs can study fusion type, aggregation and encoders within multimodal models. If it does not, the budget can shift to RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation. A single small difference should be treated cautiously, but this one-factor comparison is the most decision-relevant experiment now.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested a multimodal, single-profile model that concatenates PCA (n=2000) RNA features with ResNet50 image features. RNA encoder and profile setting were held fixed relative to the RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_001), so the comparison isolates adding the image modality under concat fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.542 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.483. Accuracy is below the RNA-only baseline (0.573) but well above image-only (0.422), and the larger drop in F1 (0.573 to 0.483) suggests less balanced per-class performance. This is an initial observation that naive concat fusion with ResNet50 features did not help and may have hurt relative to RNA alone. Each result comes from a single run with unknown seed or split variability, so the size and reliability of the roughly 0.03 accuracy gap are uncertain. It also remains open whether other fusion methods, image encoders, or multiprofile aggregation would let image features contribute complementary signal.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: RNA-only PCA single-profile is the best result (0.573 accuracy, 0.573 F1). Image-only ResNet50 is much weaker (0.422). Concat fusion with ResNet50 did not help: accuracy fell to 0.542 and F1 fell further to 0.483. The profile-setting axis (single vs multiprofile) has not been tested at all, even though it applies across every modality and many remaining configurations. 2) This run changes only the profile setting, to multiprofile with avgpool, while keeping the strongest known setup fixed (RNA-only, PCA n2000). Comparing it with config_001 isolates whether pooling multiple profiles adds signal. Avgpool is the simpler aggregator, so it gives a cleaner first test than the transformer. 3) It is the best next experiment because it builds on the strongest direction found so far and resolves a major untested design choice. Whatever the result, it will inform which of the many multiprofile configurations are worth running, for RNA, image and multimodal models alike. That makes it more useful than further fusion variants, given that fusion has so far underperformed.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested an RNA-only, multiprofile model with a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder and avgpool aggregation. It differs from the RNA-only single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001) only in the profile setting, so the comparison isolates switching to multiprofile with avgpool. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.540 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.524. Both are below the baseline (0.573 accuracy, 0.573 F1) and roughly match the concat-fusion run on accuracy (0.542), though with higher F1 (0.524 vs 0.483). This is an initial observation that average-pooling multiple profiles did not help, and may have hurt, in this RNA PCA setup. Several points remain uncertain: the roughly 0.03 accuracy gap comes from single runs with unknown seed or split variability, and it is unclear whether a learned aggregator (transformer), other RNA encoders, or other modalities would benefit from multiprofile inputs where simple averaging did not.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only single-profile with PCA (0.573 acc / 0.573 F1) is the best result so far. Image-only ResNet50 (0.422) was clearly weaker. Concat fusion (0.542) and multiprofile avgpool (0.540) both came in about 0.03 below the baseline, and these single runs cannot separate that gap from noise. The RNA encoder, which drives the strongest modality, has not been varied at all. 2. What this tests: config_004 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA n2000 to scVI n200, keeping the RNA-only single-profile setup. This isolates whether the RNA representation is a key lever for performance. 3. Why now: RNA is the dominant signal source and many remaining configurations depend on the RNA encoder choice. Learning early whether scVI beats or trails PCA tells us which encoder to carry into later aggregation and fusion experiments. It is a clean one-factor comparison against the current best baseline, with real potential to improve on it.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested an RNA-only, single-profile model with an scVI (n200) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It differs from the best-so-far baseline (llm_summary_001, PCA n2000) only in the RNA encoder setting. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.507 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.455, about 0.066 accuracy and 0.118 F1 below the baseline (0.573 / 0.573), so it is the weakest RNA-based run so far, and the large F1 drop suggests less balanced per-class performance. This is an initial observation that this scVI configuration trailed PCA n2000 and that the RNA encoder choice may matter more than the roughly 0.03 gaps seen for concat fusion and avgpool multiprofile. However, the comparison changes both the method (scVI vs PCA) and the n setting (200 vs 2000), so the effect of each cannot be separated, and with single runs and unknown seed or split variability it remains open whether other scVI settings, scGPT, or scVI combined with multiprofile or fusion would behave differently.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: RNA-only PCA n2000 single-profile (0.573 acc / 0.573 F1) is the best result so far. The other single-factor changes all fell short: concat fusion with ResNet50 (0.542), avgpool multiprofile (0.540) and image-only ResNet50 (0.422). The largest single-factor effect came from the RNA encoder, where scVI n200 dropped to 0.507 accuracy and 0.455 F1. That suggests the encoder choice may matter more than the other axes tested so far. scGPT, the third RNA encoder option, is still untested. 2. Test: config_007 changes only the RNA encoder relative to the baseline (PCA to scGPT), keeping RNA-only and single-profile fixed. This completes the RNA encoder comparison and shows whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding beats or trails PCA. 3. Why now: RNA is the strongest modality, and the encoder is the factor with the largest observed effect. Pinning down the best RNA backbone tells us which encoder to carry into later aggregation and fusion tests. It is a clean one-factor comparison, and it could either produce a new best configuration or confirm PCA as the reference. Either outcome usefully narrows the remaining search space under the limited budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 tested an RNA-only, single-profile model with a pretrained scGPT RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It differs from the best-so-far baseline (llm_summary_001, PCA n2000) only in the RNA encoder, which completes the three-way RNA encoder comparison. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.520 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.498. That is about 0.053 accuracy and 0.075 F1 below PCA n2000 (0.573 / 0.573) but above scVI n200 (0.507 / 0.455), giving an initial ordering of PCA > scGPT > scVI and suggesting that this foundation-model embedding, used as configured here, did not beat the simpler PCA features. This supports keeping PCA n2000 as the reference RNA encoder for later aggregation and fusion tests. Uncertainty remains because the scGPT vs scVI gap (about 0.013 accuracy) is small and all results are single runs with unknown seed or split variability. It is also unknown whether other scGPT settings (e.g., fine-tuning or embedding choices) would change the result, or whether scGPT would behave differently than PCA when combined with multiprofile aggregation or multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: PCA n2000 is the strongest RNA encoder so far (0.573 accuracy and F1), ahead of scGPT and scVI. Neither avgpool multiprofile nor concat fusion helped. The only image encoder tested, ResNet50, was weak on its own (0.422). The image-encoder choice is still completely untested, and it affects about half of the remaining configurations, including every multimodal option. 2) What this tests: switching from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L in the image-only, single-profile setting changes only the encoder. That shows whether the weak image signal comes from the modality or from ResNet50 features. 3) Why now: if ViT-L substantially narrows the gap to RNA, the ViT-L multimodal configurations (e.g., config_022 and config_023) become strong candidates. If it does not, we can deprioritize image-encoder variation and focus on transformer aggregation or weighted fusion with PCA. This single-factor test reduces the most uncertainty across the remaining search space for one experiment.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 tested an image-only, single-profile model with an ImageNet ViT-L image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It differs from the ResNet50 image-only run (llm_summary_002) only in the image encoder. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.715 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.687. That is far above ResNet50 (0.422 / 0.405) and also above the best RNA-only baseline, PCA n2000 (0.573 / 0.573), making it the best configuration so far. Within this encoder comparison, the result suggests that the earlier weak image performance came largely from ResNet50 features rather than from the image modality itself, and that ViT-L-based multimodal configurations (e.g., config_022/023) are now high-priority candidates. Several points remain uncertain. These are single runs with unknown seed or split variability, though the roughly 0.29 accuracy gain is large compared with gaps seen elsewhere. The F1 is somewhat below accuracy, suggesting some per-class imbalance. It is also unknown whether PCA RNA features would add complementary signal to ViT-L under concat or other fusion, given that concat with ResNet50 did not help, and whether multiprofile aggregation would help ViT-L image features.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Image-only ViT-L (config_013) is the best run so far at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. That is far above RNA-only PCA n2000 (0.573) and ResNet50 (0.422). The one multimodal run (config_016) concatenated PCA RNA with the weak ResNet50 features and did not beat RNA alone. So it is still unknown whether RNA adds complementary signal when paired with a strong image encoder. 2) Test: config_022 adds PCA n2000 RNA to ViT-L using concat fusion in the single-profile setting. It differs from config_013 only by adding RNA, and from config_016 only by the image encoder. This gives two clean one-factor comparisons: whether fusing RNA helps or hurts the best image model, and whether the earlier fusion failure was due to ResNet50. 3) Why now: whether multimodality is worth pursuing is the most important open design question, and it determines whether the many remaining ViT-L multimodal configurations deserve budget. Concat is the simplest fusion and serves as a reference for later tests of weighted fusion or multiprofile aggregation. This run is both informative and a plausible candidate for the new best result.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 tested a multimodal, single-profile model that concatenates PCA (n=2000) RNA features with ImageNet ViT-L image features. It differs from the best run, image-only ViT-L (llm_summary_007, 0.715 accuracy / 0.687 F1), only by adding RNA, and from the ResNet50 concat run (llm_summary_003, 0.542 / 0.483) only by the image encoder. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.260 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.222. That is far below ViT-L alone, PCA RNA alone (0.573 / 0.573), and every other run so far, so in this single-run comparison, adding PCA RNA to ViT-L under concat coincided with a severe collapse rather than complementary gains. Because performance fell well below both unimodal components, the result may reflect an optimization or training failure specific to this combination (for example, feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance between the two encoders) rather than a true lack of complementary signal, and seed or split variability is unknown, so a rerun or sanity check, plus tests of normalized or weighted fusion, would be needed before treating multimodal ViT-L configurations as unpromising.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Image-only ViT-L is the best run so far (0.715 accuracy / 0.687 F1). Adding PCA RNA with concat fusion (config_022) collapsed to 0.260 / 0.222, which is below both single-modality models. That pattern points to a fusion or optimization failure, such as feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance between the encoders, rather than a true absence of complementary signal. Concat also failed with ResNet50, though only mildly. 2. What this tests: config_023 differs from config_022 only in fusion (weighted instead of concat), so it isolates whether the collapse came from concat. If weighted fusion recovers to near or above 0.715, the whole ViT-L multimodal branch (config_024 to config_027) stays worth pursuing. If it also fails, the budget can go toward ViT-L image-only multiprofile extensions instead. 3. Why it is the best use of the next experiment: it resolves the largest current uncertainty, whether multimodal ViT-L is viable at all. It does so with a one-factor change and has realistic upside to beat the best configuration.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 tested a multimodal, single-profile model combining PCA (n=2000) RNA features with ImageNet ViT-L image features under weighted fusion. It differs from the collapsed concat run (llm_summary_008, 0.260 accuracy / 0.222 F1) only in the fusion method, so it isolates whether concat alone caused the collapse. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.328 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.288. That is a modest improvement over concat but still far below image-only ViT-L (0.715 / 0.687), PCA RNA alone (0.573 / 0.573), and the ResNet50 concat run (0.542 / 0.483). This initial observation suggests that switching from concat to weighted fusion did not resolve the PCA + ViT-L failure and that the problem is not specific to concat. Possible explanations include feature-scale or dimensionality mismatch, an optimization or training-pipeline issue, or a genuine lack of complementary signal, and the available evidence does not distinguish among them. The roughly 0.07 accuracy gain over concat comes from single runs with unknown seed or split variability. It also remains open whether feature normalization, per-modality projection, other fusion methods, or multiprofile settings would rescue multimodal ViT-L, or whether budget is better directed toward ViT-L image-only extensions.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Image-only ViT-L single-profile is clearly the best run so far (0.715 acc / 0.687 F1). Both PCA+ViT-L multimodal runs collapsed under concat (0.260) and weighted fusion (0.328), so the cause of that failure is unclear and multimodal ViT-L looks risky. For RNA PCA, avgpool multiprofile was slightly worse than single-profile (0.540 vs 0.573). That is a single run, and it may not carry over to image features, which could gain more from averaging across profiles. 2) Test: config_014 changes only the profile setting of the best configuration, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool. This isolates whether multiprofile aggregation helps the strongest representation. It also shows whether the multiprofile effect seen with RNA depends on the modality. 3) Why now: it builds directly on the strongest evidence and has a good chance of improving on the best score. It also answers a key design question cheaply, since avgpool is the simplest aggregator and transformer aggregation (config_015) can follow if pooling helps. Further multimodal ViT-L runs can wait until there is a clearer read on the fusion failure.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 tested an image-only, multiprofile model with an ImageNet ViT-L image encoder and avgpool aggregation. It differs from the best run so far, image-only single-profile ViT-L (llm_summary_007, 0.715 accuracy / 0.687 F1), only in the profile setting, so the comparison isolates the switch to avgpool multiprofile. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.532 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.516, about 0.18 accuracy and 0.17 F1 below single-profile ViT-L. It is also slightly below PCA RNA single-profile (0.573) and close to RNA avgpool multiprofile (0.540). This initial observation suggests that avgpool multiprofile hurt ViT-L image features as well as RNA PCA (where the drop was about 0.03), and that the drop was much larger here. Simple averaging across profiles therefore looks unhelpful in both modalities tested so far. Uncertainty remains because these are single runs with unknown seed or split variability. It is unclear whether the large drop reflects a real loss of profile-specific signal under averaging or a pipeline or optimization issue in the multiprofile setup. It is also open whether a learned aggregator (transformer, e.g., config_015) would recover or exceed single-profile performance, so single-profile ViT-L remains the reference configuration.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: no experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion method matters, and no reference point for performance. 2. What it tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, lowest-variance configuration. It gives a reference accuracy and F1 for later single-factor comparisons: changing the RNA encoder (config_004 scVI, config_007 scGPT), adding multiprofile aggregation (config_002 and config_003), switching to an image-only model (config_010) and adding fusion (config_016 and config_017). 3. Why now: under a limited budget, a simple anchor experiment makes each later experiment an interpretable one-variable change rather than a confounded jump into a complex multimodal setup. It also avoids assuming that more complex models are better before any evidence exists.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration, an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation or fusion. It was chosen as an anchor for later single-factor comparisons. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.7150 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.6872, which together suggest moderately strong performance from RNA features alone with somewhat less balanced per-class performance. This is an initial baseline only. With no other experiments completed, it is not yet known whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image-only models or multimodal fusion would improve or degrade performance. Run-to-run variance is also uncharacterized, so small future differences relative to this baseline should be read cautiously.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: only one experiment is complete. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. We have no evidence yet on profile setting, RNA encoder, image modality, aggregation or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_002 changes one factor from the baseline, switching from single-profile to multiprofile. It uses the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and keeps the RNA-only PCA setup. This cleanly isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps or hurts. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: profile setting splits nearly the whole search space, including RNA-only, image-only and multimodal configurations. Its effect therefore tells us which half of the space to prioritize. Avgpool serves as a low-complexity reference, so a later transformer run (config_003) can show whether learned aggregation adds anything. Starting with an RNA-only comparison avoids confounding the result with image-encoder or fusion choices. Any difference should still be read cautiously, since run-to-run variance is unknown.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA (2000-component) setup of the llm_summary_001 baseline and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with average-pooling aggregation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5907 (supporting F1 0.5727), about 0.12 accuracy and 0.11 F1 below the single-profile baseline (0.7150 / 0.6872). This initial observation suggests that multiprofile input with avgpool hurts performance in the RNA-only PCA setting. Because the profile-setting change is bundled with the move from no aggregation to avgpool, it is unclear whether the drop comes from multiprofile input itself or from the simple pooling. Each configuration was run only once and run-to-run variance is uncharacterized. It also remains unknown whether learned aggregation (e.g., a transformer), other RNA encoders, or image and multimodal configurations would change this picture.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only two runs exist. Single-profile RNA PCA reached 0.715 accuracy (0.687 F1). Multiprofile with avgpool dropped to 0.591 (0.573 F1). That run changed two things at once, the profile setting and the aggregation, so we cannot tell whether multiprofile input is harmful or whether simple average pooling is the problem. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 and swaps only avgpool for transformer aggregation. This isolates the effect of aggregation within multiprofile input. If accuracy recovers to near or above 0.715, the earlier drop came from naive pooling and multiprofile remains a viable direction. If it stays low, that is stronger evidence that multiprofile input itself is unhelpful here. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: Profile setting and aggregation recur across most of the remaining space, including the image-only and multimodal configurations. Resolving this question now, with a clean one-factor change, helps decide whether to deprioritize many multiprofile configurations before spending budget on encoder or fusion comparisons.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA (2000-component) setup of llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregation from avgpool to a transformer. This one-factor change was intended to test whether the earlier multiprofile drop came from naive pooling. The transformer reached 0.5420 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.4833), below both avgpool (0.5907 / 0.5727) and the single-profile baseline (0.7150 / 0.6872), so the drop was not recovered. This adds evidence that multiprofile input, with either of the two aggregators tested, underperforms single-profile input in the RNA-only PCA setting, and that transformer aggregation did not help here (the F1 decline suggests less balanced per-class performance). It remains uncertain whether this reflects multiprofile input itself or untuned or data-limited transformer aggregation, because each configuration was run once with uncharacterized variance, and the result may not transfer to other RNA encoders, image-only models or multimodal configurations.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: all three runs are RNA-only with PCA. Single-profile input (0.715 accuracy / 0.687 F1) clearly beat multiprofile input with both avgpool (0.591) and transformer (0.542). Each result is a single run, but this is a consistent signal that single-profile is the stronger setting for now. The image modality is completely untested, yet most of the remaining search space (36 multimodal and 6 image-only configs) depends on how informative image features are. 2) This experiment tests an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 encoder and no aggregation or fusion. It mirrors the config_001 anchor, differing only in modality, and gives a direct RNA-vs-image baseline under the setting that has worked best so far. 3) Why now: knowing whether images carry signal comparable to, weaker than, or stronger than RNA is the largest open uncertainty. It decides whether to spend the limited budget on multimodal fusion or on RNA encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT). It also gives a reference point for judging any later fusion gains, which makes it more informative than another RNA-only variant at this stage.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no aggregation or fusion. It mirrors the llm_summary_001 RNA-only PCA anchor except for modality and encoder, giving the first RNA-vs-image baseline under the best setting so far. It reached 0.7250 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.6847), versus 0.7150 / 0.6872 for the RNA-only baseline: about 0.01 higher accuracy and a negligibly lower F1. This initial observation suggests that image features alone carry signal roughly comparable to RNA PCA features, but with single runs and uncharacterized run-to-run variance, the gap is too small to call either modality stronger. It remains unknown whether the two modalities hold complementary information that fusion could exploit, how other image or RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT) would compare, and whether the multiprofile drop seen with RNA also occurs with images.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: single-profile RNA PCA (0.715 acc / 0.687 F1) and single-profile image ResNet50 (0.725 / 0.685) give comparable results. In RNA PCA, multiprofile input underperformed with both avgpool and the transformer, so single-profile is the strongest setting so far. Untested is whether the two modalities carry complementary information. 2) This experiment fuses exactly those two tested encoders by simple concatenation in the single-profile setting. Fusion is the only new factor, so any gain or loss over the 0.715 and 0.725 unimodal anchors can be attributed to multimodality. 3) Whether multimodal fusion helps is one of the most important open design questions. It can be answered cleanly now because both unimodal components are already measured. It also builds on the best profile setting so far rather than the setting that has looked weak. The result will show whether to spend budget on fusion variants (weighted fusion, other encoders) or on unimodal encoder alternatives. Gains of about 0.01 should still be read cautiously, given single runs.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 fused the two previously tested single-profile unimodal encoders, RNA PCA (2000 components) and image ResNet50, by simple concatenation, with no aggregation. Fusion was the only new factor relative to the unimodal anchors (llm_summary_001: 0.7150 acc / 0.6872 F1; llm_summary_004: 0.7250 / 0.6847). It reached 0.6878 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.6585), about 0.03–0.04 accuracy and 0.03 F1 below both unimodal models. This initial observation suggests that naive concat fusion did not exploit any complementary signal and may degrade performance in this setting. With single runs and uncharacterized variance, the size of the drop is uncertain. It also remains unknown whether the shortfall reflects the modalities being redundant or the fusion design itself (e.g., unnormalized or unbalanced feature scales, dimensionality, lack of tuning). Untested alternatives such as weighted or learned fusion, per-modality normalization, or other encoders might change this picture.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: In the single-profile setting, the two unimodal models perform about the same (RNA PCA 0.7150 accuracy, image ResNet50 0.7250). Concat fusion of these same encoders fell to 0.6878 accuracy and 0.6585 F1. We cannot yet tell whether the two modalities are redundant or whether naive concatenation is the problem, for example through unbalanced feature scales or the much larger PCA dimensionality swamping the image features. 2. What this tests: Config_017 changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted, keeping the single-profile setting and both encoders fixed. This directly isolates whether the fusion mechanism caused the multimodal shortfall. If weighted fusion matches or beats the unimodal models, multimodal remains a live direction worth extending to other encoders. If it also falls short, that is evidence that these features add little complementary signal, and later experiments can shift toward unimodal encoder choices such as scVI, scGPT or ViT-L. 3. Why now: The multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space and all use either concat or weighted fusion, so resolving the fusion question early tells us how much of that space deserves budget. It is a clean single-factor comparison and stays within the best-performing single-profile setting.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the single-profile multimodal setup of llm_summary_005 (RNA PCA with 2000 components plus image ResNet50, no aggregation) and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted, to test whether the fusion mechanism explained the multimodal shortfall. Weighted fusion reached 0.5375 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.5184). That is about 0.15 accuracy below concat fusion (0.6878 / 0.6585) and about 0.18–0.19 below both unimodal anchors (RNA 0.7150, image 0.7250), the largest drop observed so far. Within this single-factor comparison, weighted fusion as implemented did not recover the shortfall and performed clearly worse than concat, so neither fusion variant tested shows multimodal benefit with these encoders. However, it remains uncertain whether this reflects redundant modalities or shared fusion-design problems (untuned weights, feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance, optimization issues), because each configuration was run once with uncharacterized variance and results may differ with other encoders or normalization.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Single-profile models are clearly ahead so far. Image ResNet50 reached 0.7250 accuracy and RNA PCA reached 0.7150. Multiprofile input (two aggregators, RNA only) and both fusion methods (concat, weighted) all performed worse. Encoder choice, however, is completely untested: every result so far uses PCA for RNA and ResNet50 for images. 2. What this tests: config_013 keeps the current best setup (image-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion) and changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This isolates whether the image representation is a key performance driver. It could also produce a new best model. 3. Why now: Under a limited budget, this is a clean single-factor comparison anchored to the strongest configuration, so it combines exploitation with exploration of an important design axis. It also helps decide whether later fusion or multiprofile experiments should use ViT-L instead of ResNet50. Testing the RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) is a natural follow-up.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the strongest configuration so far (image-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion; llm_summary_004 with ResNet50: 0.7250 acc / 0.6847 F1) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. It reached 0.5362 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.5158), about 0.19 accuracy and 0.17 F1 below ResNet50 and also below the RNA PCA baseline (0.7150). In this single-factor comparison, image encoder choice is a major performance driver, and ImageNet ViT-L as used here is clearly worse than ResNet50, so ResNet50 remains the preferred image encoder for later fusion or multiprofile experiments. It remains uncertain whether the drop reflects ViT-L itself or how it was applied (e.g., frozen ImageNet features poorly matched to cellular images, preprocessing or resolution mismatch, high feature dimensionality, lack of tuning), because each configuration was run once with uncharacterized variance. RNA encoder alternatives (scVI, scGPT) are still untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Single-profile models are the strongest so far. RNA PCA reached 0.715 accuracy and image ResNet50 reached 0.725. Encoder choice proved to be a major driver on the image side, where ViT-L fell about 0.19 below ResNet50. The RNA encoder, however, has only been tested with PCA. scVI and scGPT are completely untested. Multiprofile aggregation and both fusion methods have consistently hurt, so further multimodal or multiprofile runs on the current encoders are less promising. 2. What this tests: Swapping only the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI (200 dims) in the RNA-only, single-profile anchor (config_001) isolates the effect of RNA representation. A clear gain could produce a new best model. It could also supply a better-scaled, lower-dimensional RNA feature that might change fusion outcomes later. A drop would strengthen PCA as the RNA default. 3. Why this is the best use of budget: It is a clean single-factor comparison on the largest remaining untested design dimension. It sits in the best-performing setting and has real potential to improve the top result. It also directly informs which RNA encoder to carry into any later fusion experiments.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the RNA-only, single-profile anchor of llm_summary_001 (no image encoder, aggregation or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA (2000 components) to scVI (200 dimensions). This is the first test of an alternative RNA representation. It reached 0.5191 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.4797), about 0.20 accuracy and 0.21 F1 below PCA (0.7150 / 0.6872) and below the best image-only ResNet50 model (0.7250). This is among the lowest results so far. In this single-factor comparison, RNA encoder choice is a major driver, as encoder choice was on the image side, and scVI as used here is clearly worse than PCA, which favors keeping PCA as the default RNA encoder for later work. It remains uncertain whether the drop reflects scVI itself or how it was applied (e.g., the much smaller 200-dimensional latent, scVI training or tuning, preprocessing), because the encoder change is bundled with a large dimensionality change and each configuration was run once with uncharacterized variance. scGPT remains untested, and whether scVI features would behave differently in fusion is unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Encoder choice is the largest driver so far. PCA beat scVI by about 0.20 accuracy (0.715 vs 0.519). ResNet50 beat ViT-L by about 0.19 (0.725 vs 0.536). scGPT is the only representation not yet tested, so it is unknown whether any RNA encoder can beat PCA. Multiprofile input (two RNA runs) and fusion (concat and weighted) have both underperformed the single-profile unimodal anchors. 2. Test: config_007 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT in the RNA-only, single-profile anchor. This completes the RNA-encoder comparison and shows whether a foundation-model embedding beats PCA (0.715 acc / 0.687 F1) or follows scVI's drop. 3. Why now: It is a clean single-factor experiment on an axis known to matter a lot. A strong scGPT result would open new RNA-only and fusion directions (for example scGPT with ResNet50). A weak result would firmly settle PCA as the RNA default. That makes it a better use of budget than extending the profile or fusion axes, which have shown repeated drops. Testing multiprofile with ResNet50 images (config_011) is a strong candidate for the following experiment.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the RNA-only, single-profile anchor of llm_summary_001 (no image encoder, aggregation or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA (2000 components) to scGPT, completing the planned RNA-encoder comparison. It reached 0.3316 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.3150), the lowest result so far: about 0.38 accuracy and 0.37 F1 below PCA (0.7150 / 0.6872) and about 0.19 below scVI (0.5191 / 0.4797). In single-factor comparisons on the same anchor, both foundation-model and learned-latent RNA encoders, as applied here, fall well short of PCA, which supports keeping PCA as the default RNA encoder and ResNet50 (0.7250) as the strongest overall representation. It remains uncertain whether scGPT's poor result reflects the representation itself or how it was applied (e.g., frozen embeddings, gene-vocabulary or preprocessing mismatch, embedding dimensionality, lack of fine-tuning), because each configuration was run once with uncharacterized variance and the embedding dimensionality is not reported. Whether scGPT features would add anything in fusion is also untested, though this result gives little reason to prioritize it.

selection_reason:
1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is image-only ResNet50 with a single profile (0.7250 acc / 0.6847 F1). The evidence against multiprofile input comes only from RNA PCA, where avgpool scored 0.5907 and transformer 0.5420, both below the 0.7150 single-profile baseline. It is unknown whether this drop is specific to RNA PCA features or general to multiprofile input. Encoder comparisons are largely settled: PCA and ResNet50 clearly beat the alternatives tested. Both fusion variants tested so far fell short of the unimodal models.

2. What this tests: Config_011 changes only the profile setting (single to multiprofile, with avgpool) on the strongest configuration. It isolates whether the multiprofile effect transfers to the image modality. Avgpool is the better-performing aggregator in the RNA tests, so it gives multiprofile its fairest chance.

3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It is a clean one-factor test of the most open remaining design question. It also has real upside, since image features may benefit from pooling across profiles even though RNA features did not. The result also guides whether any of the many remaining multiprofile multimodal configurations are worth testing.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 took the strongest configuration so far, image-only single-profile ResNet50 (llm_summary_004: 0.7250 acc / 0.6847 F1), and switched to multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation, the same change previously tested with RNA PCA. It reached 0.2079 validation accuracy (supporting F1 0.1718), the lowest result in the study: about 0.52 accuracy below single-profile ResNet50. That is far larger than the roughly 0.12 drop seen for RNA PCA with avgpool (0.5907 vs 0.7150). This extends the initial observation that multiprofile input with avgpool hurts performance from RNA to image features, so multiprofile configurations look like a low-priority direction, including the untested multiprofile multimodal ones. It remains uncertain whether the collapse reflects multiprofile input itself, mean-pooling of ResNet50 features (the profile change is bundled with adding aggregation), or an implementation or data-handling problem. The unusually severe, possibly near-chance drop makes a pipeline issue worth checking before drawing firm conclusions, and each configuration was run once with uncharacterized variance.
